passages.title: Oath of the ranked angels: Allah is One
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah aṣ-Ṣāffāt opens the way a courtroom opens: not with the claim, but with the oath that will carry it. Three sworn phrases pass before us — ranks drawn straight, forces held in check, a Reminder recited — and then, in ayah 4, the claim they were sworn to support: **"Surely your Deity is One!"** Ayah 5 then widens the frame to the whole cosmos, naming the One sworn by as Lord of the heavens, the earth, everything between, and every point of the sunrise. Read them apart and they are three riddles. Read them together and they are an argument.

## Why the surah begins by swearing by angels

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this surah is Makkan and that, like other Makkan surahs, matters of faith are its essential subject: beliefs about the Oneness of Allah, the mission of the messengers, and the certain eventuality of the Hereafter, each fortified with proofs presented in various ways. As a corollary come a refutation of the beliefs of the *mushriks* — those who ascribe partners to Allah — and the scenes of Paradise and Hell. The surah then turns to how Allah dealt with those who embraced these beliefs and what became of those who took the road of denial, recounting the affairs of Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, Hārūn, Ilyās, Lūṭ and Yūnus (peace be upon them).

One particular form of that shirk is in the surah's sights from beginning to end: **the mushriks of Makkah used to call the angels the daughters of Allah.** Towards the end of the surah this belief is refuted in detail, and Maʿārif observes that an overall view of the surah suggests the refutation of this specific kind of shirk has been kept in marked sight throughout. Therefore, it says, the surah has been initiated with an oath taken in the name of angels *combined with a declaration of the attributes of their servitude*.

You are not argued at first; you are simply shown what the angels do. Stand in rows awaiting orders. Hold back firmly what must be held back. Recite what they have been given to recite. Ponder those attributes of servitude, says Maʿārif, and the angels themselves become a witness before you that their relationship with Allah is not that of a father and daughters, but that of servants and their Master. Ibn Kathir introduces the passage plainly: *the angels witness to the Oneness of Allah.*

## Who are "those in ranks"?

A simple literal rendering of the three oaths, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it, is: *"(I swear) by those who stand in rows, then by those who prevent firmly, then by those who recite the dhikr."* Who are they? Maʿārif is careful here: **there is no clarification in the words of the Qur'an about it**, and therefore different views have been expressed.

- **Living warriors** who come out to wage jihad in the way of Allah and stand in rows after rows, so that they prevent the aggression of the forces of the false — and who, even as they file in readiness for combat, remain engaged in *dhikr* (remembrance of Allah), *tasbīḥ* (glorifying Allah with words that declare Him far above every defect) and the recitation of the Qur'an.
- **The performers of prayer**, who stand in rows in the masjid and, by total concentration on *dhikr* and recitation of the Qur'an, deny Shaitanic thoughts any access to them (Maʿārif cites Tafsīr Kabīr and Qurṭubī for this).
- **The angels** — and this, Maʿārif tells us, is the explanation that "found the widest acceptance with the majority of commentators," the three phrases naming three attributes credited to them.

Ibn Kathir reports that same majority reading. It was reported that ʿAbdullah bin Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said of each of the three phrases in turn: *"they are the angels."* Ibn Kathir lists this as also the view of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Masruq, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, As-Suddī, Qatādah and Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas. Qatādah added simply: *"The angels form ranks in the heavens."*

## The first attribute: ranks drawn straight (ayah 1)

**اَلصَّافَّات (aṣ-ṣāffāt)** — "those who stand in rows." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the expression to the word **صَفّ (ṣaff)** and, citing Qurṭubī, gives its meaning as *"to align some group on a straight line."* Not merely to gather; to align.

This formation appears again later in the same surah: **وَإِنَّا لَنَحْنُ الصَّافُّونَ** — "and We, surely We are those who stand in rows" (37:165).

When are these rows formed? Maʿārif reports two views:

- Ibn ʿAbbās, Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah held that the angels are **always** standing in their rows in space awaiting the command of their Lord, and when it comes, they carry it out (cited from Mazharī).
- Others particularised it to the time of worship — that when the angels are engaged in *ʿibādah*, *dhikr* and *tasbīḥ*, they are in a row formation (Tafsīr Kabīr).

**Discipline is desirable in Islam.** It is obvious, Maʿārif says, that the two objectives of worshipping Allah and implementing His command might just as well have been achieved if the angels had assembled as a disorganised mob rather than forming rows. But instead they were given the *tawfīq* to make rows. And then, by mentioning this very attribute first among their good attributes, the verse points out how much Allah likes this style of propriety. From this verse, Maʿārif concludes, we learn that doing everything in an organised and disciplined manner, with due consideration for order and skill, is expected of us and is certainly liked by Allah.

## The second attribute: an impregnable check (ayah 2)

**اَلزَّاجِرَات (az-zājirāt)** — "those who prevent firmly." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives it from **زَجْر (zajr)**, and gives the root its full range: to hold in check, block, prevent or restrain, and also to drive back, repel or reprimand. Maulānā Thānavī rendered it as *"those who place an impregnable check,"* which Maʿārif notes comprehends every possible sense of the word.

Check against *what*? Here the commentaries part ways:

- **Against the shaitans.** In view of the context of the Qur'an, Maʿārif reports, most commentators answer that the enforcing of the check here means the act of the angels by which they stop the shaitans from reaching the higher levels — something the Qur'an itself will describe in detail a little later.
- **Driving the clouds.** As-Suddī and others, Ibn Kathir reports, said the ayah means that they drive the clouds. Ibn Kathir's own rendering reads *"By those who drive the clouds in a good way"* — and the translation given with this ayah follows the same reading.

Both are the same shape of service: a created servant moving what Allah commands to be moved, and barring what Allah commands to be barred.

## The third attribute: reciting the Reminder (ayah 3)

**اَلتَّالِيَات (at-tāliyāt)** — those who recite — with **ذِكْر (dhikr)** as their object. Maʿārif notes that the core sense of *dhikr* is **"word of good counsel"** as well as **"the remembrance of Allah."** Each opens a different window:

1. Taking *dhikr* as revealed good counsel: these are angels who recite everything Allah has revealed as word of good counsel through the Scriptures — and such recitation could be a means of earning *barakah* (divine blessing) and also an act of *ʿibādah*, worship, in itself.
2. It is also possible that it means the angels who bring *waḥy* (revelation) to the prophets, since they recite these Scriptures carrying good counsel before them and thus convey the message of Allah to them. Ibn Kathir preserves As-Suddī's compact statement of exactly this: *"The angels bring the Scriptures and the Qur'an from Allah to mankind."*
3. Taking *dhikr* as remembrance: they keep busy reciting words that prove their commitment to the glory and sanctity of Allah.

**Three attributes, one portrait of servitude.** Maʿārif draws the three together: by mentioning these three attributes of the angels, the Qur'an "has put together all essential qualities of ideal servitude" — (1) to stand in perfect linear formation for *ʿibādah*, (2) to prevent rebellious forces from disobedience to Allah, and (3) to recite the good counsel and commandments of Allah in person as well as to communicate them to others. It is obvious, Maʿārif observes, that no act of servitude can remain devoid of these three departments. Hence the sense of all four verses (37:1–4) turns out to be: *by the angels who imbibe in them all ideal attributes of servitude, your true Lord is but One.*

## Why does Allah swear at all?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this as a recognised topic in the science of Qur'anic exegesis, noting that Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Qayyim wrote a whole book on the subject (*Tibyān fī Aqsām al-Qurʼān*) and that ʿAllāmah as-Suyūṭī discussed it in detail in *al-Itqān*, in the sixty-seventh category of his discussions. Three questions, with the answers the source gives:

**Does Allah need to swear?** Abulqāsim al-Qushairī answered that Allah needs not to swear before anyone, but His compassion towards His servants invited Him to do so, in the hope that after hearing such a sworn statement they may tend to accept the truth and save themselves from the punishment. Is it not, Maʿārif asks, that we already have a recognised method of settling disagreements? A witness is presented to support a claim; if there is no witness, a sworn statement is offered. Allah has elected to go by this familiar human way in our own interest. On occasions He lays stress on a subject with the word *witness*: "Allah bears witness that there is no god but He" (3:18); on other occasions with words of oath: "Yes, by my Lord, it is true" (10:53). Maʿārif preserves a bedouin's reaction on hearing 51:22–23, where Allah swears by "the Lord of the heavens and the earth" — *"Who has annoyed the Almighty to make Him swear an oath?"*

**Why swear by created things, which are inferior to Him?** Because there simply is not, nor can there be, any being or entity greater than Allah — so the oath of Allah cannot be like that of the common creation. Accordingly, on occasions He has sworn by His own pristine Being ("Yes, by my Lord," 10:53); Maʿārif counts seven places in the Qur'an where oaths are sworn by Allah Himself. Elsewhere the oaths are by Divine acts or attributes and by the Qur'an — as in "And by the sky, and One who built it, and by the earth, and the One who spread it, and by the soul, and Who made it well" (91:5–7). And most such oaths, as Ibn al-Qayyim notes, relate to objects of creation that, being the means of recognition of Allah, revert back to Allah Himself as the ultimate source of all creation. The purposes vary: sometimes to highlight the sublimity of the thing sworn by — as with the oath by the blessed life of the Prophet ﷺ in 15:72, and here Ibn Marduwayh reports from ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that Allah has not created anyone or anything in this world more sublime and esteemed than the Prophet ﷺ himself, which is why no oath by the person of any prophet or messenger appears anywhere else in the Qur'an; likewise "By the Mount" and "By the Written Book" (52:1–2) highlight the greatness of the two objects sworn by. Sometimes it is because the created thing yields a lot of benefits ("By the fig, and the olive," 95:1). And sometimes because its creation is a manifestation of Allah's great power and an important source of getting to know the Master-Creator of the universe. In most cases, Maʿārif adds, the thing sworn by does have some role to play in proving the subject being stressed — as it plainly does here, where the angels' servitude is itself the evidence that they are servants and not daughters.

**If Allah swears by creation, may we?** No. Maʿārif cites Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: *Surely, Allah has the right to swear by whatever of His creation He wills, but it is not for anyone else to swear by anyone other than Allah* (reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, as given in Mazharī). The well-known rule of the Shariʿah for people in general stands: swearing by anyone other than Allah is not permissible. The core sense, Maʿārif explains, is that taking one's own self on the analogy of the most-exalted Allah is wrong and false; once the Divine Law has prohibited it for human beings at large, any counter-argument built on what He elects to do on His own cannot be anything but false.

## The declaration and the Lord who is declared (ayat 4–5)

Ayah 4 is where the whole passage has been travelling: **إِنَّ إِلَـٰهَكُمْ لَوَاحِدٌ** — "Surely your Deity is One." Maʿārif states that the real purpose of the first four verses is to state exactly this. Ibn Kathir spells out the content: **this is the One by Whom the oath is sworn**, stating that there is no deity worthy of worship but He, Lord of the heavens and the earth. The claim, then, is not an abstraction about number. It is about who alone deserves worship.

Ayah 5 then answers, in advance, any suspicion that this One is a local or partial deity: **Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the points of the sunrise.** On "and all that is between them," Ibn Kathir says concisely: *of created beings.* And on **رَبُّ الْمَشَارِقِ**, he explains that He is the Sovereign Who is controlling His creation by subjugating it, and all that is in it of stars, planets and heavenly bodies which appear from the east and set in the west. Mentioning the east is sufficient, he notes, and there is no need for the west to be mentioned too, because it is implied in what is said — and the Qur'an states it clearly elsewhere: "So I swear by the Lord of all the points of sunrise and sunset in the east and the west that surely We are able" (70:40), and "the Lord of the two easts and the Lord of the two wests" (55:17), which Ibn Kathir says refers to the rising and setting points of the sun and the moon in both winter and summer.

Why the **plural** "sunrises"? *al-mashāriq* is the plural form of *mashriq*, east, and since the sun rises from a new point every day of the year, its orientations in the east are many — and it is on this basis, Maʿārif answers, that the plural form has been employed. And a Being, Maʿārif continues, to whom goes the credit of having created and sustained such a mind-boggling range of creations has to be the One most deserving of ownership — this entire universe being a positive proof of His existence and Oneness.

Maʿārif also notes that the particular attributes of the angels mentioned in the course of these oaths, if deliberated upon even in a modest measure, turn out to be nothing short of *initial* proofs of the belief in Tawḥīd, while in the six verses that follow a standing proof of Tawḥīd has also been supplied. This passage is the doorway, not the whole building.

## Living it: straighten the row

Because the first quality praised in the angels is the straight rank, the same thing is pressed upon us. Maʿārif puts it directly: this is not for angels only; human beings too have been induced to and bound with the need to make their rows straight and right during *ʿibādah*.

Ibn Kathir cites Muslim, from Ḥudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"We have been favoured over the rest of mankind in three ways: our ranks have been made like the ranks of the angels; the entire earth has been made a masjid for us; and its soil has been made a means of purification for us if we cannot find water."* The row you stand in tonight is listed among the distinguishing gifts of this community.

Ibn Kathir also cites Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, An-Nasāʼī and Ibn Mājah, from Jābir bin Samurah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Will you not form ranks as the angels form ranks in the presence of their Lord?"* They asked how the angels form ranks in the presence of their Lord, and he ﷺ said: *"They complete the rows nearer the front and they consolidate the rows."* Two concrete instructions: fill the front rows before starting another, and close the gaps.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this same narration of Jābir Ibn Samurah (may Allah be pleased with him) from Tafsīr Mazharī, with the answer given as: *"They complete the rows and stand compactly"* — that is, leave no gap in between the row. And it adds that so many aḥādīth stressing the need to make rows complete and keep them straight in Salah have appeared that they could fill an independent treatise on the subject. It further relates from Abū Masʿūd al-Badrī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ would touch their shoulders with his blessed hand during Salah and say: *"Stand straight, do not step ahead or fall behind, otherwise it will cause dissension to creep up in your hearts"* (Maʿārif cites this from *Jamʿ al-Fawāʼid*, with reference to Muslim and an-Nasāʼī). The outward ragged line and the inward ragged heart are connected.

**A closing note on the surah itself.** Ibn Kathir opens with a report from An-Nasāʼī, from ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to command us to make our prayers short, and he used to recite aṣ-Ṣāffāt when he led us in prayer." Ibn Kathir notes that this was recorded by An-Nasāʼī only. A surah that opens by swearing by ranked angels was recited over ranked worshippers — the meaning and the moment matching each other exactly.

passages.title: Stars adorn the sky, devils barred from heaven
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat lift the reader's eyes to the night sky and then tell them something they could never have worked out by looking: that the same stars which beautify the lowest heaven also form a barrier, and that the beings who try to slip past that barrier to steal news from the angels are hunted down by fire. The unity of the passage is that single double-purpose — **ornament (ayah 6) and guard (ayah 7)** — and everything in ayat 8–10 unpacks what that guarding looks like in practice.

## The nearest heaven, made beautiful

Ayah 6 says: *"Indeed, We have adorned the lowest heaven with the stars."* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah has adorned the lowest heaven with the heavenly bodies **for the sake of the people of the earth who look at it** — and that the stars and planets also give light to the people of earth. So the beauty is not decoration in a vacuum; it is beauty aimed at a viewer, at you.

He gathers the parallel places in the Qur'an where the same two themes — adornment and protection — appear together: *"And indeed We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and We have made such lamps (as) missiles to drive away the Shayatin, and have prepared for them the torment of the blazing Fire"* (67:5); and *"And indeed, We have put the big stars in the heaven and We beautified it for the beholders. And We have guarded it from every outcast Shaytan. Except him who steals the hearing then he is pursued by a clear flaming fire"* (15:16–18). Reading these alongside sūrah 37 shows that our passage is not an isolated image but a settled Qur'anic theme.

**A note on the words "the lowest heaven."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *as-samāʾ ud-dunyā* means the **closest** sky — the sky nearest to this world — and that Allah has made it look beautiful through the glittering presence of the stars. It then makes a careful point that saves the reader from a false problem: it is not necessary that the stars are located precisely *within* that sky. Even if they are detached from it, when they are looked at from the earth they appear to be on the sky, and they keep imparting a glow to it. (Maʿārif refers the reader who wants the full discussion of stars, the sky and astronomy to its own commentary on Sūrah al-Ḥijr, 15:16.) The ayah is describing what the sky *is and does* for the one standing beneath it, not settling a question of astronomical placement.

## What the beautiful sky is arguing

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the reasoning that this star-spangled sky presses on anyone honest enough to look: it is **an open proof that it did not come into existence on its own** — it has been created by its Creator. And a Being who can bring such enormous things into existence — why would He need any partner or sharer in His creation?

Maʿārif then presses the point one step further: even **the disbelievers** find it a settled matter that Allah is the Creator of all the heavenly bodies. Would it not then be sheer injustice that, despite His being the Creator and Master, someone or something else be taken as the object of worship? This is what Maʿārif calls the first real objective of the passage — the assertion of Allah's Oneness through a sky that anyone can see.

## Ornament and guard are the same act

Ayah 7 adds: *"and [for] protection from every rebellious devil."* Maʿārif renders it "and [have made them] a security against every rebellious shaitan," and comments that **the stars have another benefit besides being a decoration of the sky**: through them, wicked devils are restrained from approaching the higher levels to eavesdrop. One and the same creation, then, serves both ends. What delights the believer looking up is what repels the eavesdropper looking in.

Ibn Kathir glosses *wa ḥifẓan* — "and to guard" — as meaning **to protect as it should be protected**: not a token barrier, but a guarding worthy of what is being guarded.

**"Every rebellious devil" (*shayṭān mārid*).** Ibn Kathir explains *mārid* as **every insolent and impudent devil**. And he adds the consequence in the same breath: when such a devil wants to eavesdrop on the news in the heavens, a piercing fire comes and burns him.

Note also the word **"every."** Not most; not the weaker ones. The guard the ayah describes has no gaps.

## The higher assembly

Ayah 8 says they *"cannot listen to the highest assembly."* Ibn Kathir explains *al-malaʾ al-aʿlā*, the higher group, as **the heavens and the angels in them** — and specifies *what* the devils are trying to overhear: the angels speaking about **what has been revealed by Allah of His Laws and His decrees**. Maʿārif calls it the Upper Realm and says plainly that the devils are **denied the opportunity to listen to what the angels say to each other**.

Ibn Kathir points the reader to a related ayah for the same scene: *"when fear is banished from their hearts, they say: 'What is it that your Lord has said?' They say: 'The truth. And He is the Most High, the Most Great'"* (34:23) — the angels themselves overwhelmed at the descent of Allah's word, then relaying it as truth. That is the conversation the devils want a piece of. Maʿārif adds their motive: they are trying to gather **whatever news of the unseen they can** by reaching the fringes of the sky.

**Then the counter-measures, word by word.** Ibn Kathir takes the terms of ayat 8–9 one at a time:

- *wa yuqdhafūn* — "they are pelted" — **means they are hit**.
- *min kulli jānib* — "from every side" — **from all directions from which they try to reach the heaven**. Every approach angle is covered.
- *duḥūran* — "outcast" — **they are rejected, repelled and prevented from reaching it, and they are pelted**. Three things at once: refused entry, driven back, and struck on the way.
- *wa lahum ʿadhābun wāṣib* — "and theirs is a constant torment" — Ibn Kathir specifies that this is **in the Hereafter**: an ongoing, everlasting and painful torment. He cites 67:5 again for it: *"and [We] have prepared for them the torment of the blazing Fire."*

So there are two layers of consequence, and it is worth keeping them distinct. The pelting is at the boundary of the heaven. The *ʿadhāb wāṣib* is in the Hereafter, and it does not end.

## The snatched word

Ayah 10 makes a narrow exception, and the narrowness is the point: *"But whoever manages to stealthily eavesdrop is [instantly] pursued by a piercing flame."*

Ibn Kathir describes the mechanism in detail. The exception is for **the one among the devils who manages to get something — a word he has heard from the heaven**. He then throws it down to the one beneath him, who in turn throws it down to the one beneath him. **Perhaps the flaming fire will strike him before he is able to throw it down; or perhaps he will throw it — by the decree of Allah — before the flaming fire strikes him and burns him.** Then the other devil takes it to the soothsayer. (Ibn Kathir refers at this point to a ḥadīth he had discussed earlier, without naming it here, so we leave it at the teaching itself.)

Two things in that description deserve attention. First, the notice that even the rare success happens **"by the decree of Allah"** — the leak is not a hole in Allah's guard but something permitted within it. Second, notice how thin the stolen goods are: a word caught in flight, passed down a chain while its carrier is being pursued by fire.

Maʿārif reaches the same conclusion from the other end: if some devil picks up even a part of the angels' conversation and tries to decamp with it, **he is hit by a blazing flame, so that he remains unable to pass on this information to his devotees among the soothsayers in the world.**

**The words.** *Shihāb thāqib*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as a flaming fire **shining brightly**, is what Maʿārif identifies as the meteor — the streak of light that crosses the sky.

## Why the flame never missed after the Prophet ﷺ was sent

The single most illuminating report in this passage is one Ibn Kathir cites: **Ibn Jarir recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

> "The Shayatin had places where they sat in the heavens listening to what was being revealed by Allah. The stars did not move and the Shayatin were not struck. When they heard the revelation, they would come down to earth and to every word they would add nine of their own. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent, if a Shaytan wanted to take his seat in the heavens, the flaming fire would come and would not miss him; it would burn him every time. They complained about this to Iblis, may Allah curse him, and he said, 'Something must have happened.' He sent his troops out and they found the Messenger of Allah ﷺ standing in prayer between the two mountains of Nakhlah." — Wakiʿ said this means in the valley of Nakhlah — "They went back to Iblis and told him about that, and he said, 'This is what has happened.'"

Sit with that scene. Iblis, sensing that the order of the heavens has changed and unable to find out why, sends out his troops — and the disturbance in the sky turns out to be **one man standing in prayer between two mountains.** The devils' whole enterprise of counterfeit knowledge had been running on a trickle of overheard truth padded with **nine of their own words for every word they heard**; and the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ shut it down.

Ibn ʿAbbās's report also lets you feel the ayah as the Companions did: it is not only a statement about how the cosmos works, it is tied to the moment the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent. Where before "the stars did not move," now the sky itself was defending the message.

## What the mention of the sky, the stars and the meteors achieves

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers this up under a heading it calls "The Real Objective," and says that by mentioning the skies, the stars and the meteors here, **two objectives** have been achieved.

**The first real objective: the Oneness of Allah.** He has, all by Himself, created and managed a universal system this magnificent — and therefore He alone is worthy of being worshipped.

**The second objective: the demolition of devil-worship.** The false notion of those who take devils as their objects of worship is refuted by telling them what those beings actually are: **the most accursed of the creation**, with **nothing to do with the supreme station of godhead.** You cannot worship something you have just watched being pelted away from the gates of heaven.

**And in addition to that** — Maʿārif introduces this separately, as a further thing refuted here — the objection of **those who used to degrade the Divine revelation (*waḥy*) sent to the Prophet ﷺ as the predictions of the soothsayers.** Maʿārif shows how these ayat dismantle that charge: the Qur'an itself **rejects the soothsayers**, because the sum total of their information is what they receive through the devils — and the Qur'an states that the devils **do not have access to the higher echelons** and cannot bring back true information out of what remains in the realm of the Unseen (*al-ghayb*). When the Qur'an states *that* as its creed about soothsaying, how can it itself be soothsaying? So, in Maʿārif's words, these ayat carry clear hints of both Allah's Oneness and the veracity of the mission of the Prophet ﷺ — and Maʿārif notes that later on, through the example of these very cosmic creations, belief in the Hereafter is established.

## On meteors, and on not flinching

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes time here with a reader who finds the idea of devils struck by meteors hard to accept, and its handling is instructive.

It records that **early Greek scientists** believed meteors to be terrestrial substance that rose up with vapours and burned up on reaching the "fire zone," whereas the words of the Qur'an here seem to suggest that a meteor is not terrestrial substance but something generated in the upper atmosphere. Earlier commentators, it notes, have been saying all along that the Greek assumption was **no more than a conjecture** and therefore cannot be used to raise an objection against the Qur'an — while also observing that even the other possibility, of some terrestrial substance rising and igniting in the upper atmosphere, offers no contradiction with the Qur'an.

Maʿārif then reports what astronomers say — citing *Tafsīr al-Jawāhir* by Ṭanṭāwī — that meteors (*shihāb thāqib*) are small pieces from countless stars, generally the size of large bricks, which stay in space; that one of their groups is known as *asadiyyah* (Leo, of the signs of the Zodiac), which keeps revolving around the sun on its path, completing one orbit in thirty-three years; that light is emitted in these pieces because of their speed and abrasion against heavenly bodies; and that they fall mostly during the nights of 10 August and 27 November, with their falling tapering off on other named nights. Maʿārif's judgement is that this investigative approach of modern science **corresponds to the Qur'anic description**.

Then it quotes Ṭanṭāwī's advice, which is really about how a believer should hold their nerve:

> "Our forebears and scholars also took it with a heavy heart that the noble Qur'an would say something counter to contemporary astronomy of their time. But the commentators of the Qur'an did not compromise their position… Instead of doing something like that, they bypassed their philosophical assumptions and continued to stay with the Qur'an. After the passage of some time, it became automatically established that the early Greeks were wrong in their assumptions. Now, if we were to acknowledge that these stars hit, hurt and burn shaitans, what is there to stop us from doing so?"

The lesson is not that the Qur'an needs science to certify it. It is that the confident consensus of an age is not a court above revelation, and that the scholars who declined to bend the text to the science of their day were, as Ṭanṭāwī points out, later vindicated.

## Living it

**Look up on purpose.** Ibn Kathir says the adornment is for the people of the earth *who look at it*. The ayah's benefit is only collected by someone who actually raises their eyes and lets the sight lead them where ayah 6 is pointing: to a Creator with no partner.

**Take the doors of the unseen seriously.** These ayat show the Unseen guarded and defended. Maʿārif's point about soothsaying cuts at the root of any claim to news of *al-ghayb*: the whole stock of the soothsayers is what they receive through the devils, and the devils have no access to the higher echelons and cannot bring true information out of the Unseen. And in Ibn ʿAbbās's report, even the scraps of an earlier age came padded with nine of the devils' own words for every word heard. The Qur'an is itself the refutation of that trade.

**Measure the enemy correctly.** The devil is real and hostile — *mārid*, insolent and impudent, still trying to eavesdrop. He is also pelted from every side, rejected and repelled, and awaiting a torment in the Hereafter that does not end. Ayat 7–9 keep both halves in view: do not be casual about him, and do not be impressed by him.

**Recognise what a praying servant is worth.** In Ibn ʿAbbās's report, Iblis sent out his troops to investigate a change in the heavens, and what they found was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ standing in prayer. That is the standing of revelation, and of prayer, in the order of things.

passages.title: They mock the raising of dust until the Blast
passages.tafsir:
These eleven ayat turn from the oneness of Allah — established in the verses just before — to the second great truth the disbelievers threw back in the Prophet's ﷺ face: that the dead will be raised and judged. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, having proved the belief in the Oneness of Allah, what is described here is the belief in the Ākhirah, together with an answer to the doubts the disbelievers entertained about it.

What holds the unit together is a movement from argument to event. **Ayah 11** puts one question to them that settles the matter by reason. **Ayat 12–15** record how they received it: mockery, deafness, and the charge of magic. **Ayat 16–17** state their one real objection. **Ayah 18** answers it in a few words. Then **ayat 19–21** stop arguing altogether and simply show the moment the argument ends — a single Blast, and the mockers are standing there, staring, crying out.

## Ayah 11: the argument from the greater to the lesser

*"So ask them: which is harder to create — them, or those We have created?"*

Ibn Kathir unfolds the question: Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ to ask the deniers of resurrection whether they are more difficult to create, or the heavens, the earth, the angels, the devils, the mighty creatures, and everything between them. **Ibn Masʿūd said that they admitted that these things were harder to create than they were.** That admission is the whole hinge. Ibn Kathir presses it: if that is the case, why do they deny the resurrection, when they see before them things far greater than the thing they deny? He cites the same logic elsewhere in the Qur'an — *"The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind; yet most of mankind know not"* (40:57).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point from the other direction. It reads ayah 11 as referring back to the huge heavenly bodies of the universe mentioned in the previous verses, and pointing out the obvious weakness of human beings measured against them: when the disbelievers already recognise that such great objects of creation as the angels, the moon, the stars, the sun and the meteors were made by Allah through His infinite power, how could it be difficult for Him to make a weak creature like a human being die and then live once again? The way they were fashioned in the beginning out of sticky clay and then had spirit breathed into them — in just that way, once they have died and become dust, Allah will give them life once again.

**"A sticky clay" (ṭīn lāzib).** Notice that the ayah does not answer its own question with a lecture; it drops one phrase and lets it do the work. Ibn Kathir gathers the early explanations of *lāzib*: Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Ad-Dahhāk said it is the useful kind of mud which sticks to itself; Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrimah said it is sticky and useful; Qatādah said it is that which sticks to the hand. So the material is humble but cohesive — clay you can actually shape, mud that clings to your fingers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes two readings of *"We created them from sticky clay"*: either it refers to their forefather Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him), who was created from clay; or it may mean every human being. On the second reading, with a little deliberation, water-based clay turns out to be the essence of every person cyclically: human creation is from sperm, sperm from blood, blood from food; and the essence of food, in whatever form, is vegetation, and vegetation comes from the combination of clay and water. You are eating the earth, becoming the earth, and returning to the earth — and being told that the One who ran that cycle once can run it again.

Maʿārif also observes why the argument is stated so briefly: since it was posed as a question aimed straight at them — *who is more difficult to create, you, or the many objects of creation We have mentioned?* — no elaborate explanation was considered necessary. A hint sufficed.

## Ayat 12–13: astonishment on one side, mockery on the other

*"In fact, you are astonished, while they ridicule. And when they are reminded, they are never mindful."*

Ibn Kathir reads *bal ʿajibta* as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: you were astounded, O Muhammad, at these people who denied the resurrection while you were certain that it is true; they disbelieved in what Allah told you of this wondrous matter — the re-creation of their bodies after they have disintegrated — and out of the intensity of their disbelief they oppose you and make fun of what you tell them. **Qatādah said, "Muhammad ﷺ was astounded by the mockery of the misguided ones among the sons of Adam."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the contrast in the same two ayat: here is the Prophet ﷺ wondering how these people, with such clear proofs in front of them, still remain reluctant to accept the truth — and here are they, making fun of the very proofs and beliefs he brings before them.

That is the psychology worth sitting with. **Mockery here is not an argument; it is a substitute for one.** Ayah 13 names the same hardness in a different register: *when they are reminded, they are never mindful.* Maʿārif renders the line, *and when any advice is given to them, they pay no heed to it*, and adds the diagnosis: in fact, no amount of advice and counsel given to them works — they are simply averse to any understanding. The sound reaches the ear; nothing reaches the heart.

## Ayat 14–15: "nothing but pure magic" — and what an āyah is

*"And whenever they see a sign, they make fun of it, saying, 'This is nothing but pure magic.'"*

Ibn Kathir explains *āyah* here as clear evidence and proof, and *yastaskhirūn* as: Mujāhid and Qatādah said, "They make fun of it." Their words *"This is nothing but evident magic"* mean: this that you have brought is nothing but plain magic.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stops here for a substantial point of doctrine. The word *āyah* literally means "sign," and in this place it means **muʿjizah — a miracle**. Some who deny that the Prophet ﷺ was given miracles claim that *āyah* here means rational arguments, and others that it means the verses of the Qur'an. Maʿārif answers both from the wording itself:

- **Against "rational arguments":** look at the very next ayah — they say *"this is nothing but open magic."* It makes no sense to declare an evidence and argument to be open magic. People could say something like that only when they had seen a miracle.
- **Against "verses of the Qur'an":** the ayah says *raʾaw* — "they **saw**." The verses of the Qur'an were not seen; they were heard. Wherever the Qur'an mentions its own verses, the words used are those of hearing, not of seeing.

Maʿārif adds that *āyah* carries the sense of miracle in place after place in the Qur'an — for instance Pharaoh's demand of Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him): *"If you have come with a sign, bring it out, if you are one of the truthful"* (7:106), in response to which Mūsā showed the miracle of his staff turning into a serpent. The conclusion drawn is that Allah gave the Prophet ﷺ miracles besides the Qur'an — which refutes those who treat his miracles as effects of physical causes and claim that no miracle other than the Qur'an was shown at his blessed hands.

**Then why were miracles sometimes refused?** Maʿārif answers the obvious objection from those verses where the Prophet ﷺ did not accede to a demand for a miracle. Miracles had been repeatedly shown; what these people were doing was asking for an ever-new miracle of their own choice almost every day, and it was those demands that were turned down. A prophet of Allah shows miracles at the will and command of Allah, not on request; if a person still refuses the true message, producing a new miracle every day is counter to the dignity of the prophet and counter to the will of Allah. And there is a mercy in the refusal: it has been Allah's customary practice that when a people were granted the very miracle they demanded and still failed to believe, they were destroyed through a mass punishment. In view of the intended survival of the community of the Prophet ﷺ, and to keep it safe from any such mass punishment, no miracle on demand was shown before it.

## Ayat 16–17: the objection stated plainly

*"When we are dead and reduced to dust and bones, will we really be raised? And our forefathers as well?"*

Ibn Kathir's comment is spare: they thought this was unlikely to happen, and they did not believe it. Maʿārif frames it as their problem of comprehension — how in the world could they, once they and their forefathers had become dust and bones, be brought back to life all over again? And it notes the hardness underneath the question: they were really not willing to admit any proof in the matter, neither that of reason nor that of miracle.

The mention of *"our forefathers"* sharpens the sneer. Generations gone, bones scattered, nothing left to identify — and they take that as the end of the discussion.

## Ayah 18: four words that are also a complete proof

*"Say: 'Yes! And you will be fully humbled.'"*

Ibn Kathir: tell them, O Muhammad — yes, you will be raised on the Day of Resurrection after you have become dust and bones, and you will be humiliated, put to shame before His great might. He links the word *dākhirūn* to two other places: *"And all shall come to Him, humbled"* (27:87), and *"Verily, those who scorn My worship, they will surely enter Hell in humiliation"* (40:60). The mockery of ayah 12 and the humbling of ayah 18 are the same people at two different moments.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that outwardly this is a dismissive answer, the kind usually given to rigid people — but a little deliberation reveals it to be a full-fledged argument as well, as **Imām Rāzī has explained in Tafsīr Kabīr**. The reasoning runs in two steps. First, the rational proof given earlier has already established that the rising of human beings after death is not something impossible. Second, the rule is that the physical happening of anything rationally possible can be proved on the authority of the statement of one who is a harbinger of nothing but the truth. So once possibility is settled, a true prophet of Allah simply saying *"Yes, you shall definitely rise again"* is an absolute proof that the event is bound to happen. That is why "Yes" is enough: reason had cleared the ground, and revelation only had to confirm the fact.

## Ayah 19: one Blast, and the mockery is over

*"It will only take one Blast, then at once they will see."*

Ibn Kathir: it will be a single command from Allah; He will call them once to come forth from the earth, and then they will be standing before Him, staring at the horrors of the Day of Resurrection.

The word repays attention. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **zajrah** is a noun derived from *zajr*, which is used to carry many meanings in Arabic; one of them is to utter the kind of sounds which, when heard by cattle, motivate them to rise and get moving. Here it refers to the second *Ṣūr* — the Horn or Trumpet — that will be blown by the angel, Sayyidnā Isrāfīl, and it is called a *zajrah* precisely because, just as such sounds are produced to prompt cattle to rise and get moving, this Horn will be blown to make the dead rise. There is something withering in the image for people who had spent their lives laughing: one call, and up they come.

Maʿārif adds a point from Tafsīr Kabīr on the wisdom of it: though Allah is in His infinite power inherently capable of making the dead rise again without the Horn being blown at all, the Horn will be blown in order to highlight the awe of the Resurrection.

**"Then at once they will see."** Maʿārif explains that the way they could see in the mortal world, in the same way they would be able to see there — the faculty they used to look at signs and laugh at them is handed back to them at the very moment the signs turn real. Some other commentators, it notes, explain it as their starting to look at one another, overtaken by wonder (Qurṭubī).

## Ayat 20–21: the confession, and the answer that stings

*"They will cry, 'Oh, woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment!' — 'This is the Day of Final Decision which you used to deny.'"*

Ibn Kathir: Allah tells us what the disbelievers will say on the Day of Resurrection — how they will blame themselves and admit that they wronged themselves in this world. When they see the horrors of that Day with their own eyes, they will be filled with regret, at a time when regret will not avail them anything.

Two names for the Day sit side by side. In ayah 20 they call it the Day of Recompense — that is Ibn Kathir's rendering of *yawm al-dīn* — the Day on which, as Maʿārif said earlier in this passage, human beings will account for their deeds. In ayah 21 it is called the Day of Final Decision. Ibn Kathir tells us who speaks that second line: **the angels and the believers** will say to them, *"This is the Day of Judgement which you used to deny"* — and this will be said to them as a rebuke and reproof. Ibn Kathir adds what follows: Allah will command the angels to separate the disbelievers from the believers in the very place where they are standing.

So the sentence they mocked becomes the sentence read out over them, in the same words they used to laugh at — *the Day you used to deny.* Nothing new has to be proved to them at that point. They are simply shown.

## Living with these ayat

**Take the argument of ayah 11 seriously in your own thinking.** The Qur'an's case for resurrection here is not sentiment; it is a comparison you can make any day. Look at what already exists — the sky, the earth, the vast orders of creation the deniers themselves conceded were harder to make — and then look at yourself, assembled out of clay by way of vegetation, food and blood. The second making is the easier of the two.

**Watch for ayah 13 in yourself.** *When they are reminded, they are never mindful* was said about deniers, but the disease it names — hearing the reminder and remaining unmoved — has a mild form that can live quietly in a believing heart. The remedy is simply to let a reminder land: to hear an ayah about the Day of Final Decision and let it change something before the day is out.

**And notice what mockery costs.** These people had reasoning put to them and miracles shown to them, and they answered both with a joke and the word "magic." Ridicule feels like strength in the moment; ayah 18 tells you exactly where it ends — *and you will be fully humbled.* The believer's posture is the opposite and is available now, voluntarily, while it still counts: humbling yourself before Allah's greatness today, rather than being humbled before it on a Day when regret will not help.

passages.title: Wrongdoers gathered and detained for questioning
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are a set of orders. Allah speaks, the angels move, and a crowd of wrongdoers is gathered up, led away, halted, and questioned. What holds the passage together is that single unbroken chain of commands — **gather them, lead them, stop them, question them** — followed by a rebuke put to them (ayah 25) and then Allah's own statement of what their condition will actually be: total surrender (ayah 26).

## The scene just before

Ibn Kathir sets the passage in its immediate context. In the two ayat before ours, the deniers finally see the Day they had mocked. They cry, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense!" — Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us how the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection **will blame themselves and admit that they wronged themselves in this world**. Seeing the horrors of that Day with their own eyes, "they will be filled with regret at the time when regret will not avail them anything."

Then comes the reply — "This is the Day of Judgement which you used to deny" — which Ibn Kathir says the **angels and the believers** will say to them "as a rebuke and reproof."

And immediately after that, according to Ibn Kathir, "Allah will command the angels to separate the disbeliever from the believers in the place where they are standing." That is the hinge into ayah 22. A moment ago the two groups stood together in one place. Now they are pulled apart, and one group is taken in hand.

## "Gather the wrongdoers" (ayah 22)

The command is **ٱحۡشُرُوا** (*uḥshurū*), rendered "Assemble those who did wrong" by Ibn Kathir and "Muster all those who were unjust" by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. It is the same verb that appears in the ayah Ibn Kathir quotes as a parallel: "and We shall gather them together on the Day of Resurrection on their faces, blind, dumb and deaf; their abode will be Hell; whenever it abates, We shall increase for them the fierceness of the Fire" (17:97). That parallel tells you the manner of this gathering — not people making their own way somewhere, but people brought.

Those gathered are **ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا** — "those who did wrong," "those who were unjust." Ibn Kathir's framing earlier in the passage tells you the wrong at issue: they *wronged themselves*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads them as the Mushriks — those who set up partners with Allah — which fits what is gathered alongside them in the rest of the ayah.

## Who are "their azwāj"?

The most discussed word in this passage is **وَأَزۡوَٰجَهُمۡ** (*wa azwājahum*).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up carefully. Literally, *zawj* means **"pair"** — one of two things that go together. From there, Maʿārif notes, the word "is very commonly used in the sense of spouses. That is why some commentators have said that it means wives of the Mushriks who were also Mushriks."

But that is the minority reading. **In the sight of most commentators**, says Maʿārif, *azwāj* here "means nothing but people of the same persuasion" — cohorts, fellow travellers, the crowd you belonged to. Partners, then, not in marriage but in mentality.

Ibn Kathir lines up the early authorities behind exactly this. An-Nuʿmān bin Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with him) said their companions "means their counterparts, those who are like them" — and Ibn Kathir reports that this was also the view of **Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, As-Suddī, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Abū Al-ʿĀliyah and Zayd bin Aslam**. Mujāhid and Saʿīd bin Jubayr also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās a plainer gloss: *azwājahum* means **"their friends."**

Then comes the line that makes the whole thing concrete. Sharīk narrated, from Simāk, from An-Nuʿmān: "I heard ʿUmar say" that the phrase means "those who are like them" —

> "So those who committed *zinā* will be gathered with others who committed *zinā*, those who dealt in *ribā* will be gathered with others who dealt in *ribā*, those who drank wine will be gathered with others who drank wine."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same statement of Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) and notes that **Imām al-Baihaqī, ʿAbd-ur-Razzāq and others** reported it in their explanation of this very verse: the word means "other people like them," so that huddled together there will be "the people of the same interest, fornicators with other fornicators and drunkards with other drunkards." (Maʿārif attributes its sourcing here to *Rūḥ-ul-Maʿānī* and *Mazharī*.)

Notice what this does. The gathering of the Last Day, on this reading, is not random. People are placed with those who were like them, and the crowd you chose in this world becomes the crowd you are assembled with in the next. *Zinā* with *zinā*, interest with interest, drink with drink.

## "...and what they used to worship, instead of Allah" (ayat 22–23)

The muster does not stop at people. **وَمَا كَانُوا يَعۡبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ** — "and what they used to worship, instead of Allah." Ibn Kathir: this means "their idols and false gods will be gathered together with them in the same place."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why. It says the ayah "expressly laid out" that along with the Mushriks, **all those false objects and entities like idols and shaitans they used to worship and equate with Allah as His associates** in the life of the world "will all be mustered together" — and gives the purpose: **"so that, at that time, the helplessness of these false objects of worship could be demonstrated publicly."**

That is the design of the scene as Maʿārif reads it. Every rescuer they ever counted on is brought into the same place with them, so that the emptiness of the claim is not argued about but *seen*.

## "Then lead them to the path of the Blaze" (ayah 23)

**فَٱهۡدُوهُمۡ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطِ ٱلۡجَحِيمِ** — Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: "take them to the way to Hell." Maʿārif renders it "show them the way to Jahannam."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then traces the sequence: "When the angels will take them away, and reach close to the Bridge of Sirat," the next command comes.

## "And detain them — they are to be questioned" (ayah 24)

**وَقِفُوهُمۡ** — stop them. The march halts. Ibn Kathir: "stop them so that they may be questioned about the things they **did and said** in this world." Ad-Daḥḥāk, narrating from Ibn ʿAbbās, put it as: **"detain them, for they are to be brought to account."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this halt near the Bridge of Sirat and says that at this place "they will be questioned about their beliefs and deeds — that have been mentioned in the Qur'an and Hadith at many places."

## The first thing a man is asked about

Ibn Kathir records here a striking statement from the early generations. ʿAbdullāh bin Al-Mubārak said: "I heard ʿUthmān bin Zāʼidah say, **'The first thing about which a man will be asked is the company that he kept.'**"

This is the word of an early believer as Ibn Kathir transmits it, not a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ — but see where it sits. The ayah before gathered them **with their *azwāj***, their counterparts and friends. So the questioning, as Ibn Kathir places this narration, opens on exactly the thing the gathering has just made visible: *who were you with?*

## "What is the matter with you? Why do you not help one another?" (ayah 25)

**مَا لَكُمۡ لَا تَنَاصَرُونَ.** Ibn Kathir says this is said to them **"by way of rebuke,"** and unpacks the sting: "as you claimed that you would all help one another."

So the words are not a request for information; Ibn Kathir calls them a rebuke. That mutual help was the claim of the worldly crowd — our people stand by their own. And now the crowd is all present in one place: their counterparts, their friends, and, as Ibn Kathir said of ayah 22, their idols and false gods gathered with them there too. The rebuke is put to the assembled group: *so help each other.*

## "In fact, on that Day they will be fully submissive" (ayah 26)

**بَلۡ هُمُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ مُسۡتَسۡلِمُونَ** — "Nay, but that Day they shall surrender," in Ibn Kathir's rendering; "In fact, on that Day they will be ˹fully˺ submissive."

No mutual rescue comes. Ibn Kathir explains the state described: "they will be subjected to the command of Allah, and they will not be able to resist it or avoid it. And Allah knows best."

That is the last note of the passage, and it is worth sitting with. Ibn Kathir's words describe a surrender with no capacity to resist left — the crowd that was to help one another has nothing left to offer, not even refusal.

## What this passage asks of us

The passage is short on argument and long on picture, and its practical weight falls on two things it sets side by side.

**First: your company is not a neutral detail of your life.** The *azwāj* of ayah 22 — on the reading of ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, An-Nuʿmān bin Bashīr, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and the majority Maʿārif ul Qurʼān speaks for — are the people of your own persuasion, those who are like you. If those who dealt in *ribā* are gathered with others who dealt in *ribā*, then the honest question is not only *what do I do?* but *whose crowd am I in, and what does that crowd make normal for me?* And it is the question ʿUthmān bin Zāʼidah says gets asked first.

**Second: count nothing as a rescuer that will be standing in that place with you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān said the false objects of worship are mustered in with their worshippers precisely so their helplessness is demonstrated publicly. Anything leaned on in place of Allah — an idol of stone or an idol of status, a network, a patron, a group that will "look after its own" — meets the rebuke of ayah 25, and ayah 26 records that no help arrives.

The mercy hidden in these hard ayat is that we are being shown the scene **now**, while the regret Ibn Kathir describes has not yet become the regret that "will not avail them anything."

passages.title: Followers and leaders trade blame in Hell
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are a recorded argument. Allah lets us listen in on the moment when those who followed falsehood and those who led them into it come face to face after death — and instead of standing together, they turn on one another. What holds the passage together is that it is one continuous exchange: an accusation (ayah 28), a two-part rebuttal (ayat 29–30), and then a reply from the accused that ruins both sides at once (ayat 31–32).

## Where this scene is happening

The setting comes from the ayat just before. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that a command goes out to the angels, **"and show them the way to Jahannam"** (37:23). The angels take them away, and when they draw close to the Bridge of Sirāt, the order comes: **make them stop — they are to be questioned** (37:24). At that place they are questioned about their beliefs and their deeds — matters, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, that the Qur'an and Hadith mention in many places.

So ayah 27 — *"They will turn on each other, throwing blame"* — is not a random flare-up. It happens under interrogation, on the way to Jahannam, at the exact moment when each soul most wants somewhere else to put the weight of what it did. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the human scene plainly: when the leading elders among the disbelievers, who had misled their common followers, appear before those followers on the plains of Resurrection, then rather than help each other they start arguing among themselves. These ayat are a sample of that argument, and of the sad end both parties face.

Ibn Kathir adds an important observation: this mutual blaming is not confined to one place. The disbelievers **blame one another in the arena of Resurrection, just as they will argue with one another in the levels of Hell**. The quarrel begins on the plain of gathering and continues inside the punishment. He brings two other passages to show the same scene from different angles:

- *"The weak will say to those who were arrogant: 'Verily, we followed you, can you then take from us some portion of the Fire?' Those who were arrogant will say: 'We are all (together) in this (Fire)! Verily, Allah has judged between (His) servants!'"* (40:47–48)
- *"…how they will cast the (blaming) word one to another! Those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant: 'Had it not been for you, we should certainly have been believers!' And those who were arrogant will say…: 'Did we keep you back from guidance after it had come to you? Nay, but you were criminals.' Those who were deemed weak will say…: 'Nay, but it was your plotting by night and day, when you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him!' And each of them will conceal their own regrets, when they behold the torment… Are they requited aught except what they used to do?"* (34:31–33)

Read together, a pattern emerges. The followers always open with *you did this to us*. The leaders always answer *you were already willing*. And in the passage from Sūrah Ghāfir, the one request that is actually made — *take from us some portion of the Fire* — is refused outright.

## The accusation: "you used to come at us from the right"

Ayah 28 is the followers' charge: **إِنَّكُمْ كُنتُمْ تَأْتُونَنَا عَنِ ٱلْيَمِينِ** — *"It was you who used to come to us from the right side."* The phrase is compressed, and the early scholars unpacked it in several complementary ways, all of which Ibn Kathir preserves:

- **Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn ʿAbbās**: they will say, *"You used to force us because of your position of power over us, for we were weak and you were strong."*
- **Qatādah**: men will say to the jinn, *"You used to come to us from the right side to block every good deed, and you told us not to do it and you tried to put obstacles in our way."*
- **As-Suddī**: *"You used to come to us to block the truth, and you made falsehood look attractive to us, and you prevented us from seeing the truth."*
- **Ibn Zayd**: *"You stood in the way between us and goodness, and you repelled us from Islam and faith and doing the good deeds that we had been commanded to do."*
- **Yazīd Ar-Rishk**: it means coming at them to block them *"from Lā ilāha illallāh"* — the kalimah itself.

What most of these explanations share is a picture of interception rather than mere temptation: not simply luring a person toward evil, but positioning yourself between him and the good he was headed for. Qatādah speaks of blocking *every good deed* and putting obstacles in the way; As-Suddī of blocking the truth and dressing falsehood up attractively; Ibn Zayd puts it most directly — *you stood in the way between us and goodness*. And by Yazīd Ar-Rishk's reading, what was blocked was the kalimah, *Lā ilāha illallāh*, itself.

**A second reading of the word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that يَمِين (*yamīn*) may carry several meanings here, and that one possible sense of the expression عَنِ الْيَمِين is *"powerfully"* or *"forcefully"* — hence the rendering *"you were the ones who used to come to mislead us forcefully"* (37:28), a meaning it describes as fairly clear and cloudless. In addition, *yamīn* is also used to mean an **oath**, and some commentators explained the phrase as *"you came to us with oaths"* — that is, *you made us believe on oath that our creed was correct and that the teaching of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was false.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges that, in terms of the words of the Qur'an, both these explanations are possible and can be accepted comfortably.

Sit with that for a moment. The reports and readings together give us more than one picture of how people are led to ruin: raw pressure from those stronger than you; an interference that dresses falsehood up as attractive and stands guard over your good deeds; and confident swearing — *trust me, we are right and he is wrong.* Anyone who has watched a person talked out of religion will recognise all of these.

## The rebuttal, part one: "you were never believers"

Ayah 29 turns the microphone over: **قَالُوا بَلْ لَّمْ تَكُونُوا مُؤْمِنِينَ** — *"Nay, you yourselves were not believers."* Ibn Kathir identifies the speakers as **the leaders of the jinn and mankind** answering their followers, and paraphrases them: *"It is not as you say; your hearts denied faith and were open to disbelief and sin."*

This is the hinge of the whole exchange. The followers' defence rests on a claim about their inner state: *I would have believed, but for you.* The leaders demolish exactly that claim. In their telling, you did not believe and then get dragged away from belief — your heart already denied faith and stood open. Notice the two words Ibn Kathir uses: the heart *denied*, and the heart was *open*. Refusal on one side, availability on the other.

## The rebuttal, part two: "we had no authority over you"

Ayah 30 completes it: **وَمَا كَانَ لَنَا عَلَيْكُم مِّن سُلْطَانٍ** — *"And we had no authority over you."* Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and easy to pass over, and it changes the whole meaning of the sentence. It means, he says, *'we had no proof of the truth of that to which we called you.'*

So the leaders are not merely saying *we never held a whip over you*. On Ibn Kathir's reading they are conceding something more damning: there was never any proof behind the invitation. They called, and their followers came, and there had been nothing to come for.

Then the counter-charge: **بَلْ كُنتُم قَوْمًا طَاغِينَ** — *"Nay! But you were a transgressing people."* Ibn Kathir expands: *'You yourselves were evildoers and transgressors against the truth, so you responded to us and neglected the truth which the Prophets brought with proof, and you went against them.'*

That single sentence carries the moral logic of the passage, and it turns on one repeated word. The leaders had **no proof**. The Prophets came **with proof**. Two invitations reached these people, and they answered the one with nothing behind it while neglecting the one that came with evidence — and then, says Ibn Kathir, went against the Prophets who brought it. That is what earns them the description *transgressors against the truth*.

Notice also what this does to the followers' opening charge. If the leaders had no proof, then whatever the followers were given, it was never a reason. On the leaders' own account, they were not out-argued. They responded.

## The reply: shared ruin, not shared excuse

The tone changes in ayah 31. **فَحَقَّ عَلَيْنَا قَوْلُ رَبِّنَا إِنَّا لَذَائِقُونَ** — *"So now the Word of our Lord has been justified against us, that we shall certainly taste (the torment)."* Ibn Kathir explains this as the arrogant saying to those who were deemed weak: *'the Word of Allah has been justified against us, that we are among the doomed who will taste the punishment of the Day of Resurrection.'*

Watch the pronouns. Through ayat 29 and 30 the leaders spoke in *you* — *you* were not believers, *you* were transgressors. Here, for the first time, they say *us* and *we*, and the verdict they announce includes themselves. They are not pleading. They are reporting a sentence that has already been established against them.

Then ayah 32: **فَأَغْوَيْنَاكُمْ إِنَّا كُنَّا غَاوِينَ** — *"So we led you astray because we were ourselves astray."* Ibn Kathir gives each half:

- **فَأَغْوَيْنَاكُمْ** — *"So we led you astray"* means, *'so we called you to misguidance.'*
- **إِنَّا كُنَّا غَاوِينَ** — *"because we were ourselves astray"* means, *'we called you to follow the path which we were on, and you responded.'*

This is an admission, but read it carefully: it exonerates nobody. The leaders concede they issued the call — and in the same breath explain that they were walking that road themselves. There was no secret exit they kept for themselves and hid from their followers. On Ibn Kathir's wording they called others onto the very path they were on. And the sentence does not end with the call; it ends with *and you responded*. Even in confessing, the leaders hand part of the weight back.

## Why the quarrel changes nothing

Nothing in these six ayat moves a single portion of blame from one party to the other. That is the shape of the passage: charge, counter-charge, and an admission that settles no account.

The parallels Ibn Kathir brings to explain ayah 27 make the point explicitly. In Sūrah Ghāfir the followers put the only request that would actually matter — *"can you then take from us some portion of the Fire?"* — and the answer is **"We are all (together) in this (Fire)! Verily, Allah has judged between (His) servants!"** (40:47–48). The share is not transferable, and the matter is already judged. And Sūrah Sabaʾ closes its version of the same quarrel with a question that leaves no room for the whole argument: *"Are they requited aught except what they used to do?"* (34:33) — while both parties, having said everything, **conceal their own regrets when they behold the torment**.

The follower's *you made me* does not shift his share upward to the leader. The leader's *you were already willing* does not shift his share downward to the follower. Each is requited for what he used to do.

## Living it

**Ask for the proof now, while asking still helps.** The whole quarrel turns on ayah 30 as Ibn Kathir reads it: *we had no proof of the truth of that to which we called you.* There is a question worth putting to every voice that shapes what you believe — and to your own reasons for what you already believe: *what is the evidence for this?* The Prophets came **with proof**, in Ibn Kathir's words on the very next line. Anything asking you to leave that has, by its own eventual admission, nothing.

**Blame will not be transferable.** Every excuse a person is quietly saving up — *my family, my crowd, my teacher, the pressure I was under* — is spoken aloud in these ayat, by people who mean it, and it changes nothing. In the parallel Ibn Kathir cites, the request to have some portion of the Fire lifted is simply refused. Better to spend that energy now, on what can still be changed.

**Watch what you invite others into.** Ayah 32 is the confession of anyone who called others onto a road he had not checked: *we called you to follow the path which we were on, and you responded.* Walking the path yourself did not make it safe for the leaders and did not save the followers. Whoever has influence — over children, students, friends, an audience — should be sure the path he recommends is one he has evidence for, and not merely one he happens to be standing on.

**And notice, too, what the followers claim they were kept from.** By Yazīd Ar-Rishk's reading, the blocking described in ayah 28 was a blocking *from Lā ilāha illallāh* — the shortest sentence in the religion, and the one thing that, on this reading, all that pressure and interference and swearing was aimed at. Whatever stands between a person and those words is worth naming now, while there is still time to step around it — because in these ayat, once the words are out of reach, the only thing left to argue about is whose fault that was.

passages.title: Shared punishment for those who scorned tawhid
passages.tafsir:
These ayat close the courtroom scene that began a few verses earlier. The misguided leaders and their followers have finished blaming one another, and Allah delivers the verdict: the blame they are trading changes nothing — they will all be inside the same punishment (ayah 33). Allah then names the attitude that brought them there: they could not bear to say *lā ilāha illā Allāh* (ayah 35), and they sneered at the Messenger ﷺ who brought it (ayah 36). Allah answers that sneer Himself (ayah 37), and the passage ends by telling them what they will receive and on what basis (ayat 38–39).

What holds the seven ayat together is a single line of argument: **shared guilt produces shared punishment, arrogance is the root of that guilt, and the reckoning is measured strictly by what people actually did.**

## Prior context: the quarrel that ayah 33 interrupts (ayat 27–32)

Ibn Kathir treats ayah 33 as the closing comment on an argument that begins several verses earlier, so a brief look back helps. In those verses the disbelievers "turn to one another and question one another," and the followers open the accusation: *"It was you who used to come to us from the right side."* Ibn Kathir gathers several early explanations of that phrase — Ad-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas ("You used to force us because of your position of power over us, for we were weak and you were strong"); Qatadah, that men will say this to the jinn, who came "to block every good deed"; As-Suddi ("you made falsehood look attractive to us, and you prevented us from seeing the truth"); Ibn Zayd ("You stood in the way between us and goodness"); and Yazid Ar-Rishk, who takes the blocking to be "from *Lā ilāha illā Allāh*." The readings differ over *who* is blamed — the powerful among men, or the jinn — but agree on the charge: someone stood between them and the good, whether by pressure or by making falsehood attractive.

The reply is blunt. **"Nay, you yourselves were not believers."** Ibn Kathir: the leaders of the jinn and mankind will tell their followers, "It is not as you say; your hearts denied faith and were open to disbelief and sin." Then, **"And we had no authority over you"** — which Ibn Kathir explains as, *we had no proof of the truth of that to which we called you.* The leaders are not claiming they forced anyone; they are admitting they never even offered an argument. Hence **"Nay! But you were a transgressing people"** — Ibn Kathir: you were "evildoers and transgressors against the truth," who responded to their call and neglected "the truth which the Prophets brought with proof."

Finally the leaders concede their own doom: the Word of their Lord has been justified against them, they are "among the doomed who will taste the punishment of the Day of Resurrection," and — **"so we led you astray because we were ourselves astray,"** which Ibn Kathir renders: *we called you to misguidance… we called you to follow the path which we were on, and you responded.*

## Ayah 33: sharers in the punishment

After all that mutual accusation, Allah's comment lands: **"Surely on that Day they will all share in the punishment."** *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* renders it, "they will be sharers in the punishment."

Ibn Kathir is careful about what that sharing means: **"all of them will be in Hell, each according to what he deserves."** Being together in the punishment does not mean an identical sentence. The leader who called others to misguidance and the follower who responded are both inside it, but each carries his own measure. This is exactly why the blame-trading is futile — nobody is transferring a portion of anything to anyone.

Ibn Kathir sets this alongside two other scenes of the same argument, so you can hear that the Qur'an describes one consistent reality:

> "The weak will say to those who were arrogant: 'Verily, we followed you, can you then take from us some portion of the Fire?' Those who were arrogant will say: 'We are all together in this Fire! Verily, Allah has judged between His servants!'" (40:47–48)

And the longer passage of Sūrah Saba' (34:31–33), where the weak say *"Had it not been for you, we should certainly have been believers,"* the arrogant answer *"Did we keep you back from guidance after it had come to you? Nay, but you were criminals,"* the weak come back with *"it was your plotting by night and day, when you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him"* — and the passage closes the file with: *"Are they requited aught except what they used to do?"* Ibn Kathir notes that the disbelievers will blame one another in the arena of Resurrection, just as they will argue with one another in the levels of Hell.

## What this asks of us now: the ruling in ayah 33

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* draws out of ayah 33 a principle that is uncomfortably practical:

**1. Inviting someone to sin is itself a punishable act.** If a person invites someone else to participate in what is impermissible and uses his clout to coax him into sin, "he will certainly incur the punishment of so inviting that person to sin." The invitation is a crime in its own right.

**2. Accepting the invitation is your own act.** A person who accepts of his own volition and choice "cannot be absolved from the sin of his deed. He cannot appear in the Hereafter and get away by saying that he was made to go astray by this or that person." Peer pressure, a persuasive friend, a culture that expects it — none of that transfers the file to someone else's name. This is precisely the excuse the earlier verses dramatise and ayah 33 dismisses.

**3. Genuine coercion is a different matter.** *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* adds: if the sin was not committed by his own volition and choice but under coercion, just to save his life, "then, insha'Allah, it is hoped that he will be forgiven." Note the careful wording — hope, not a bare guarantee — and note that the case described is coercion to save one's life, not social awkwardness.

So the passage cuts in two directions at once. It warns anyone with influence — an older sibling, a boss, a friend with a strong personality, anyone with a following — that leading others into wrong is itself charged to their account. And it removes from the follower the comfort of saying "they made me."

## Ayah 34: not an exception but a rule

**"That is certainly how We deal with the wicked."** Ibn Kathir's rendering of the same words is "that is how We deal with criminals." The ayah generalises: what happened to those particular idolaters is not a one-off, but how Allah deals with people who do this. And what they did is named in the very next breath.

## Ayah 35: the arrogance behind it all

**"For whenever it was said to them, 'There is no god but Allah,' they puffed themselves up with pride."**

Here the Qur'an traces the whole scene at Judgement back to a single moment, repeated many times in the world: a sentence was offered to them, and they were too proud to say it. Ibn Kathir's comment is precise: "in this world they were too arrogant to say these words **as the believers said them**." The obstacle was never intellectual difficulty; a short sentence is not hard to pronounce. What was hard was saying it the way a believer says it — as surrender rather than as a slogan.

It is worth noticing that this is the very trait the parallel verses Ibn Kathir quotes pin on the ringleaders: "those who were arrogant." The same pride that stopped them from saying the words in this world puts them, on the Day of Judgement, in front of the crowd they misled.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir narrates here from Ibn Abi Hatim, that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"I have been commanded to fight the people until they say Lā ilāha illā Allāh. Whoever says Lā ilāha illā Allāh, he and his property are safe from me except for his obligation, and his reckoning will be with Allah, may He be glorified."*

Placed beside ayah 35, the hadith shows how much weight that one sentence carries. It is a boundary line: the person who says it comes under protection of life and property — with what he owes still owed — and his reckoning is with Allah. The people of ayah 35 refused to say it, and everything in the passage follows from that refusal.

## Ayah 36: "a mad poet"

**"And argued, 'Should we really abandon our gods for a mad poet?'"**

Ibn Kathir unpacks the sneer: *"Shall we stop worshipping our gods and the gods of our forefathers just because of the words of this mad poet?"* — and "this mad poet," he notes, means the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Two things are worth sitting with. First, what they think is an argument is not one: inherited habit on one side (*our gods and the gods of our forefathers*), mockery on the other, and nothing in between. Second, look at the two labels — *shāʿir*, a poet, and *majnūn*, out of his mind. Both are ways of dismissing a message without answering it: treat it as mere wordcraft, or as illness.

Recall the leaders' own admission in the earlier verses: *we had no proof.* Mockery is what stands in for proof when proof is missing.

## Ayah 37: Allah answers on His Prophet's behalf

**"In fact, he came with the truth, confirming the earlier messengers."**
