The ayah opens with the word rendered "Nay!" — and Ibn Kathir introduces it as *"Allah said in refutation of their attitude."* The answer to the insult does not come from the Prophet ﷺ defending himself; Allah refutes them.

Ibn Kathir explains the two halves:

- **"He has come with the truth"** — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "has brought the truth with all that Allah has revealed to him of stories and commandments." Both the accounts of what happened and the rulings of what to do are truth.
- **"And he confirms the Messengers"** — he "fulfills their prophecies of his praiseworthy characteristics and his perfect way, and he tells people of the Laws and commands of Allah, as they said he would." His coming is what earlier Prophets foretold, and his message matches theirs. So the charge is doubly answered: he is neither an inventor nor an outlier, but the confirmation of a line of Messengers.

Ibn Kathir then quotes: *"Nothing is said to you except what was said to the Messengers before you"* (41:43) — what is said against him had already been said to the Messengers who came before him.

## Ayat 38–39: the sentence, and its exact measure

**"You will certainly taste the painful torment, and will only be rewarded for what you used to do."**

Ibn Kathir introduces these two ayat with "Allah says, addressing the people" — the third-person account of "them" turns into "you." The reader is no longer watching someone else's judgement from a safe distance.

And the wording echoes what the arrogant leaders had already admitted about themselves a few verses earlier: they conceded that *"we shall certainly taste"* the torment; now the same certainty of tasting is announced in the second person, to all who took that road.

Then ayah 39 fixes the measure: **you "will be requited nothing except for what you used to do."** No inflation, nothing invented and added on. It is the deed handed back. This is the same seal that closes the Sūrah Saba' passage above: *"Are they requited aught except what they used to do?"*

## The door that opens right after

Ibn Kathir points out something about ayat 38–39 that a reader who stops at ayah 39 might miss: the sweeping address is immediately followed by an exception — *"Save the chosen servants of Allah"* (ayah 40). He notes that Allah "makes an exception in the case of His sincerely believing servants," and that this is like other ayat:

- *"By the Time. Verily, man is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds…"* (103:1–3)
- *"Verily, We created man in the best stature. Then We reduced him to the lowest of the low. Save those who believe and do righteous deeds"* (95:4–6)
- *"There is not one of you but will pass over it (Hell); this is with your Lord, a decree which must be accomplished. Then We shall save those who have Taqwa"* (19:71–72)
- *"Every person is a pledge for what he has earned, except those on the right"* (74:38–39)

Of those excepted servants Ibn Kathir says: "they will not taste the painful torment nor will they be brought to account. Their evil acts, if there are any, will be overlooked, and each good deed will be rewarded in multiples of between ten and seven hundred, or as much as Allah wills."

So the arithmetic here is not symmetrical. Wrongdoing is repaid at exact cost — *nothing except what you used to do.* Good, for those servants, is repaid many times over. The threat is measured; the mercy is generous.

## Carrying it

- **Watch what you invite people into.** Influence is recorded. Ayah 33 and *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* together mean that a nudge or a bit of pressure that pulls someone into wrong is not free.
- **Stop outsourcing blame.** Every excuse the followers offer in this passage is answered. Willing participation is your own deed, and it cannot be moved to another name in the Hereafter.
- **Guard the heart against the pride of ayah 35.** What ruined those people was not confusion but arrogance — refusing to say the words *as the believers say them*. The same pride can live in a believer who knows the truth and resists submitting to some particular part of it.
- **Expect mockery, and do not be shaken.** They called the Prophet ﷺ a mad poet, and Allah answered: *he came with the truth.* And nothing was said to him that had not already been said to the Messengers before him (41:43).

passages.title: The chosen servants and the delights of Paradise
passages.tafsir:
These ayat are one long sentence of rescue. The preceding verses had just told the deniers that they were going to taste a painful torment and be repaid for exactly what they used to do — and then ayah 40 breaks in with a single word of exception: **"Save the chosen servants of Allah."** Everything from ayah 41 to 49 is the unfolding of that exception: who these servants are is answered not by a definition but by a description of where they end up, what is set before them, who sits with them, and — just as importantly — what their delight will *not* contain.

## The great exception

Ibn Kathir draws attention to a pattern the Qur'an uses again and again: a sweeping verdict on humanity, then a narrow door left open. He lines up the parallels:

- "By the Time. Verily, man is in loss, **except** those who believe and do righteous deeds" (103:1–3)
- "Verily, We created man in the best stature. Then We reduced him to the lowest of the low. **Save** those who believe and do righteous deeds" (95:4–6)
- "There is not one of you but will pass over it (Hell) … Then We shall save those who have Taqwa. And We shall leave the wrongdoers therein to their knees" (19:71–72)
- "Every person is a pledge for what he has earned, **except** those on the right" (74:38–39)

Here in ayah 40 the same door opens. And Ibn Kathir spells out just how wide it is: the chosen servants "will not taste the painful torment nor will they be brought to account. Their evil acts, if there are any, will be overlooked, and each good deed will be rewarded in multiples of between ten and seven hundred, or as much as Allah wills."

Notice the honesty of that phrase — *if there are any*. These are not people without failings. They are people whose failings are passed over, and whose small acts are multiplied beyond all proportion.

**The word itself.** The translation renders *al-mukhlaṣīn* as "the chosen servants"; Ibn Kathir speaks of them as Allah's "sincerely believing servants." The two readings sit comfortably together: the quality being praised is *ikhlāṣ*, doing what you do purely for Allah with nothing else mixed in — and the wording of the ayah frames such a servant as one Allah has set apart. Sincerity is not a badge a person pins on himself.

**A word about the verses just before.** Commenting on ayah 33 ("So, this day, they will be sharers in the punishment"), Maarif ul Quran notes that whoever invites another to participate in what is impermissible and uses his clout to coax him into sin will certainly incur the punishment of that invitation — but the one who accepted, of his own volition and choice, cannot be absolved either. He cannot appear in the Hereafter and get away by saying that this or that person made him go astray. If, however, he did not sin by his own volition and choice but under coercion, just to save his life, then, *insha'Allah*, it is hoped he will be forgiven. That is the crowd ayah 40 is carving the believers out of: a crowd busy blaming one another.

## A provision that is *known* (ayah 41)

*Rizq maʿlūm* — "a known provision." Qatadah and As-Suddi said simply: "This means Paradise." But the word "known" is doing real work, and Maarif ul Quran records three explanations of it, citing Qurtubi and others:

1. **Known because it has already been described.** It refers to the detailed description of the provisions of Paradise given in different surahs of the Qur'an. Maulana Ashraf Thanavi elected to go by this reading.
2. **Known in its timing.** Its timings are determined and known: it will be bestowed punctually all mornings and evenings, as another ayah says explicitly of the people of Paradise — "and for them there is their provision in it, morning and evening" (19:62).
3. **Known because it is certain and everlasting.** This is the reading that stings most, because it names something about our own lives. In this world no one can say with any degree of certainty what provision he will receive, or how much, or how long it will remain available to him. Every human heart is all the time under the fear that the blessings it has may disappear tomorrow. Jannah will be free of that danger: the provision there will be certain and everlasting, both.

Read the three together and "known" comes to mean: *described in advance, delivered on time, and never in doubt.* Precisely the three things our provision here is not.

## Fruits — eaten for pleasure, not out of need (ayah 42)

Ayah 42 answers immediately what that provision consists of: *fawākih*, fruits — "of different kinds," says Ibn Kathir.

Maarif ul Quran opens the word up. *Fawākih* is the plural of *fākihah*, and *fākihah* denotes everything eaten **for the taste and not to remove hunger**. It is conveniently translated as "fruit," since fruit is eaten for the taste, but the sense of *fākihah* is much wider than that. Imam Razi culled a subtle point from exactly this choice of word: the cuisine offered in Jannah will be for the taste of it, and not for removing hunger. The reason is that in Jannah there is nothing one would really need — no food or energy-giving intake required to sustain life or preserve health. What remains is *wish*: the fulfilment of the wish will bring the pleasure of satiation, and that, Razi says, would be the objective of all the blessings of Paradise (Tafsir Kabir).

This quietly reframes the whole passage. These are not descriptions of needs being met. They are descriptions of desires being honoured.

**"And they shall be honoured."** Ibn Kathir glosses *wa hum mukramūn*: they will be served and will live a life of luxury. Maarif ul Quran adds the emphasis on *manner*: this provision will be presented to the people of Jannah with the full protocol of hospitality and honour, for an absence of that would leave even the most delicious offering without relish. And from this the commentary draws a lesson for our own tables: the right of a guest is not fulfilled simply by feeding him. The warmth of hospitality and the according of honour are themselves included under his rights. Food handed over grudgingly has already lost the thing that made it a gift.

## Facing one another (ayat 43–44)

*Jannāt al-naʿīm* — the Gardens of Delight — and in them, "facing one another on thrones."

Mujahid's comment is one line and it is the whole picture: "One of them will not look at one another's backs." Nobody is turned away from anybody. There is no seat at the back of the room, no one left out of the conversation.

How that seating arrangement would turn out in practice, Maarif ul Quran says frankly, only Allah knows best. But it reports what commentators have suggested. Some say the circuit of the seating arrangement would be so extensive that no one will need to sit with his back towards anyone, and that Allah Taʿālā will bless the people of Jannah with such power of sight, audition and speech that they would be able to converse comfortably with people sitting at varying distances. Others have said that these couches, thrones or settees will be revolving — readily zooming towards whomsoever one wishes to talk to. And Allah knows best.

Either way the point stands: in Paradise, companionship has no logistics. The pleasure being described here is not furniture. It is the end of social distance.

## The cup (ayat 45–47)

Now the passage slows down and lingers, and it does something striking: it describes the drink of Paradise largely by listing what is *absent* from it.

**"Round them will be passed a cup of pure wine" (45).** Ibn Kathir explains this as wine from a flowing stream which they do not fear will ever be cut off or cease. He sets alongside it the parallel scene: "Immortal boys will go around them (serving), with cups, and jugs, and a glass of flowing wine, from which they will get neither any aching of the head nor any intoxication" (56:17–19). Note also the shape of the verb — the cup is *passed round to them*; they are, as Ibn Kathir says of *mukramūn*, the ones served.

**"White, delicious to the drinkers" (46).** Malik narrated that Zayd bin Aslam said, "White flowing wine" — meaning with a bright, shining colour, unlike the wine of this earth with its ugly, repulsive colours of red, black, yellow and turbid shades, and other features which are repugnant to anyone of a sound nature. Ibn Kathir continues: its taste will be as good as its colour, and a good taste indicates that it has a good smell too — again unlike the wine of this world.

On the word *ladhdhah* itself, Maarif ul Quran notes a fine grammatical question. *Ladhdhah* is essentially a verbal noun meaning "to be tasteful," so some commentators have said that an adjunct stands elided here — originally *dhāti ladhdhatin*, "having taste." But, Maarif ul Quran says, there is no need for this laboured approach. A verbal noun is frequently used in the sense of an active participle, in which case the sense is that the drink would be "a taste personified" for those who drink. In addition, alongside *ladhīdh* there is another adjectival form, *ladhdh* — and the *ladhdhah* used here may possibly be its feminine (Tafsir Qurtubi), giving the plain meaning: "delicious for those who drink."

**"Neither will they have Ghawl from that nor will they suffer intoxication therefrom" (47).** This is the heart of the passage's realism about pleasure. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah refined the wine of Paradise from the bad effects of the wine of this world, which causes headaches and stomach aches — which is the meaning of *ghawl* — and causes people to lose their minds completely.

- On *ghawl*: it will not have any effects on them such as causing stomach aches. This was the view of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Maarif ul Quran records that *ghawl* has been variously explained as "headache" or "abdominal pain" or "smell or corruption" or "muddling of reason" — and the fact is that the word is used to convey all of these meanings. Hafiz Ibn Jarir says that *ghawl* appears here in the sense of **bane, trouble or unwelcome consequences**, which yields the widest and cleanest meaning: the drink offered in Jannah will have no such evil consequences as are found in the wines consumed in this mortal world — no hangovers of headache, stomach pain, bad breath or loss of reason (Tafsir Ibn Jarir).
- On *lā hum ʿanhā yunzafūn*: Mujahid said, "It will not cause them to lose their minds" — also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Muhammad bin Kaʿb, Al-Hasan, ʿAtaʾ bin Abi Muslim Al-Khurasani, As-Suddi and others.

Ad-Dahhak reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said, "Wine causes four things: intoxication, headache, vomiting and urine." So, when Allah mentions the wine of Paradise, He states that it is free of these characteristics.

Sit with what this implies. Every pleasure we know in this world arrives with a bill attached — the enjoyment, and then the cost. The Qur'an is not promising a larger version of the world's pleasure; it is promising pleasure with the defect removed. Even the *dignity* of the drinker is protected: he keeps his mind. Nothing in Paradise makes a fool of you.

## The company (ayat 48–49)

**Qāṣirāt al-ṭarf — "restricting their gazes."** Ibn Kathir reports the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Zayd bin Aslam, Qatadah, As-Suddi and others: chaste females, who will not look at anyone other than their husbands. Maarif ul Quran puts it the same way — except for the mate to whom Allah Taʿālā gives them in marital bond, they will not raise their eyes to cast a look at any other male.

ʿAllamah Ibn-ul-Jauzi reports that these women will tell their spouses: "By the honour of our Lord, I see no one better than you in this Jannah. Praised be Allah who made me your spouse and made you mine."

Ibn-ul-Jauzi also gives a second, elegant sense of "those with lowered gaze": that *they* will cause the gaze of their spouses to remain lowered — they will be so beautiful and so faithful that their spouses would simply not have a wish to look at anyone else (Tafsir Zad-ul-Masir). Read either way, the quality being praised is not confinement but contentment: a love in which no one is looking elsewhere. Set that beside the restless appetite this world trains in us, and you see why the Qur'an counts it among the delights.

**ʿĪn — "with (wide and beautiful) eyes."** Ibn Kathir: it means with beautiful eyes; it was also said that it means with wide eyes, which is connected to the first meaning — they are wide-eyed and beautiful, and their eyes are described as being beautiful and chaste.

**Ka-annahunna bayḍ maknūn (49).** This last image is the one that most needs a guide, because a literal English rendering lands strangely on a modern ear. Maarif ul Quran renders it "as if they were hidden eggs"; the translation given with the ayah reads "as if they were pristine pearls." Ibn Kathir says their bodies are being described as having the most perfect colour, and gathers the early explanations:

- Ibn ʿAbbas, as reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah: **as if they were hidden pearls**.
- Al-Hasan: **protected, never touched by any hands**.
- As-Suddi: "The well preserved egg in its nest" — and elsewhere, "The white of the egg when its shell is removed."
- Saʿid bin Jubayr: **"The inside of the egg."**
- ʿAtaʾ Al-Khurasani: **"It is the membrane which is between its outer shell and its inner contents."**

Ibn Jarir's view concerning the meaning of *maknūn* ("well preserved") is that the outer shell is touched by the wing of the bird and the nest, and by people's hands, unlike the interior of the egg. And Allah knows best.

Maarif ul Quran fills in the cultural sense. The simile was popularly recognised among the people of Arabia: the egg hidden under feathers remains safe from pollution, therefore it is always neat and clean; and its colour is yellowish white, which was deemed by the Arabs the most attractive colour for women. Other commentators, it adds, say that the simile does not relate to eggs as such but to the membrane hidden in the egg — the sense being that the skin of those women will be as soft as the membrane of the egg (Ruh-ul-Ma'ani). Allah knows best.

So the image is not really about eggs. It is about the two things *maknūn* guarantees: **untouched** and **unblemished** — something kept from every hand and every stain.

## What the passage is doing

Look back over ayat 41 to 49 and notice how much of it is negation. Provision that is never uncertain. A stream that they do not fear will ever be cut off. A drink with no headache, no stomach pain, no stupor, no foul aftertaste. A gathering with no one behind anyone's back. A companionship with no eye wandering. A beauty never touched by any hands.

That is the passage's argument, and it is aimed straight at people whose pleasures always came with a price. Ibn Kathir titles this section "The Punishment of the Idolators and the Reward of the sincere Believers" — and the chosen servants of Allah are given the same categories of delight that this world offers in defective form: food, drink, seating, company, honour — with every defect taken out.

And all of it hangs on one word in ayah 40: *illā*, "save," "except." The verdict of ayah 38 is real, and the exception is real, and there is nothing in these nine ayat about lineage, wealth or status. The single qualification named is *ikhlāṣ* — being Allah's servant purely, with nothing else mixed in.

Three things to carry away:

1. **Sincerity, not flawlessness, is the entry condition.** Ibn Kathir explicitly allows that these servants have evil acts "if there are any," which will be overlooked, while each good deed is rewarded in multiples of between ten and seven hundred, or as much as Allah wills.
2. **Learn what pleasure is for.** Imam Razi's point about *fawākih* — taste rather than hunger — teaches us to read every one of these descriptions as generosity rather than provisioning. Allah is not meeting a requirement. He is honouring a guest.
3. **Honour your own guests properly.** Maarif ul Quran lifts a practical rule straight out of *wa hum mukramūn*: the right of a guest is not fulfilled simply by feeding him. Serve him with warmth and with honour, or the food arrives without its relish — a small imitation, at your own table, of how Allah receives those He has chosen.

passages.title: A believer sees his old scoffing companion in Hell
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are a single scene: the people of Paradise, settled and at ease, fall into conversation about their past — and one of them remembers a friend from the world who used to mock him for believing in the Resurrection. He asks to look down, sees that man in the middle of the Fire, and speaks the two sentences that hold the whole passage together: *you nearly ruined me*, and *had it not been for the grace of my Lord*.

What unites ayat 50–57 is that they are almost all one man's speech, framed by a look. Ayah 50 opens the setting, 51–53 replay the taunt he once endured, 54–55 are the request and the sight, and 56–57 are what he says once he has seen. Read as a unit, the passage is about how a friendship looks from the far side of death.

## The setting: Paradise in conversation (ayah 50)

The translation of ayah 50 reads: *Then they will turn to one another inquisitively.* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us how the people of Paradise "will turn to one another, asking one another about their situation, how they were in this world and what they suffered." Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah is "Then they will turn to one another, mutually questioning" — the exchange is mutual, each asking the other, not one man interrogating a silent companion.

Ibn Kathir sets the scene generously. This talk, he says, is part of their conversation when they get together to converse and drink, sitting on their thrones, servants coming and going, bringing all kinds of good food, drink, clothes and other delights that no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and that the mind of man has never comprehended. That is the setting in which the memory of the mocking friend surfaces.

## The taunt, quoted back (ayat 51–53)

**"I once had a companion."** The word in ayah 51 is قَرِين (*qarīn*), which Ibn Kathir's text renders as "a companion (in the world)"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān speaks of the man as a "disbelieving acquaintance" and, in one report it mentions, of the two as "comrades." Ibn Kathir reports that Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that this refers to an idolater who had a companion among the believers in this world. So the relationship was a real one: not an enemy across a battle line, but someone in his circle.

**"Do you actually believe?"** In ayah 52 the taunt is أَءِنَّكَ لَمِنَ ٱلۡمُصَدِّقِينَ — "Do you actually believe ˹in resurrection˺?", or in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "Are you among those who believe...?" Ibn Kathir explains the sense: *do you believe in the resurrection after death, and the Reckoning and reward or punishment?* And he notes exactly the tone in which it was said — "by way of astonishment, disbelief and stubbornness." Not an honest question. The kind of question that is really a laugh at your expense: *you don't actually believe that, do you?*

**"Dust and bones."** Ayah 53 gives the argument behind the mockery: once the body has crumbled to dust and bare bones, how can anything be owed? The key word is لَمَدِينُونَ (*madīnūn*), which Ibn Kathir's text renders as being *indebted* — held liable, called to settle a bill. The early authorities read it in two complementary ways. Mujahid and As-Suddi said it means "brought to account." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi said it means "rewarded or punished according to our deeds." Ibn Kathir's judgement is that **both views are correct** — the word covers the summons and the settlement, being called in and being paid out.

Notice what the scoffer's whole objection rests on: that once the body is dust, there is nothing left to answer for. Ayat 55–57 are the reply, and the Fire he is looking down into is the proof.

## "Would you care to look?" (ayat 54–55)

In ayah 54 the believer says هَلۡ أَنتُم مُّطَّلِعُونَ — "Would you care to see ˹his fate˺?" Ibn Kathir glosses the word as meaning "look over," and the ayah is rendered "Will you look down?" He also clarifies who is being addressed: **the believer says this to his companions among the people of Paradise.** He is not shouting at the man in the Fire; he is turning to the friends around him — *come and see*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important qualification about how this is possible at all: it is **with the permission of Allah** that he is given an opportunity to speak to his old acquaintance by peeping into Jahannam. Even this glance is something granted, not something arranged by the man himself.

Then ayah 55: فَٱطَّلَعَ فَرَءَاهُ فِي سَوَآءِ ٱلۡجَحِيمِ — he looked, and spotted him in the *sawā'* of the blazing Fire. On سَوَآء a striking number of early authorities agree. Ibn Kathir names Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Sa'id bin Jubayr, Khulayd Al-'Usari, Qatadah, As-Suddi and 'Ata' Al-Khurasani: it means **in the middle of Hell**. Al-Hasan Al-Basri adds an unforgettable line — "in the middle of Hell as if he were a burning star." That is what became of the man who thought the whole idea was absurd.

## What the saved man says (ayat 56–57)

**The oath.** Ayah 56 begins تَٱللَّهِ — *by Allah*. He swears on it. Then: إِن كِدتَّ لَتُرۡدِينِ, "You nearly ruined me." Ibn Kathir supplies the clause the believer has in mind, addressing the disbeliever: "By Allah, you nearly caused me to be doomed, **if I had obeyed you**." That conditional is the hinge. The ruin he escaped is tied not to what his companion did to him but to what he himself might have done in response — obeying him. On this reading, the peril of bad company lies in going along with it.

Read the words also as an admission of how close the call was. *You nearly* — not *you never came near me*. The man in Paradise is saying, with the Garden already under him, that there was a version of his life in which he ended up down there.

**The credit.** Ayah 57 is where he places it: وَلَوۡلَا نِعۡمَةُ رَبِّي لَكُنتُ مِنَ ٱلۡمُحۡضَرِينَ — "Had it not been for the grace of my Lord, I would certainly have been among those brought forth." Ibn Kathir unfolds it: "Were it not for the favour of my Lord towards me, I would have been like you in the middle of Hell where you are, brought forth with you for punishment. But He bestowed His grace upon me, had mercy upon me and guided me to faith and to belief in Him Alone."

Three things are worth noticing.

First, he says *my Lord* — رَبِّي. At the very moment his stand in the world is vindicated, he speaks of Allah in that personal way.

Second, he does not say *had it not been for my intelligence*, or *my discipline in resisting him*. He was the one who held firm; and according to Ibn Kathir's explanation he traces it entirely to his Lord's favour, His mercy, and His guiding him to faith and to belief in Him alone — that is, to *tawḥīd*, the worship of Allah alone. Ibn Kathir follows the point with the Qur'an's own words: **"and never could we have found guidance, were it not that Allah had guided us!"** (7:43).

Third, look at what the speech does *not* contain. He states what nearly happened to him and Whose favour prevented it. There is no boast in it — the comparison he draws is not *look how much better I was* but *look what I was saved from*.

This is the passage's deepest lesson for anyone who has held on to faith while being laughed at. When the vindication finally comes, the sentence on his tongue is not *I was right*. It is *my Lord was gracious to me*.

## Who were these two men?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: **the identity of this man has not been given in the Qur'an**, and therefore "it cannot be said with any degree of certainty as to who this person could be." What follows are reports, offered as possibilities, not as part of the revealed text.

**One opinion**, from Tafsīr Mazharī: some commentators held that the believer's name was Yahudah and his disbelieving acquaintance's name was Matrus, and that they were the same two comrades mentioned earlier in Sūrah al-Kahf — "And give them an example. There were two men…" (18:32).

**A second report** reaches us through two channels in our sources, with details that differ. Ibn Kathir records it from Abu Ja'far bin Jarir, who reported it from Furat bin Tha'labah Al-Bahrani, about two men among the Children of Israel who were partners. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a version that 'Allāmah as-Suyūṭī reported from several *tābi'īn* (the generation after the Companions), cited from *Tafsīr ad-Durr ul-Manthūr* with reference to Ibn Jarir and others.

In Ibn Kathir's telling, two partners had collected eight thousand dinars. One of them had a craft and the other did not, so the one with the craft said, "You do not have a craft, so I think I will divide the money with you and leave you," and left him. Then he bought a house belonging to a king who had died for the price of one thousand dinars, called his old partner over and showed it to him. The man said, "How beautiful it is" — and on his way out prayed: "O Allah, this companion of mine has bought this house for one thousand Dinars; I ask You for one of the houses of Paradise," and gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then as much time passed as Allah willed. The first man married a woman with a dowry of a thousand dinars, invited him and made food for him. Same reply — "How beautiful this is" — and on the way out: "O Lord, my companion has married a woman with a dowry of one thousand Dinars; I ask you for a wife from among *Al-Hur Al-'Iyn*," and another thousand in charity. Time passed again. The first man bought two gardens for two thousand dinars and showed them to him. "How beautiful this is" — then: "O Lord, my companion has bought two gardens for two thousand Dinars; I ask you for two gardens in Paradise," and two thousand dinars in charity.

Then the angel came to them and took their souls in death. The one who had given his money in charity was put in a house that he liked; there was a woman in it so beautiful that the ground shone under her; then the angel took him to two gardens, and gave him other things which are known only to Allah. He said, "This is like a man who has such and such" — and the angel answered, "That is exactly what it is; this house, these gardens and this wife are all for you." Then he said, "I had a companion who used to say: *Are you among those who believe?*" It was said to him, "He is in Hell." He said, "Will you look down?" So he looked down and saw him in the midst of Hell, and said the words of ayat 56–57.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's version runs differently and has a harder edge. There, the two partners earned eight thousand dinars and took four thousand each. The worldly partner spent a thousand on land, then a thousand on a house, then a thousand on marrying a woman, then a thousand on attendants and other things; and each time, the pious partner asked Allah for the equivalent in Jannah and gave away a thousand dinars in charity. Afterwards this believing servant of Allah was caught in some dire need and thought of his former partner, hoping he would help, and told him about it. The partner asked what had become of his share of the money, and heard the whole story. Wondering at it, he said: "Do you really believe it as true that, once we die and become dust, we shall get another life and, in that life, we shall be given the return for our deeds? Get lost. I am not going to give you anything." After that, both of them died — and in this account the man of Jannah in these ayat is the one who gave all his wealth in charity for the sake of the Hereafter, while his acquaintance in Jahannam is the partner who had chided him for affirming the life to come.

Handle these reports as the sources themselves do: illustrative material, helpful for feeling the shape of the ayat, not doctrine. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says so plainly — **"whoever this person may be — it does not matter."** What matters is why the episode is mentioned at all.

## Living it: audit your circle

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out that purpose. The noble Qur'an, it says, is alerting people to a beneficial rule operative in human relations: **let everyone make a careful survey of his or her circle of friends, and try to find out whether there is someone in it who may actually be dragging them towards the sad end of the Jahannam.**

Three observations from that commentary are worth taking personally.

**The damage is hard to see while it is happening.** There are occasions and circumstances, it says, when one does not foresee what would happen after forming relationships with someone who disbelieves or disobeys. What ultimately happens is that "one starts becoming affected by his ideas, thoughts and way of life without having any sense of that which is happening to him." Nobody announces that they are being pulled off course. And this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, "proves lethal for one who is so affected in terms of the end he would have in the Hereafter."

**The full reckoning arrives too late.** The destruction bad company can bring about "can only be discovered fully and truly in the Hereafter — and that will be a time when there will be no escape from such destruction." Ayah 55 shows us exactly that discovery, in advance, while there is still time to act on it.

**Therefore choose now, with care.** The conclusion Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches: it is better to take one's guard right here in this world in matters concerning the taking of friends and the promoting of relationships, "something that must be done with due caution and judgment."

And beside the warning stands the model in the reports: a man who watched a friend spend on a house, a marriage, gardens — answered "how beautiful this is" each time — and then, on his way out, asked Allah for the equivalent in the Hereafter and gave the same sum in charity. He simply invested in the world his friend denied. And ayah 57 tells us that even then, he refused to call any of it his own achievement.

The passage continues past ayah 57. Ibn Kathir explains ayat 58–59 — "Are we then not to die any more? Except our first death, and we shall not be punished?" — as what the believers will say when they feel joy at what Allah has given them and realise that they are to remain in Paradise forever, with no punishment and no death to come; Al-Hasan Al-Basri notes that they know death brings an end to every delight, and they are answered that this is indeed the supreme success. Then, on "For the like of this let the workers work," Ibn Jarir said: "These are the Words of Allah, and it means: for the like of this pleasure and this success, let the workers work in this world, so that they may attain it in the Hereafter."

But the moral centre is already fixed here, in ayah 57: the whole difference between the man in the Garden and the burning star in the middle of the Fire is *ni'mah* — the grace of his Lord.

passages.title: "Are we then not to die?" — the honour worth striving for
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are words spoken **inside Paradise**. A believer has just looked down and seen the old companion who used to mock his belief in the resurrection now in the midst of the Fire; he turns back to what surrounds him and breaks out in wonder — are we really never to die again, never to be punished? Ayah 60 answers him: *this* is the supreme success. And ayah 61 turns from the scene to us: this is what a lifetime of effort is for.

What holds the four together is that they are the closing movement of one scene. Ayat 58–59 are the cry of joy, ayah 60 is the verdict passed on that joy, and ayah 61 is the lesson drawn out of the whole episode for anyone still alive and still able to work.

## The scene these ayat close

Ibn Kathir sets it up: Allah tells us how the people of Paradise will turn to one another, asking one another about their situation — how they were in this world and what they suffered. This is part of their conversation when they get together to converse and drink, sitting on their thrones, servants coming and going, bringing all kinds of good food, drink, clothes and other delights no eye has seen and no ear has heard and that never entered the mind of man.

In the middle of that ease, one of them speaks (ayah 51): *"Verily, I had a companion"* — the Arabic word is **qarīn**, which the tafsir renders simply as "companion." Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said this refers to an idolater who had a companion among the believers in this world.

What that companion used to say is quoted in ayah 52: *"Are you among those who believe (al-muṣaddiqīn)?"* Ibn Kathir explains the sense: do you believe in the resurrection after death, and the Reckoning, and reward or punishment? — and adds that he used to say it *"by way of astonishment, disbelief and stubbornness."* Not a sincere question; a sneer.

Ayah 53 gives his objection: when we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be **madīnūn** — the word Ibn Kathir's text renders "indebted"? Mujāhid and as-Suddī glossed it "brought to account." Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) and Muḥammad bin Kaʿb al-Qurazī glossed it "rewarded or punished according to our deeds." Ibn Kathir's verdict on the two readings: **both views are correct.**

Then, in ayah 54, the believer says: *"Will you look down?"* — meaning, look over. Ibn Kathir notes he is saying this **to his companions among the people of Paradise**. And what he sees (ayah 55) is his companion *fī sawāʾ al-jaḥīm*. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Khulayd al-ʿUṣarī, Qatādah, as-Suddī and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasānī all read this as "in the middle of Hell." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī put it starkly: "In the middle of Hell as if he were a burning star."

His first words to the man (ayah 56) are an oath: *"By Allah! You have nearly ruined me."* Ibn Kathir supplies the unspoken clause: *by Allah, you nearly caused me to be doomed, if I had obeyed you.* And then ayah 57, which is the hinge of the whole scene: *"Had it not been for the grace of my Lord, I would certainly have been among those brought forth."* Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: were it not for the favour of my Lord towards me, I would have been like you in the middle of Hell where you are, brought forth with you for punishment — but He bestowed His grace upon me, had mercy upon me, and guided me to faith and to belief in Him alone. Ibn Kathir places beside it the words of the people of Paradise elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"and never could we have found guidance, were it not that Allah had guided us"* (7:43).

That is the mood in which ayat 58–61 are spoken: relief, gratitude, and the knowledge of how close the other outcome came.

## The words of ayat 58–59

*Afamā naḥnu bi-mayyitīn — illā mawtatanā al-ūlā wa-mā naḥnu bi-muʿadhdhabīn.*

Two things are named and then set aside. Ayah 58 denies death; ayah 59 makes the one exception — *our first death*, the death already behind them, the one they died in the world — and then denies punishment too. Ibn Kathir draws out exactly that: this is what the believers will say when they feel joy at what Allah has given them, and they realise that they are to remain in Paradise forever **with no punishment and no death to come**. There is no second death waiting.

## Wonder, not doubt

An honest reader may pause here: if he is in Paradise, why is he *asking*? Doesn't he know?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers this directly. It does not mean he will not be certain of the eternal life of Jannah. It is like the case of a person who achieves the highest degree of happiness: such a person would occasionally break into exclamations that show as if he does not believe his eyes on having received such enormous blessings. "These remarks are of the same nature." It is the speech of overwhelmed joy, not of shaky faith — the way a man who has just been handed everything says *is this really mine?*

## Why death is mentioned at all

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī gave the reason the thought of death even occurs to them: **"They know that death brings an end to every delight."** That is the one shadow over every happiness a human being has ever had — that it will be taken away. So, in al-Ḥasan's telling, they say, *are we then not to die, except our first death, and we shall not be punished?* — and the answer comes back: *No —*

*"Truly, this is the supreme success!"*

## Ayah 60: the verdict

*Inna hādhā la-huwa al-fawzu al-ʿaẓīm* — "Truly, this is the supreme success."

Notice who is speaking. Ibn Kathir introduces the ayah with "Allah says," presenting it as Allah's own word on their joy; in al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's narration it is the reply given to them. Either way it is not the believer congratulating himself — the ayah settles from above what he has just been marvelling at.

And notice what is being called the supreme success. Not the house, not the gardens, not the servants. What the ayah points at, in the flow Ibn Kathir traces, is **the state itself**: remaining in Paradise forever, with no punishment and no death to come.

## Ayah 61: the lesson that comes out of the scene

*Li-mithli hādhā fal-yaʿmal al-ʿāmilūn* — "For the like of this let the workers work."

Ibn Jarīr said: "These are the Words of Allah, and it means: for the like of this pleasure and this success, let the workers work in this world, so that they may attain it in the Hereafter."

So the goal is set by pointing back at what the passage has just shown — *the like of this* — and the ayah names not admirers but **workers**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah as the closing turn of the whole episode: towards the end, the noble Qur'an turns our attention to the essential lesson embedded in this event and says, *for this kind of achievement, all workers must work.*

## Who was the man?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: the identity of this man has not been given in the Qur'an, "therefore it cannot be said with any degree of certainty as to who this person could be." It then reports two separate attempts at identification, as alternatives rather than as one story:

- Some commentators have opined that the believer was named Yahūdah and his disbelieving acquaintance Matrūs, and that they were the same two comrades mentioned earlier in Sūrah al-Kahf — *"And give them an example. There were two men…"* (18:32). This is from Tafsīr Mazharī.
- ʿAllāmah as-Suyūṭī reported "yet another event" from several of the tābiʿīn — the account of two business partners given below (Tafsīr ad-Durr ul-Manthūr, with reference to Ibn Jarīr and others).

Ibn Kathir, for his part, introduces his own narration with "they mentioned," and describes the two partners in it as men "who are included in the meaning of this Ayah" — that is, material that falls under the ayah's meaning, not the Qur'an's own statement of who these people were.

So the right posture is Maʿārif's own: "whoever this person may be — it does not matter." Read the narrations as illustrations of the passage's meaning, not as settled history.

## The story of the two partners

Ibn Kathir records, under the heading "The Story of Two Israelites," from Abū Jaʿfar bin Jarīr, that Furāt bin Thaʿlabah al-Baḥrānī said about *"Verily, I had a companion"*: there were two men who were partners and had collected eight thousand dīnārs. One of them had a craft and the other did not, so the craftsman said he would divide the money with him and leave him — and he did.

Then the man bought a house belonging to a king who had died, for a thousand dīnārs, and called his companion and showed it to him: what do you think of this house? I bought it for a thousand dīnārs. He said, "How beautiful it is" — and when he went out he said: *"O Allah, this companion of mine has bought this house for one thousand dīnārs; I ask You for one of the houses of Paradise"* — and he gave a thousand dīnārs in charity. Then as much time passed as Allah willed should pass.

The first man married a woman with a dowry of a thousand dīnārs, invited his companion and made food for him, and told him. "How beautiful this is." And when he left: *"O Lord, my companion has married a woman with a dowry of one thousand dīnārs; I ask You for a wife from among al-Ḥūr al-ʿĪyn"* — and he gave a thousand dīnārs in charity. Then as much time passed as Allah willed should pass.

Then the first man bought two gardens for two thousand dīnārs and showed them to him. "How beautiful this is." And when he came out: *"O Lord, my companion has bought two gardens for two thousand dīnārs; I ask You for two gardens in Paradise"* — and he gave two thousand dīnārs in charity.

Then the angel came to them and took their souls in death. The one who had given his money in charity was put in a house that he liked; there was a woman there so beautiful that the ground shone under her; then the angel took him to two gardens and gave him other things which are known only to Allah. The man said, "This is like a man who has such and such." The angel said: *"That is exactly what it is; this house, these gardens and this wife are all for you."* The man said, "I had a companion who used to say: *Are you among those who believe?*" It was said to him, "He is in Hell." He said, "Will you look down?" So he looked down and saw him in the midst of Hell — and said the words of ayat 56–57.

This is what ayah 61 looks like as a life, and it is why Ibn Kathir places the story here: every time his friend showed him a purchase, he asked Allah for its like in Paradise and gave the same sum away in charity.

The version Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from as-Suyūṭī runs a little differently. There the two partners earned eight thousand dīnārs and took four thousand each. The friend spent a thousand on a plot of land; the pious partner prayed for a plot in Jannah and gave a thousand in charity. The friend spent a thousand building a house; the pious man asked for a house in Jannah and gave another thousand. The friend married a woman and spent a thousand on her; the pious man asked for one of the women of Jannah and gave another thousand. Finally the friend spent a thousand on attendants and things, and the pious man again gave a thousand in charity and asked Allah for attendants and things of Jannah.

After that, this believing servant of Allah was caught in some dire need and thought of his former partner, hoping he would help, and told him of it. The partner asked what had become of his share of the money; hearing the whole story, he said in astonishment: *"Do you really believe it as true that, once we die and become dust, we shall get another life and, in that life, we shall be given the return for our deeds? Get lost. I am not going to give you anything."* After that, both of them died. As-Suyūṭī's account concludes by identifying the man of Jannah in these ayat with the servant of Allah who gave his wealth in charity for the sake of the Hereafter, and the acquaintance in Jahannam with the partner who chided him for affirming the life to come.

That identification belongs to that narration, not to the Qur'an — Maʿārif offers it as one of two candidate accounts and still holds that certainty about the man's identity is not available. Which is exactly why it adds: whoever he may be, it does not matter. The purpose is elsewhere.

## Living it

**Audit your circle.** This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lands the passage. The event has been mentioned with a purpose: the Qur'an is alerting people to a beneficial rule operative in human relations. Let everyone make a careful survey of his or her circle of friends and try to find out whether there is someone in it who may actually be dragging them towards the sad end of Jahannam. The destruction bad company can bring about can only be discovered fully and truly in the Hereafter — and that will be a time when there will be no escape from it. So it is better to take one's guard right here in this world, in the taking of friends and the promoting of relationships, with due caution and judgment. What ultimately happens, Maʿārif warns, is that one starts becoming affected by such a person's ideas, thoughts and way of life *without having any sense of what is happening* — and that proves lethal in terms of the end one meets in the Hereafter.

**Notice the word "nearly."** In ayah 56 the believer does not say "you ruined me." He says *you have nearly ruined me* — and Ibn Kathir fills in the condition: *if I had obeyed you.* The harm was not imaginary; it came that close. Anyone with a friend who mocks the Hereafter should hear ayah 56 as a description of a live risk, not of someone else's story.

**Claim nothing for yourself.** The man at the summit of success in ayah 60 got there saying the words of ayah 57 — *had it not been for the grace of my Lord* — and Ibn Kathir pairs it with 7:43: we could never have found guidance had Allah not guided us. Faith is Allah's favour before it is anyone's achievement, and the people of Paradise are still saying so in Paradise.

**Aim at the right thing, then work.** Ayah 61 names the workers, and Ibn Jarīr's gloss is the whole practical programme: for the like of this pleasure and this success, let the workers work **in this world**, so that they may attain it in the Hereafter.

passages.title: The tree of Zaqqum and the boiling drink
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat turn on a single question that Allah puts to His creation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that after describing the conditions prevailing in Jahannam and Jannah briefly, Allah has invited every human being to compare the two and decide which is better. Then comes the unfolding of what the second option actually involves: a tree rooted in the Fire (ayah 64), fruit too hideous to look at (65), bellies filled with it anyway (66), a scalding drink poured on top (67), and a return to the blaze itself (68).

## Ayah 62: a question that is really an invitation

**"Is this ˹bliss˺ a better accommodation or the tree of Zaqqûm?"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as an open invitation: having sketched the conditions of Jahannam and Jannah briefly, Allah now asks every human being to compare and decide. Its own paraphrase of the ayah puts it plainly — "there are these blessings of Jannah mentioned here; are they better? Or, is it the tree of Zaqqum the fruits of which will be fed to the people of Jahannam?" Nothing is being forced. The question is put to the reader's own judgement.

Ibn Kathir spells out the two sides of the comparison: on the one hand everything just mentioned of the delights of Paradise — "its food, drink, companions and other joys" — and on the other, the tree of Zaqqum, "which is in Hell."

Notice the word chosen for what is on offer (*nuzul*). Our translation gives **"accommodation"**; Ibn Kathir's rendering is **"entertainment."** Either way, the question is about what a person will find at his destination — and the only real question is which destination he is heading towards.

And there is a bitter symmetry here that the rest of the passage develops. In Ibn Kathir's summary, Paradise was described through what its people eat and drink. Hell is now described in exactly the same terms — by what will be fed to its people.

## What is Zaqqum?

Both commentaries stop to ask a natural question: is this an actual tree, and do we know it?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that a tree called Zaqqum is found in the territory of **Tihamah**, a part of the Arabian Peninsula, and that ʿAllamah ʿAlusi has written that it is also found in other barren deserts. Some say this is the same tree known as *thohar* in Urdu and Hindi (*Euphorbia neriifolia* or *antiquorum*); others point to another tree known as *nagphan* — "hood of serpent" — found in India, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says appears to be the more likely of the two.

But then it flags a genuine difference among the commentators, and does not settle it: **is the Zaqqum whose fruit the people of Jahannam will eat one of the trees found in this world, or some other tree entirely?** Some support the view that it is what is found growing in this world. Others say the Zaqqum of Jahannam is an entirely different thing, with nothing to do with the earthly zaqqum.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then offers a middle way with an illuminating comparison. Apparently, the way there are snakes and scorpions in the mortal world, it seems they are there in Jahannam as well — though it goes without saying that the snakes and scorpions of Jahannam will be far more ferocious than their counterparts here. Similarly, the Zaqqum of Jahannam will be like the Zaqqum of this world in terms of its genus, but far too gruesome to look at, and far too unpalatable to eat. It then closes the discussion with the phrase that should close every discussion of the unseen: **"And Allah is pure and high who knows best."**

Ibn Kathir's own point is simpler and worth holding on to: the meaning here is a specific kind of tree which is called Zaqqum. He draws the parallel with Allah's words about "a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, that grows (produces) oil, and (it is a) relish for the eaters" (23:20) — which, he says, is the olive tree, a real and nameable tree. And he notes that this is supported by the ayah: *"Then moreover, verily, — you the erring-ones, the deniers! You, verily, will eat of the trees of Zaqqum"* (56:51-52).

## Ayah 63: the tree that became a test — and how Abu Jahl failed it

**"We have surely made it a test for the wrongdoers."** This is the hinge of the whole passage, and the place where the sources give us a scene from the Prophet's ﷺ own Makkah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that according to some commentators *fitnah* here means **punishment** — that Allah has turned this tree into a source of punishment. But most commentators, it says, hold that it is more appropriate to translate *fitnah* here as **"trial"** or **"test"**: the purpose is that Allah wishes to test who believes in it and who ridicules it.

Then comes the report of those who ridiculed it. Qatadah, quoted by Ibn Kathir, said that the tree of Zaqqum is mentioned as a test for those who are misguided, and preserves the objection they raised: *"Your companion tells you that in the Fire there is a tree, but fire consumes trees."* It sounds almost like a reasonable argument — fire burns wood; a tree inside a furnace is a contradiction.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the man who turned that objection into a joke. When the ayat came down mentioning that the disbelievers would be made to eat the fruit of Zaqqum, Abu Jahl said to his accomplices: "Your friend (Sayyidnā Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ) says that there is a tree in the Fire — although, fire eats the tree — while we … do know this much that zaqqum is the name of butter-topped dates. So, come and eat this date and butter." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from **ad-Durr-ul-Manthur** (p. 277, v. 5), and adds the linguistic detail that makes the sneer land: in the language of the Berbers, dates topped with butter or cream were known as *zaqqum* — so Abu Jahl made use of this opportunity to ridicule the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir preserves the same line in briefer form: Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, said, "Zaqqum means dates and butter which I eat."

So a warning of the Fire was met with a dinner party. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict is blunt: **the disbelievers of Arabia failed this test.** Rather than fear this punishment and believe, they opted for the method of confrontation and ridicule.

Ibn Kathir then gives the ayah its widest meaning: *"We have told you, O Muhammad, of the tree of Zaqqum as a trial with which We test the people to see who will believe and who will disbelieve."* He anchors this in a striking parallel: *"And We made not the vision which we showed you but a trial for mankind, and the accursed tree in the Qur'an. We warn and make them afraid but it only increases them in naught save great disbelief, oppression and disobedience to Allah"* (17:60).

That parallel is the key to the passage. Revelation about the unseen sorts people. The same words that make a believer tremble and turn back give a mocker fresh material. The warning does not change; the hearts differ. And Allah tells us plainly that He intended it as a trial.

## Ayah 64: the answer, in one sentence

**"Indeed, it is a tree that grows in the depths of Hell."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that Allah gave an answer in a single sentence. Two things collapse at once: neither does *zaqqum* mean date and butter, nor does the objection as to how a tree could survive in fire hold valid — particularly when that tree owes its very origin to the fire itself.

Ibn Kathir reports the same understanding from Qatadah, who said of this ayah that **"it is nourished by the fire, for it was created from fire."** Ibn Kathir adds the plain sense of the words: its roots grow at the bottom of Hell — *aṣl al-jaḥīm*, the very base of the blaze. Where a normal tree would draw water, this one draws fire.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point further: Allah has placed such properties in it that instead of getting burnt in fire, it is actually nurtured by it — and notes, as an aid to the imagination, that there are many life forms that would survive only in a fire that does not burn them but in fact makes them grow. The lesson is about the limits of our intuitions. Abu Jahl reasoned from the fire he knew to the Fire he had never seen. That is exactly the mistake the ayah closes off.

## Ayah 65: fruit like devils' heads

**"bearing fruit like devils' heads."** The word rendered "fruit" here (*ṭalʿuhā*) Ibn Kathir renders as "the shoots of its fruit stalks" — the emerging fruit, the part of a tree that on any ordinary tree is the promise of sweetness. On this tree, what emerges is horror.

Ibn Kathir says the comparison is simply "a description of how ugly and repulsive it is." And he raises the obvious objection: how can something be likened to the heads of *Shayatin* when people have never seen them? His answer: because it is a well-established idea in people's minds that devils are ugly in appearance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops this into a point about how the Qur'an speaks. Some commentators, it notes, have translated *ash-shayāṭīn* here as **"serpents"**, since the fruit of Zaqqum resembles the hood of the serpent — which is precisely why it is called *nagphan* in Urdu and Hindi. But most commentators say the word should be taken in its well-recognised sense: devils. On that reading, in its ugliness the fruit of Zaqqum is like the head of the satans — and this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is **an imaginative simile**. Speaking metaphorically, things ugly and grotesque are commonly likened to Shaitans, Jinns and ghosts; the purpose is only to express an extreme degree of ugliness. It attributes this explanation to Ruh-ul-Maʿani and others.

This is worth understanding properly. The Qur'an is not describing a shape you could sketch. It is reaching for the ugliest thing the human imagination already holds and saying: like that.

## Ayah 66: they will fill their bellies with it

**"The evildoers will certainly ˹be left to˺ eat from it"** — and, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, they "fill their bellies therewith." He catches the pathos of this. They will eat of this extremely ugly tree even though its fruit tastes and smells so bad — and they will eat because **they will be forced to**: they will not find anything else to eat except this tree and similar things. He cites the ayah: *"No food will there be for them but a poisonous thorny plant, Which will neither nourish nor avail against hunger"* (88:6-7).

Set that beside ayah 62's question. The people of Paradise have food, drink and companions set before them. These are starving people who fill their bellies with what revolts them, and are not even nourished by it. Hunger drives them to eat; the food does nothing for the hunger.

## Ayah 67: the drink poured on top

**"Then on top of that they will be given a blend of boiling drink."** Ibn Kathir gathers the interpretations of *shawb min ḥamīm*. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said this means they will be given boiling *ḥamīm* to drink **after** they have eaten from Zaqqum; according to another report from him, it means a mixture made from boiling water. Someone else said it means boiling water mixed with the pus and offensive discharges that leak from their private parts and eyes.

Ibn Kathir then records, from **Ibn Abi Hatim**, that Saʿid bin Jubayr traced the whole sequence of ayat 66-67 as a single ordeal. When the people of Hell get hungry they will ask for food from the tree of Zaqqum. They will eat from it, and then the skin of their faces will fall off — if someone were to pass by, he would recognise them from their faces. Then thirst will be sent upon them, so they will ask to be given something to drink, and they will be given water like boiling oil that has been heated to the ultimate degree. When it is brought near to their mouths, the flesh of their faces from which the skin has fallen off will be baked by its heat, and whatever is in their stomachs will melt. They will walk with their guts falling out and with their skin falling off; then they will be beaten with hooked rods of iron, and every part of their bodies will burst into loud lamentations.

Note the shape of it: hunger, so they ask for food; the food makes thirst, so they ask for drink; the drink destroys them further. Every relief they seek deepens the punishment. In this world, eating and drinking are how a body is restored. There, the same two acts are the instruments of ruin.

## Ayah 68: and then back to the Fire

**"Then they will ultimately return to ˹their place in˺ Hell."** Ibn Kathir explains: after that interval, they will be sent back to the burning fire, searing heat and scorching flames, and **they will rotate between the one and the other**. He supports this with the ayah: *"They will go between it (Hell) and the fierce boiling water!"* (55:44) — an ayah Qatadah himself recited when discussing this one. Ibn Kathir calls this a good interpretation.

That is the closing note of the passage, and it is deliberately without exit. This is not a punishment that arrives and is over. It is a circuit: fire, then the tree, then the scalding drink, then back to the fire.

Ibn Kathir also records a second reading. ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud recited the ayah differently, with the meaning **"Their return in the afternoon"** — and ʿAbdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, midday on the Day of Resurrection will not come until the people of Paradise will be in Paradise and the people of Hell will be in Hell." He then recited: *"The dwellers of Paradise will, on that Day, have the best abode, and have the fairest of places for repose"* (25:24). On that reading the ayah says something about speed as well as severity — the matter will be settled before the day is half done.

Ibn Kathir presents both readings side by side without forcing a choice, and it is right to leave them as he did.

## Living it

**Answer the question.** Ayah 62 is addressed to you, not only to Abu Jahl. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames this whole passage as Allah inviting every human being to compare and decide. A passage like this has done its work not when you have learned what Zaqqum is, but when you have honestly answered which of the two you are travelling towards.

**Fear mockery more than doubt.** The men of ayah 63 were not defeated by a hard question. They had one — "fire consumes trees" — and instead of asking it sincerely, they turned it into a joke and a plate of dates. Ayah 64 shows the question had an answer waiting in a single sentence. What ruined them was not the difficulty; it was the sneer. Anyone who has ever laughed off something in the revelation because it sounded strange should sit with ayah 63 for a while.

**Do not measure the unseen by what you have handled.** Both a tree nurtured by fire (ayah 64) and fruit like devils' heads (ayah 65) are described in terms our imagination can only reach for, never grasp. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's posture before such things — *and Allah is pure and high who knows best* — is the believer's posture: affirm what Allah has told us, without pretending to a picture He has not given.

**Let the warning do what warnings are for.** Ibn Kathir's parallel at 17:60 is sobering: Allah warns and makes them afraid, "but it only increases them in naught save great disbelief." The warning is doing nothing wrong when it fails to land. The heart is. So take these ayat as most commentators understood them — as *fitnah* in the sense of a trial, a test you can still pass, while the door is open.

passages.title: Blindly following forefathers into ruin
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat answer a question the reader is bound to ask about the terrifying scene just described: *how did people end up there?* Ibn Kathīr's answer, drawn straight from ayah 69, is that they inherited a wrong path from their fathers and followed it "with no evidence or proof." Ayat 69–70 diagnose the disease; ayat 71–73 show that it is an ancient disease, that Allah sent warners among those nations, and that the outcome is on record; ayah 74 names the exception.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Just before this, the sūrah sets two futures side by side: the delights of Paradise — "its food, drink, companions and other joys," as Ibn Kathīr puts it — or "the tree of Zaqqūm" that grows in Hell (ayah 62). Ibn Kathīr explains that this means a specific kind of tree, whose roots grow at the bottom of Hell. The people of the Fire eat from it and fill their bellies (ayah 66) — not because they want to, Ibn Kathīr notes, but because they will find nothing else — then boiling *ḥamīm* on top of it (ayah 67), and then a return to the blazing Fire (ayah 68), rotating between the two.

**Then ayah 69 supplies the cause.** Ibn Kathīr's comment is precise: *"We will punish them for that because they found their fathers following misguidance and they followed them with no evidence or proof."* Everything above is the end of a road; ayah 69 shows where the road started.

## Ayah 69: "they found their forefathers astray"

Notice what the ayah does **not** say. It does not say their fathers argued them into it, or produced a case for it. As Ibn Kathīr frames it, they found their fathers following misguidance, and they followed — and the decisive words in his explanation are *with no evidence or proof*.

That is the whole indictment: not that they were persuaded, but that they never asked to be persuaded. The Qurʼān is not condemning them merely for having fathers who erred; on Ibn Kathīr's reading, the fault is in following without evidence or proof — treating "this is what my people do" as though it settled the matter.

## Ayah 70: hastening in their footsteps

"So they rushed in their footsteps!" Two of the early commentators open up this ayah. **Mujāhid** said of it: "This is like running." **Saʿīd bin Jubayr** said: "They followed ignorance and foolishness."

Put the two glosses together and you have the picture: not a considered walk but a run, and a run whose content is ignorance and foolishness. They are moving fast, and they are moving *in their footsteps* — along tracks already trodden out for them.

Two things are worth sitting with:

- **Speed is not evidence of truth.** Mujāhid's "like running" and Ibn Kathīr's "no evidence or proof" belong together. Momentum, and a crowd all moving the same way, can feel like confirmation. It is not.
- **Haste and ignorance travel together.** Saʿīd bin Jubayr does not describe them as calculating; he describes them as foolish. The faster the movement, the less room there is for the question that would have saved them.

## Ayat 71–73: this is an old story, and it has an ending

Ayah 71 widens the lens: "most of the earlier generations had strayed before." Ibn Kathīr states plainly what their straying consisted of: **most of the previous nations went astray, worshipping other gods alongside Allah.** So the crowd in ayah 70 is not merely one tribe's crowd; according to this ayah, most of those who came earlier had already gone the same way. If the number of people on a road settled the question, this road would win — and the ayah says outright that this road was the road of the majority.

Ayah 72 closes off the excuse: "although We had certainly sent warners among them." Ibn Kathīr explains that Allah sent warners **among them** — from within those very nations — to alert them to the anger, wrath and vengeance of Allah towards those who disbelieve in Him and worship others besides Him. Those nations were not left in the dark. The inherited misguidance was interrupted by warners raised up among the very people who needed the warning.

And still, Ibn Kathīr continues, **they persisted in their opposition to their Messengers and their disbelief in them** — so Allah destroyed those who disbelieved in Him, and saved the believers and caused them to prevail.

Ayah 73 then turns to the listener with a command: **"See then what was the end of those who had been warned."** *Fa-nẓur* — look. Not "believe blindly," but *look at the record*. The ayah asks for the very thing the people of ayah 69 refused to do: consider the evidence. And note the pointed wording — "those who had been *warned*." They were not the uninformed; they were the informed. Their end is not a mystery. Ibn Kathīr has just told us what it was.

## Ayah 74: the exception that carries all the hope

"But not the chosen servants of Allah." After the majority, the warners and the destruction, the passage closes on a small, luminous exception. Ibn Kathīr quotes ayat 73 and 74 together as one statement — see the end of those who were warned, **except** the chosen servants of Allah — and this comes immediately after his sentence about those whom Allah *saved and caused to prevail* when the deniers were destroyed.

Two things stand out. First, they are named as the **servants of Allah**: that is the alternative to hastening along in someone else's footsteps — to belong to Allah rather than to the crowd. Second, in Ibn Kathīr's own account of these nations, the rescue is Allah's act: *He* destroyed the deniers and *He* saved the believers and caused them to prevail. Their escape is His doing, not their cleverness. That is why this exception is a comfort and not a boast.

## Living it

The passage is unusually practical, because the failure it describes is a familiar one.

- **Distinguish inheritance from proof.** Much of what we hold — religious habits, cultural certainties, family assumptions — arrived the way it arrived in ayah 69: we *found* it. That is not an argument against it; it is an argument for checking it. Ibn Kathīr's standard is the standard: *evidence or proof*.
- **Be suspicious of the rush.** Mujāhid's "like running" and Saʿīd bin Jubayr's "ignorance and foolishness" describe one state, not two. Whenever you find yourself moving quickly because everyone else is, that is the moment to stop and ask for the proof.
- **Do what ayah 73 asks.** *Fa-nẓur* — look. Refusing to examine the case was the ruin of the people in ayah 69; examining it is the command given to us.
- **Value the warners.** Ayah 72 shows Allah sending warners into the middle of the very nations that had gone astray. Wanting to be that voice inside your own circle — and being willing to hear it — is exactly what breaks the chain.
- **Ask to be among the exception.** Since Ibn Kathīr's reading has Allah Himself saving the believers when the rest were destroyed, the natural response is to ask Him for it — for sincerity, and for the strength to stand still and think when everyone around you is running.

passages.title: Noah answered, delivered, and honoured
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are the whole life's work of a prophet compressed into eight lines: a cry for help, an answer, a rescue, a legacy — and, at the very end, the fate of those he had spent nearly a thousand years warning. What holds them together is a single pattern that the surah will now repeat for prophet after prophet: **Nuh called, Allah answered, Nuh was saved and honoured, and the deniers were drowned.** Ayah 75 is the call; ayat 76–81 are the answer, unfolded; ayah 82 is the other half of the answer, the half that fell on his people.

## Where these ayat sit in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the preceding ayat had made a brief, general statement: Allah sent messengers to warn the earlier communities too, but most of the people did not listen, and so they met a very sad end. From ayah 75 onward the Qurʼān stops summarising and starts naming. The details of that brief statement now come as a series of stories about individual prophets — and the first of them is Nuh, peace be upon him.

Ibn Kathir frames it the same way. When Allah tells us how most of the early people went astray from the path of salvation, He begins the detailed explanation with the story of Nuh and his people's rejection of him. So this passage is not an isolated story. It is exhibit one in an argument the surah is building.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes that the full narrative of Nuh has already been given, with sufficient detail, in Sūrah Hūd (sūrah 11). Here the Qurʼān is not retelling the story; it is drawing out its meaning. That is why the passage moves so fast — it assumes you know what happened, and wants you to see what it means.

## Nine and a half centuries, and one cry

Ibn Kathir gives the human weight behind ayah 75. Only a few of Nuh's people believed in him, and this was not for want of effort or time: **he stayed among them for a thousand years less fifty.** Nine hundred and fifty years of calling. And the pattern of those centuries was not slow progress but the reverse — every time he called them, they turned away from him even more. His call did not soften them; it hardened them.

Eventually, Ibn Kathir says, their disbelief became too much for him to bear, and he prayed to his Lord: *"I have been overcome, so help me!"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies which prayer ayah 75 is pointing to. According to most commentators, the "calling" here is either the supplication recorded in Sūrah Nūḥ — *"My Lord, do not leave on earth even a single inhabitant surviving from the disbelievers"* (71:26) — or the one in Sūrah al-Qamar: *"I am overpowered, so defend me"* (54:10). And it adds the circumstance that makes such a prayer intelligible: Nuh, peace be upon him, made this supplication at a point when his people had crossed every limit in their wickedness and hostility toward him, and had gone as far as **conspiring to kill him.**

So when ayah 75 says *"Indeed, Noah cried out to Us,"* understand what stands behind that verb. This is not a passing request. It is what a man says after nine and a half centuries of patience, when the door has finally closed and his own life is being plotted against.

**One line worth pausing on.** Ibn Kathir writes that after all this, "Allah became angry because Nuh was angry with them." Allah's anger is a reality He has told us about, and we affirm it as He affirmed it for Himself — without imagining it to be like the anger that rises in a human chest, and without explaining the word away into something else. What the sentence conveys here is honour: the distress of a beloved servant is not a small thing with his Lord. Nuh's grievance became the ground on which the divine response fell.

## "And how excellent are We in responding"

Ayah 75 does not end with the cry. It ends with Allah's own comment on how He receives such cries: *fa-la-niʿma l-mujībūn* — rendered in the translations before us as *"how excellent are We in responding"* and *"We are the best of those who answer."*

Notice the shape of the ayah. It could have said "and We answered him." Instead it turns aside to praise the answering itself — a general statement of what Allah is like as a Responder, hung at the end of one particular man's prayer. The specific case becomes an advertisement of a permanent divine quality. Ibn Kathir leaves the phrase almost without comment, and rightly: what follows in ayat 76–81 *is* the commentary. Six ayat of answer for one line of prayer. If you want to know what "the best of those who answer" means in practice, read on and count what Nuh was given.

## Rescued from "the great distress"

Ayah 76: *"We delivered him and his family from the great distress."*

A reader might assume the "great distress" (*al-karb al-ʿaẓīm*) means the Flood — the water, the terror of drowning. Ibn Kathir reads it otherwise, and his reading is quietly devastating: it means **"their disbelief and their insults."**

That is, the great affliction Nuh was rescued from was not the deluge. It was his people. Nine and a half centuries of watching men reject their Lord to their own ruin, and of being mocked for trying to stop them — *that* was the crushing thing, and the rescue was rescue from that. The Flood was the instrument of the deliverance, not the danger he was delivered from.

There is a lesson here for anyone who carries a burden of conscience. The heaviest weight a believer bears is often not physical danger. It is living among rejection, hearing truth insulted, and being scorned for caring. The Qurʼān calls that *al-karb al-ʿaẓīm* — the great distress — and it names being lifted out of it a deliverance worthy of mention alongside surviving a flood.

## Ayah 77: "and made his descendants the sole survivors"

Ayah 77 makes a claim about the entire human race. Ibn Kathir brings the early authorities on it. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him): *"There was no one left apart from the offspring of Nuh, peace be upon him."* Saʿīd bin Abī ʿArūbah narrated from Qatādah on this same ayah: *"All people descended from the offspring of Nuh, peace be upon him."*

### The three sons

Ibn Kathir cites two reports here. At-Tirmidhī, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Samurah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said, concerning this very ayah: **"Sam, Ham and Yafith."** And Imām Aḥmad recorded from Samurah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Sam was the father of the Arabs, Ham was the father of the Ethiopians and Yafith was the father of the Romans"** — a report At-Tirmidhī also recorded. Ibn Kathir clarifies that "Romans" here means the original Romans, i.e. the Greeks who claimed descent from Ruma, son of Liti, son of Yunan, son of Yafith, son of Nuh, peace be upon him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the same map with a little more breadth: from Sam came the peoples of Arabia and Persia; from Ham, the populations of the African lands, and some scholars included the people of India in that stock; from Yafith came the peoples known as Turk, Mongol, and Gog and Magog. It adds a precision that explains the wording of the ayah: of all those who boarded the ark and survived the Flood, the three sons of Nuh were the only ones whose progeny continued afterwards. That is why the ayah can say *his descendants* were the survivors, even though others were saved with him in the ark.
