On the grading of the report about the three sons, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Imām Tirmidhī calls this hadith *ḥasan* (good), while Imām Ḥākim rates it *ṣaḥīḥ* (sound), citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī.

### How far did the Flood reach?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine difference of opinion here, and it is worth knowing where the scholars stood.

**The first view** — held by most commentators — is that the majority of the world's population was destroyed in the Flood, and that afterwards every race on earth came from the three sons of Nuh.

**A second view**, held by a very small number of scholars, is that the Flood was not worldwide but confined to the land of ancient Arabia. On this reading, it was in that region that the progeny of Nuh survived and flourished, and from them came the Arab race; the fact that other peoples spread through other parts of the world would then not contradict the ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this position to Bayān ul-Qurʼān.

**A third view**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes to Qurṭubī, is that the Flood was worldwide but that humanity's stock did not descend from Nuh's sons alone — it spread from all those who were aboard with him. This group reads the restriction in the ayah as a *relative* restriction: the point being made is simply that the line of the drowned did not continue.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges that, given the context of the Qurʼān, this third view is very weak, and that the first view is the best — because it is supported by the ahadith which Imām Tirmidhī and others reported directly from the Prophet ﷺ under the tafsir of this very ayah. That is a sound way to weigh opinions: the reading the Prophet's ﷺ own words point to takes precedence.

There is also a quiet human consequence in this ayah. On the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges best, every reader of this passage descends from the man who was mocked for nine and a half centuries. The people who laughed at him had the numbers; not one of them left a line behind. He was the one whose family the future came through.

## Ayat 78–79: the good name Allah left behind

Ayah 78: *"And We blessed him with honourable mention among later generations."* The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites all gloss it in the same direction. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said: *"He is remembered in a good way."* Mujāhid said it means *"an honourable mention by all the Prophets."* Qatādah and As-Suddī said: *"Allah caused him to be praised constantly by others."* Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said it means *"Salam and praise."*

Then ayah 79 states the mention itself — as if Allah, having said "We left him a good name," now reads the name out: *"Peace be upon Noah among all peoples."* Ibn Kathir says this ayah "explains for us the extent of the honourable mention and praise, for he is greeted with peace by all groups and nations."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how far that reaches: Nuh, peace be upon him, was made so revered in the eyes of those born after him that they would go on praying for his peace and well-being right up to the last day, the Day of Resurrection. And, it observes, this is exactly how it turned out. Every religion that claims a link to divine scripture accepts his mission as a prophet and holds him in great reverence; besides the Muslims, even the Jews and the Christians regard him as a spiritual leader of theirs.

Put ayah 79 next to ayah 75 and you see the trade. Nuh spent nine hundred and fifty years being insulted by his contemporaries. Allah answered by giving him the good word of every generation after them — peace pronounced on him, in the very words of the Qurʼān, and prayed for him by those who came after, on and on to the Day of Resurrection. His enemies had him for a lifetime; he has the world's blessing forever.

## Ayat 80–81: why, and on what basis

Ayah 80 turns the particular into a rule: *"Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers."* Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: *"This is how We reward those of Our servants who do deeds of obedience to Allah. We gave him an honourable mention so that after he died he is still remembered in a manner that befits his status."*

Two things follow from that. First, the honour given to Nuh is not a one-off favour to one prophet — it is a sample of a standing divine practice: this is how Allah rewards those of His servants who obey Him. Second, note *what* the reward consists of: a name that outlives the man. The Qurʼān treats being remembered well after death as a genuine reward from Allah, not a vanity.

Ayah 81 then supplies the reason underneath the whole passage: *"For he was truly one of Our faithful servants."* Ibn Kathir explains: one of the sincere believers in the Oneness of Allah, one of those who had certain faith.

This is the load-bearing ayah. Nuh was not honoured for his nine centuries of endurance as a feat of stamina; he was honoured because underneath the endurance lay sincere belief in the Oneness of Allah and a faith that was certain. And notice the title the ayah chooses for him: not "one of Our messengers," but *"one of Our believing servants."* At the summit of prophetic achievement, the honour named is servanthood and faith. Those are ranks open to us too.

## Ayah 82: "Then We drowned the others"

The passage ends in one short line. Ibn Kathir: *"We destroyed them, and there was no trace whatsoever left of them, and they are only known by this unfavourable description."*

Read ayah 82 against ayah 78 and the design becomes visible. In ayah 78 Allah *left something for Nuh* among "the later generations"; in ayah 82 He drowned "the others." Both ayat are about what remains after a person is gone. Nuh's people had the numbers, the majority, the power to threaten his life — and no trace whatsoever was left of them; they are known now only by that unfavourable description, *the drowned*. Nuh had almost no followers, and what survives of him is a blessing pronounced among all peoples.

That contrast is the argument the surah is making, laid bare in eight ayat: the cry of one rejected servant reached the Best of Responders; the noise of a whole civilisation left no trace at all.

## Living it

- **Take your grievance to Allah, and take it late rather than never.** Nuh called after nine hundred and fifty years. Ayah 75 does not scold the delay; it praises the Responder. No hardship is too old and no complaint too long-standing for the One who is "best of those who answer."
- **Name the real distress.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 76 teaches us that the crushing weight in a believer's life is often the disbelief and the insults around them, not physical danger. Relief from that is worth asking for.
- **Measure results the way ayah 82 does.** By the standards of his own time Nuh's mission looked like failure — only a few believers in nearly a millennium. By the standard of what lasted, his people left no trace and he was given honourable mention among all who came after. Faithfulness, not visible success, is what Allah rewards.
- **Aim at what ayah 81 names.** Sincere belief in Allah's Oneness and certainty of faith. That is what the honours of ayat 76–80 were built on, and it is available to anyone.

passages.title: Abraham confronts his people's idols
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) — not with the fire he was thrown into, but with the heart he brought to Allah and the words he spoke to his own household. Ayah 83 places Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in the way of Nuh (peace be upon him); ayah 84 describes the heart with which he came to his Lord; and ayat 85–87 give his words to his father and his people, put as three questions one after the other.

## Where this sits in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after relating the event concerning Nuh (peace be upon him), the Qur'an mentions **two events from the blessed life of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)**, and that both events highlight the great sacrifices he offered for the sake of Allah alone. The first of the two is the one beginning in these ayat: the event of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) being thrown into the fire. Maʿārif adds that the details of that event have already appeared in Sūrah al-Anbiyāʼ (21:51–70), and that the way it is described here calls for some explanatory notes.

## Ayah 83: "one of his shīʿah"

*"And indeed, one of those who followed his way was Abraham."*

The Arabic is **min shīʿatihi** — literally, "from his shīʿah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this word is used in the Arabic language for a group or party **whose individuals are similar to each other in basic concepts and methods**. It is a word about shared convictions and shared ways of doing things.

And whose shīʿah? Maʿārif states that here it is obvious the pronoun in *shīʿatihi* ("his") reverts to Nuh (peace be upon him), the prophet just spoken of. So the meaning is that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) adhered to the way of Nuh (peace be upon him), the prophet preceding him, and that there was **perfect agreement between them on the basic principles of faith** — and Maʿārif adds that it is also possible the religious codes they had could have been the same, or similar.

Ibn Kathir reports the same reading from the earliest authorities. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that it means "he was one of the followers of his religion," and Mujahid said, "He was following his path and his way."

**Why this is striking.** Maʿārif asks us to bear in mind that, according to some historical narratives, there is a gap of **two thousand six hundred and forty years** between the two of them, and that there was no prophet during that period except Hud and Salih (peace be upon them). (Maʿārif cites *Kashshāf*, p. 48, v. 4.)

Sit with that. Across a span that some historical narratives put at more than two and a half thousand years, with only those two prophets named in between, Allah still describes Ibrahim (peace be upon him) as being *of Nuh's shīʿah*. On the definition Maʿārif gives, what makes people one party is similarity in basic concepts and methods — and here Maʿārif specifies the substance of it: perfect agreement on the basic principles of faith.

## Ayah 84: the heart he came with

*"˹Remember˺ when he came to his Lord with a pure heart."*

**"He came to his Lord."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *coming to his Lord* here means "to turn to Allah, to zero in one's attention towards Him and to worship Him." So it is not a matter of physical arrival, but of the whole self turning in one direction.

**"With a qalb salīm."** Ibn Kathir's translation leaves the word standing as *Salim*, and the early commentators he cites explain it in several ways. Four statements are gathered there:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (may Allah be pleased with him): "This means that he bore witness that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah."
- **Muhammad bin Sirin**, when ʿAwf asked him what the *Salim* heart is (recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim): "One which knows that Allah is true and that the Hour will undoubtedly come to pass, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves."
- **Al-Hasan**: "One that is free from Shirk."
- **ʿUrwah**: "One that is not cursed."

These are set down in Ibn Kathir as they stand, one after another, without one being preferred over the others. It is worth reading each on its own terms and letting it sit.

**And here is the point Maʿārif draws out.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that "with a pure heart" is placed as a *restriction* — and that by placing this restriction, it has been indicated that **no act of devotion (ʿibādah) to Allah is acceptable until the heart of the devotee is cleansed pure from false beliefs and ill intentions.** Maʿārif spells out both halves of that:

- If a certain act of devotion is performed while **laced with some false belief**, then no matter how hard the devotee has worked in the process, it will still not be acceptable.
- And if the devotee's main purpose happens **not** to be the seeking of the sole pleasure of Allah — but is a simple show off, or some material gain — then that act of devotion is not praiseworthy.

"The passion with which Sayyidna Ibrahim (peace be upon him) turned towards Allah," Maʿārif concludes, "was free of all such adulterations."

## Ayah 85: he begins with a question

*"…and said to his father and his people, 'What are you worshipping?'"*

Ibn Kathir's comment on these words is direct: **he denounced his people for their worship of idols and false gods**.

Notice who is addressed: **"his father and his people."** The man closest to him and the wider community, named together in the ayah itself. And notice the form the denunciation takes — not a statement or a threat, but a question: *mādhā taʿbudūn*, "What is it that which you worship?" And the two ayat that follow are questions as well.

## Ayah 86: what they desire is called a falsehood

*"Is it false gods that you desire instead of Allah?"*

Ibn Kathir renders the Arabic — *a-ifkan ālihatan dūna'llāhi turīdūn* — as **"Is it a falsehood – gods other than Allah – that you desire?"**

This is the continuation of the denunciation Ibn Kathir described at ayah 85. The wording itself is the argument: what they are pursuing is named a **falsehood** (*ifk*), and the "gods other than Allah" they set up are exactly that falsehood. Nothing further is added by way of proof — the question is left for them to answer.

## Ayah 87: the question he does not answer

*"What then do you expect from the Lord of all worlds?"*

*Fa-mā ẓannukum bi-rabbi'l-ʿālamīn.* Ibn Kathir renders it, "Then what think you about the Lord of the all that exists?" and quotes Qatadah's explanation: "This means, 'what do you think He will do with you when you meet Him, given that you worshipped others alongside Him?'"

So the question is about a meeting. On Qatadah's reading, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is not describing a punishment; he is asking them what they suppose will be done with them when they stand before their Lord, having worshipped others alongside Him. The answer is left to them to supply.

## Living it

**The heart is the qualifying condition, not a bonus.** Maʿārif's reading of ayah 84 is the most immediately practical thing in this passage: an act of devotion laced with false belief is not acceptable no matter how hard the devotee has laboured at it, and an act done for show or for material gain rather than for Allah's sole pleasure is not praiseworthy. Before adding to what we do, this passage asks us to look at what we are doing it *with*.

**Belonging is by shared conviction.** Ayah 83 names Ibrahim (peace be upon him) as being of the shīʿah of Nuh (peace be upon him) across a gap that some historical narratives put at two thousand six hundred and forty years, with only Hud and Salih (peace be upon them) named in between. What Maʿārif identifies as the bond is similarity in basic concepts and methods, and perfect agreement on the basic principles of faith.

**Start with those closest, and start by asking.** Ayah 85 has Ibrahim (peace be upon him) addressing his own father alongside his people, and ayat 85–87 have him putting his case as questions — the last of which, on Qatadah's explanation, asks them what they think will be done with them when they meet Allah.

**Keep the meeting in view.** Muhammad bin Sirin's answer about the *Salim* heart included knowing that the Hour will undoubtedly come to pass and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves — and ayah 87, as Qatadah explains it, is a question precisely about that meeting.

passages.title: Abraham turns from the stars to the silent idols
passages.tafsir:
Five ayat cover a single episode. Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān read them together: a festival day in the city of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), an excuse that leaves him behind while everyone else goes out, and then his approach to statues with two questions they cannot answer.

## The occasion: a festival and a counter-plan

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the background that the Qur'an here leaves unspoken. Ibrahim's people held a festival on a particular day, and when the day came they invited him to come along. Their purpose, the commentary says, was that if he joined them he might be impressed with them and forget about calling them to his faith (the report is traced to ad-Durr ul-Manthūr, Ibn Jarīr and others).

But Ibrahim had something else on his mind. As Ibn Kathir puts it, the time was approaching for them to go out to celebrate a festival of theirs, and he wanted to be alone with their gods so that he could break them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the aim behind the plan: while the people were away at their festival he would have the time to go into their temple, so that when they returned they would see the helplessness of their false gods with their own eyes. It was quite possible, the commentary adds, that such a scene would light someone's heart with the spark of true faith, and that he would repent and shy away from shirk. The aim was never destruction for its own sake; it was their guidance.

So he needed to stay behind — and ayah 90 tells us the excuse worked: *"So they turned their backs on him and went away."* Ibn Kathir comments on this ayah that he went to the idols after they had left, "quickly and secretly."

## Ayah 88: why a glance at the stars deserved a whole ayah

*"He later looked up to the stars ˹in contemplation˺."*

One answer, reported by some commentators, is that it was simply a matter of chance — a man with something important on his mind sometimes starts looking at the sky quite unintentionally. Invited to the festival, Ibrahim was left thinking how to excuse himself, and it was in that state of indecision that the glance happened, with his answer following after. Ibn Kathir preserves a version of this from Qatādah, who said, "The Arabs say of one who thinks deeply that he is looking at the stars"; what Qatādah meant, Ibn Kathir explains, is that he looked at the heavens thinking of a way to distract his people. Al-Hasan al-Basrī's account, recorded by Ibn Abī Hātim, has the same texture: his people went out to their festival and wanted to make him go out too, so he lay down on his back, said *"Verily, I am sick,"* and started looking at the sky; when they had gone out, he turned to their gods and broke them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges this explanation difficult to call correct, for two reasons.

**First, the Qur'an's manner of narration.** Its style is to limit itself to the important and necessary units of an event and leave off unnecessary details. In these very ayat whole units of the story are elided — even the entire background of the festival invitation is not spelt out. It is not possible, then, to believe that the Qur'an would leave out the background of the event lest the account grow too long, and yet take an absolutely involuntary action, not even distantly related to the event, and give it a whole ayah.

**Second, the preposition.** The text says **فِي النُّجُوم** (*fī an-nujūm*), literally "*into* the stars," not **إِلَى النُّجُوم** (*ilā an-nujūm*), "*towards* the stars." According to the grammatical rules of Arabic, the commentary notes, an involuntary glance in the sky's direction would call for *ilā*. What the text actually gives is a full, animated look — a looking *into* the stars.

So what was the expedient consideration behind the look? Most commentators answer: his people believed in astrology and used to do everything they had to do by looking at the stars. By answering them in that way, Ibrahim let them understand that what he said about his indisposition rested on his assessment of the movement of the stars, exactly the kind of grounds they would find trustworthy. And note the restraint in it: he was not a believer in astrology personally; he made no verbal reference to astrology, and never declared that he was drawing on knowledge of the stars. What he did was no more than look at the stars rather fully — which is why, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, this had no aspect of some lie in it either. Maulānā Ashraf Thānavī followed this same interpretation in Bayān ul-Qur'ān.

Did this not risk encouraging his people in a false science — people who not only believed in astrology but took the stars to be effective agents in the events of the world? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the likelihood of such encouragement would exist only if he had not clearly warned them about their erroneous conduct later on. In fact this entire plan was enacted for the sole purpose that the invitation to pure monotheism be communicated to them in the most effective manner possible, and it was after a short while that he laid bare every possible error of their conduct before them. Considered ambiguity for a purpose like that, the commentary concludes, is based on nothing but wisdom, and no reasonable objection can be raised against it.

## Astrology, weighed by the Shariah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out what Islam does and does not accept here.

This much is a settled matter: Allah has placed specific properties in the sun, the moon and the stars that affect human lives, some of them observable by anyone — the feeling of heat or cold as the sun draws near or far, the high and low tides of the seas with the waxing and waning of the moon. Beyond that, positions divide. Some commentators limit themselves to what common observation yields. Others say there are additional and particular properties in the position and movement of the stars which affect most human matters; and among those, some believe the stars are the sole effective agents in all success and failure, while others say there is no effective agent but Allah, who has endowed the stars with such properties so that, like other causes, they too serve as a cause of human success and failure.

**The false position is clear.** Those who believe the events and revolutions of the world depend on the stars alone and they alone decide what happens, hold a notion that is wrong and false without any doubt — a belief that takes one to the borderline of shirk, the ascribing of partners to the pristine divinity of Allah. This was the kind of belief the people of Arabia entertained about rainfall: a particular star (*nawʼ*) brought the rain and was itself the effective agent in the matter. The Prophet ﷺ strongly refuted this belief, and the detailed description of that refutation appears in ahadith.

**The intermediate position is not shirk**, but it is fenced in. Those who hold that Allah is the ultimate effective agent in world events, while allowing that He has endowed the stars with properties affecting human lives in the degree of a general cause, stand on the same ground as saying that Allah alone brings rain while clouds are its obvious cause. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges that this thinking is no shirk, and that neither the Qur'an nor the Hadith confirms or rejects it — so it is not too far out to think that Allah may have embedded some such effects in the position, movement, rising and setting of the stars.

**What is prohibited** is acquiring the knowledge of astrology in order to pursue and discover those effects, then placing reliance on that knowledge and issuing decrees about the future on its basis; the ahadith forbid this. According to a narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, the Prophet ﷺ said: *"When destiny is mentioned — observe restraint; and when stars are mentioned — observe restraint; and when my Companions are mentioned — observe restraint"* — that is, do not deliberate or debate or dwell on differences (ʿIrāqī on Iḥyā' ul-ʿUlūm, with reference to Tabarānī, and rating as *hasan*). And ʿUmar said: *"Acquire knowledge of stars to the extent you are guided right on land and at sea — then, stop"* (Iḥyā' ul-ʿUlūm, al-Ghazālī). This prohibition does not require rejecting that the stars have properties and effects at all; what is prohibited is the relentless digging into them and the wasting of precious time in hankering after them.

Discussing this subject in Iḥyā' ul-ʿUlūm, Imām al-Ghazālī identified several elements of wisdom behind the prohibition. **The first** lies in a person's accelerated devotion to the subject: experience bears out that he gradually starts taking the stars as the be-all and end-all of everything, and that false perception then drags him on to the polytheistic belief of taking the stars as the real effective agents. **Another** is that even if Allah has placed some properties and effects in the stars, we have no certain source of knowledge about them except through *wahy*, revelation. It appears in ahadith about Idrīs (peace be upon him) that Allah had given him some knowledge of this nature — but knowledge based on revelation of that sort is no longer in this world. Whatever the so-called experts have with them is merely a collection of inferences, conjectures and whims from which no certain knowledge can be acquired, which is why countless predictions of astrologers keep being proved false. Someone made a lively comment on the field: *the useful of it is unknown, and the known of it is useless.* ʿAllāmah Ālūsī, in his Tafsīr Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, cited several historical cases where events that should have transpired one way under the accepted rules of astrology transpired almost contrarily, so that many great people who devoted their lives to it were finally compelled to confess that the field's ultimate end is no more than conjecture and estimation; he quotes the famous astrologer Koshyār Dailamī, in *al-Mujmal fi-l-Aḥkām*, that astrology is a field not supported by evidence, proof or argument, with a lot of leeway for human scruples and conjectures. More serious still, false pride in it pushes some of its votaries into claiming that they have knowledge of the unseen (*al-ghayb*). **A further reason** is that it lets a dear life be consumed in a pursuit with no benefit in the real sense — and running after something useless for no valid reason is totally against the spirit and temperament of the Shariah.

## Ayah 89: "I am really sick" — and the question of truthfulness

Ibn Kathir explains **سَقِيم** (*saqīm*) here as "weak," and notes that Ibrahim told his people something that was true, for he was indeed sick of the implications of what they believed in — one reported meaning of the words being, *I am sick at heart of your worshipping idols instead of Allah.*

Ibn Kathir then cites a hadith that Ibn Jarīr narrates from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Ibrahim (peace and blessings be upon him) did not lie except in three cases: two of them for the sake of Allah — his words *"Verily, I am sick,"* and his words *"Nay, this one, the biggest of them, did it"* — and the third when he said concerning Sarah, *"She is my sister."* Ibn Kathir says this hadith is recorded in the books of the Sahih and Sunan with various chains of narration, and immediately guards it: this is not the kind of real lie for which a person is to be condemned — Allah forbid. One calls it a lie for lack of a better word, because it is abstruse speech used for a legitimate religious purpose.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works the same problem more finely. Was he really sick at that time? The Qur'an gives no clarification; but from a hadith of the Sahih of al-Bukhari it seems he was not so sick as would make him unable to go with his people. The majority of commentators answer that he employed **تَوْرِيَة** (*tauriyah*), equivocation — saying something whose apparent sense runs counter to the actual fact, while the speaker means a remote sense in it that does match the fact. On what exactly he meant, the commentators differ:

- **Instinctive aversion at their shirk.** This view is supported by the word chosen: *saqīm* is much lighter than **مَرِيض** (*marīḍ*, "sick"), closer to English "indisposed."
- **"I am going to be sick."** In Arabic the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) is frequently used for the future tense. The Qur'an itself says, addressing the Prophet ﷺ, **إِنَّكَ مَيِّتٌ وَإِنَّهُم مَّيِّتُونَ** — literally "you too are dead and they too are dead," meaning *certainly, you will die and they will die* (az-Zumar 39:30). On this reading Ibrahim meant that sickness would come to him, since one has to fall sick at some time or other well before death.
- **A real but minor indisposition** — the explanation Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls most reasonable and satisfactory: he really was somewhat indisposed at the time, though not so much as would have prevented his going, and he mentioned that casual indisposition in a particular setting where his listeners concluded he was suffering from some major disease and was truly unable to come.

Either way, the word *kadhibah* ("lie") used of this statement in the hadith of Bukhari means *tauriyah* — something with the apparent form of a lie that is no lie in terms of the sense the speaker intends. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some narrations of that same hadith carry the additional words: *out of these, there is no lie that has not been spoken for the sake of defending and supporting the religion of Allah.*

## Ayat 91–92: two questions no idol can answer

*"Then he ˹stealthily˺ advanced towards their gods, and said ˹mockingly˺, 'Will you not eat? What is wrong with you that you cannot speak?'"*

Ibn Kathir explains that **food had been placed before the idols as a sacrifice, so that the food might be blessed**. So when Ibrahim looked at the food that was before them, his first question was the obvious one — *Will you not eat?* Then the second, sharper: *What is the matter with you that you speak not?*

He is not really asking. He is inviting the stone to prove it is more than stone, and the silence in that empty temple is the whole argument. And because the offering was laid there precisely to draw blessing from them, their inability even to touch it makes the claim collapse at the exact point where it was meant to work.

Ibn Kathir observes that the story is told here in brief, while Sūrah al-Anbiyā' tells it in more detail.

## What this passage asks of us

**Wisdom belongs to the work of calling people to Allah.** Ibrahim chose the occasion, secured the conditions, and worked so that the invitation to pure monotheism could be communicated in the most effective manner possible — and the aim throughout was their guidance, that someone's heart might be lit with the spark of true faith and turn away from shirk.

**Where there is genuine need, veiled speech is permitted.** From these very ayat Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives the ruling that resorting to *tauriyah* on occasions of need is permissible, in two forms. Verbal *tauriyah* is saying something whose apparent sense is counter to the fact while its inward sense corresponds to it. Practical *tauriyah* — also called *īhām* — is acting in a manner that makes an onlooker read one's intention in a certain way while one's real intention is quite different; on the view of most commentators, Ibrahim's look towards the stars was *īhām*, and calling himself *saqīm* was verbal *tauriyah*. Both kinds stand proved from the Prophet ﷺ in person. On his journey of hijrah, while the disbelievers were looking for him frantically, someone on the road asked Abū Bakr about him, and Abū Bakr answered, "He is my guide; he shows me the way" — the listener gathered that he meant some ordinary desert pathfinder and did not bother further, while Abū Bakr had still not surrendered the truth that this was his guide in religion. And Kaʿb ibn Mālik reports that when the Prophet ﷺ had to go in a certain direction for jihad, he would come out of Madinah marching towards some other direction, so that onlookers would not find out the destination he was really headed for (Sahih Muslim and others). *Tauriyah* is proved of him ﷺ in light humour too: according to a narration from the Shamā'il of Tirmidhi, he ﷺ said humorously to an old woman that no old woman will go to Paradise; when she became very anxious, he explained that he meant no old woman goes there *in the state of her old age* — she goes there after having been turned young.

Note the condition the commentary attaches: *occasions of need*. Every case above carries one — protecting a hunted life, shielding a military movement, clearing space for the call to pure monotheism. The words themselves stay true; it is only the hearer's inference that is left free to wander.

**Finally, weigh where your reliance sits.** Ibrahim's people used to do everything they had to do by looking at the stars; he looked at them once, and only as a device, without believing in astrology at all. The passage sets the two ways side by side: consulting created things about our affairs, or holding to the truth that there is no effective agent but Allah. And it leaves two questions hanging in a silent temple — *Will you not eat? What is the matter with you that you speak not?*

passages.title: The idols struck, and the argument that follows
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the turning point of Ibrahim's story in this surah: alone with the idols his people worship, he smashes them; the crowd comes racing back at him; and instead of defending himself he puts a question to them that cannot be answered. What holds the passage together is a single movement — **from action to argument**. Ayah 93 is the deed, ayah 94 is the reaction, and ayat 95 and 96 are the reasoning the deed was designed to make unavoidable.

## The scene just before

Ayah 93 begins with "then," so a word about what it follows. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the background: Ibrahim's people held a festival on a particular day, and when the day came they invited him along, hoping that if he joined the celebration he might be impressed by it and let go of his call to faith. Ibrahim had something else in mind. He wanted the occasion for himself — when they had all gone out he would have time to go into their temple and break their idols, so that on their return they would see the helplessness of their false gods with their own eyes. The aim was not vandalism; it was that some heart among them might be lit with the spark of true faith and turn away from shirk.

Ibn Kathir's comment on the moment of departure is quietly vivid: after they had left, he went to the idols *quickly and secretly*. Al-Hasan Al-Basri described the same sequence — Ibrahim lay down on his back, said he was sick, and kept looking at the sky; when they had gone out, he turned to their gods and broke them (recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim).

And the two ayat immediately before ours are the irony that sets up the blow. Food had been placed before the idols as an offering, so that the food might be blessed. Ibrahim looked at that spread and asked the statues, "Will you not eat? What is the matter with you that you speak not?" A god that cannot lift a morsel laid at its feet, and cannot answer a question put to its face, has already been refuted before a single blow falls.

## Ayah 93: the striking

فَرَاغَ عَلَيْهِمْ ضَرْبًا بِالْيَمِينِ — "Then he turned upon them, striking them with his right hand."

Two renderings of the opening verb are reported. Al-Farra' explained it as *he started to hit them with his right hand*. Qatadah and Al-Jawhari explained it as *he turned to them, hitting them with his right hand*. Either way the picture is of real striking, not a symbolic gesture.

Why does the ayah specify **the right hand**? Ibn Kathir answers plainly: he struck them with his right hand because the right hand is stronger and more powerful. The detail tells you he was not being delicate. And the result, Ibn Kathir says, was that he left them broken to pieces — all except the biggest of them, which was left *so that they might turn to it*. For that point Ibn Kathir refers the reader back to his own commentary on Surat Al-Anbiya' rather than retelling it here, so we will leave it where he left it: the largest idol was spared on purpose, and its survival was part of the plan.

## Ayah 94: the crowd comes running

فَأَقْبَلُوا إِلَيْهِ يَزِفُّونَ — "Then they came hastily towards him."

Mujahid and others explained *yaziffūn* as: **they came rushing**. Picture a crowd returning from a festival to find their sanctuary in ruins, then converging on one man at speed.

Ibn Kathir notes that the story is told here in brief, while in Surat Al-Anbiya' it is told in more detail — and he adds, in his commentary on this ayah, that when they returned they did not at first know who had done this, until they investigated and found out that it was Ibrahim. So these three words compress an entire sequence: the discovery, the questioning, the identification, the mob.

And then the reversal. In Ibn Kathir's words, **they came to rebuke him, and he started rebuking and criticising them** — and what he said to them is ayah 95. The accused takes over the courtroom. This is the hinge of the passage: the smashed idols were never the argument itself; they were the exhibit that made the argument impossible to dodge.

## Ayat 95–96: the argument

أَتَعْبُدُونَ مَا تَنْحِتُونَ — "Do you worship what you carve?"

The force is in the verb *tanḥitūn*, from the carving and chiselling of stone or wood. Ibn Kathir spells the meaning out: do you worship, instead of Allah, idols which you yourselves carve and fashion with your own hands? Not "idols you inherited," not "idols that came down from heaven" — objects whose entire existence, shape and features passed through your own fingers. You know exactly where they came from, because you made them. The question is not seeking information; it is meant to make them hear their own practice said out loud.

Then ayah 96 removes any escape: وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ — "while Allah has created you and what you make."

The carver is himself something carved. The worshipper is a creature, the object is the handiwork of a creature, and the only Creator in the room is the One they have set aside.

**A point of language.** Ibn Kathir notes that *wa mā taʿmalūn* may be read in two ways: "Allah has created you **and what you do**" — that is, your deeds — or "Allah has created you **and what you make**" — that is, the manufactured idols. He says both views are synonymous in import, and that the former is the more apparent, because of the report recorded by Al-Bukhari in the book *Afʿāl al-ʿIbād* from Hudhayfah, attributed to the Prophet ﷺ:

> "Allah has created every doer of deeds and what he does."

— after which, Ibn Kathir relates, he recited this very ayah. So on the reading Ibn Kathir considers more apparent, the ayah is not only demolishing idol-carving; it is stating that the doer and the doing both fall under Allah's creating.

**How they answered.** Ibn Kathir draws the immediate consequence: when the proof had been established against them, they resolved to seize him by force, saying, "Build for him a building" — that is, a furnace — "and throw him into the blazing fire!" They had no counter-argument, so they reached for violence. And Allah's verdict, in the ayah that follows: "So they plotted a plot against him, but We made them the lowest." Allah saved him from the fire, caused him to prevail over them, and made his proof supreme and supported it.

That is worth sitting with. The argument of ayat 95 and 96 was so sound that the only available reply was to try to burn the man who made it — and the outcome of that attempt was that the plotters, not the lone believer, ended up at the bottom.

## Living it

**Nothing made can be worshipped.** The test Ibrahim applies in ayah 95 is simply: where did this thing come from? If you can trace a thing's existence to human hands, you already know it is not a lord. That test does not expire with stone statues; it applies to anything a person builds up and then bows to.

**The maker is himself made.** Ayah 96 goes one step behind the idol, to the man holding the chisel. Whatever hands and skill went into shaping the statue were themselves created by the One being neglected. It is a humbling thought for anyone impressed with what he has produced.

**Proof first, then patience.** Ibn Kathir describes the sequence exactly: the proof was established against them, and only then did they reach for force. When the truth has been made plain and the reply is anger rather than argument, that is not a sign the argument failed.

**And courage.** Perhaps the most striking thing in ayah 94 is what Ibrahim did *not* do. A furious crowd is bearing down on him and he neither runs nor apologises; he asks them a question. When you are certain of what you are standing on, you do not need the crowd's permission to say it.

passages.title: The furnace built, and the plotters humiliated
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the moment Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) confrontation with his people turns from argument into force. He has just taken their religion apart with a question they cannot answer, and in ayah 97 they answer him not with a counter-argument but with a construction project: *"Build for him a building and throw him into the blazing fire!"* Ayah 98 then tells us in one short clause how that project ended — *"And so they sought to harm him, but We made them inferior."* The two ayat belong together as scheme and outcome: human plotting in the first, the divine reversal of it in the second.

## The argument that left them nothing to say

To feel ayah 97 you have to hear what came immediately before it. Ibn Kathir walks through the sequence. Ibrahim excused himself from his people's festival, stayed behind in the city while they went out, and went to their idols "quickly and secretly." He put the questions to them that no idol can answer — *"Will you not eat? What is the matter with you that you speak not?"* (ayat 91–92) — and then *"he turned upon them, striking them with his right hand"* (ayah 93), leaving them broken to pieces, all but the biggest of them, so that his people might turn to it. When they came back "rushing" (Mujāhid's gloss on ayah 94) to rebuke him, he rebuked them instead: *"Do you worship that which you carve?"* (ayah 95) — which Ibn Kathir explains as: do you worship, instead of Allah, idols that you yourselves carve and fashion with your own hands? And then ayah 96: *"While Allah has created you and what you make!"*

At that point Ibn Kathir writes a single sentence that is the hinge of the whole passage: **"When the proof had been established against them, they resolved to seize him by force."** Ayah 97 is not a rival argument. It is what people reach for when their position can no longer be argued for. They had nothing left to say, so they built something instead.

## Ayah 97: "Build for him a building"

Their decision, in the Arabic, is *ibnū lahu bunyānan fa-alqūhu fī l-jaḥīm.* Ibn Kathir glosses the *bunyān* — the "building" — as a **furnace**. They do not say "light a fire." They say *build*. That single word carries planning, materials and labour in it: this is a considered, communal response, not a mob's flash of temper. And the translation renders their words as spoken to one another — an instruction passed around a group. *Al-jaḥīm* is what the structure is for: "the blazing fire."

It is worth noticing what the passage sets side by side. In ayah 95 they were rebuked for worshipping what their own hands carve; in ayah 97 their answer to that rebuke is to have their hands build something else. Their gods came out of their own workshop, and now so does their verdict.

## Ayah 98: "but We made them inferior"

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah: *"So, they plotted a plot against him, but We made them the lowest."*

What the ayah records of their side is the plot — the design against him. And that is all it records. The Qur'an here does not narrate the fire at all. Ibn Kathir does not retell it either; he simply refers the reader back to what he had already explained at Sūrat al-Anbiyā' 21:68–70, and sums up the outcome in one line: **Allah saved him from the fire and caused him to prevail over them, making his proof supreme and supporting it.**

Then the speaker changes. The verb of the first half is theirs — *they* plotted; the verb of the second half is Allah's — *"**We** made them the lowest."* And the word for what became of them is *al-asfalīn*: **the lowest**. They set out to put Ibrahim in the lowest place — down inside a furnace — and it was they who were left lowest. Read with Ibn Kathir's two-part summary, that lowness has two faces: the fire failed to touch him, and his argument stood over theirs, upheld by Allah.

## "Allah has created you and what you make"

This is where the passage quietly becomes doctrine, and it explains why ayah 98 can afford to be so brief. On ayah 96 Ibn Kathir gives two readings of *wa-Llāhu khalaqakum wa mā taʿmalūn*: it may mean "Allah has created you and what you **do**" — your actions — or "Allah has created you and what you **make**" — the idols themselves. He says both views are synonymous, and holds the first to be the more apparent of the two, on the strength of the report recorded by al-Bukhārī in the Book *Afʿāl al-ʿIbād* from Hudhayfah, attributed to the Prophet ﷺ: **"Allah has created every doer of deeds and what he does"** — after which he recited this very ayah.

Hold that next to ayah 97. The builders and their building, the plotters and their plotting, are themselves inside Allah's creation. Their furnace was never a power standing outside His reach that He then had to overcome. That is why the ayah needs only "but We made them the lowest," and no drama.

## Wisdom on one side, a furnace on the other

The contrast with that furnace is sharpened by how carefully Ibrahim had handled his own side of the affair. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the background the Qur'an compresses: his people held a festival on a particular day and invited him along, hoping (as Maʿārif reports, citing ad-Durr ul-Manthūr, Ibn Jarīr and others) that he might be won over by it and drop his call to faith. He had a different use for the day — to go into their temple while the town was away and break the idols, so that on their return they would see the helplessness of their gods with their own eyes, and perhaps someone's heart would catch the spark of true faith and turn away from shirk.

His refusal, the commentators say, was *tauriyah* — equivocation: "to say something that is apparently counter to the actual fact, but the speaker means a remote sense in it that matches the actual fact." His full look at the stars was the practical form of the same thing (called *īhām*), since his people ran their affairs by the stars and would find an answer given after such a look credible — though he neither mentioned astrology nor claimed to be relying on it. On what he inwardly meant by *"I am indisposed,"* Maʿārif reports the differing views rather than settling on one: that it expressed his instinctive aversion to their idolatry — supported by his choosing the lighter word *saqīm* over *marīḍ* ("sick"); or that it meant "I am going to be sick," since Arabic often uses this participle form for the future (as in *innaka mayyitun*, "you will die," Az-Zumar 39:30); or — the explanation Maʿārif calls most reasonable — that he really was somewhat indisposed, just not so unwell as to prevent his going, and he mentioned it in a setting where his hearers took it for something serious. Ibn Kathir's own note is in the same spirit: he told them something that was true, "for he was indeed sick of the implications of what they believed in."

This is the setting of the hadith that Ibn Kathir's passage here reports **Ibn Jarīr** as having narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Ibrahim (peace and blessings be upon him) did not lie except in three cases. Two were for the sake of Allah: (one is) when he said, 'Verily, I am sick'; and (the second) when he said, 'Nay, this one, the biggest of them (idols) did it'; and (the third) when he said concerning Sarah, 'She is my sister.'" Ibn Kathir adds that this hadith is recorded in the books of the Ṣaḥīḥ and Sunan with various chains of narration; Maʿārif refers to it as a hadith of the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī. Both are emphatic that this is not lying in the blameworthy sense — Ibn Kathir: "this is not the kind of real lie for which a person is to be condemned – Allah forbid! One calls it a lie for lack of a better word, because it is abstruse speech used for a legitimate religious purpose." Maʿārif notes that in some narrations of this same hadith these words also appear: "Out of these, there is no lie that has not been spoken for the sake of defending and supporting the religion of Allah."

From this Maʿārif derives the ruling that *tauriyah*, in both its verbal and its practical form, is permissible on occasions of need, and points to the Prophet's ﷺ own practice. On the journey of hijrah, when someone on the road asked Abū Bakr about the Prophet ﷺ, he answered, "He is my guide. He shows me the way" — and the listener, taking him for an ordinary hired desert guide, did not bother and went his way, while Abū Bakr had surrendered nothing of the truth. Kaʿb ibn Mālik reported likewise that when the Prophet ﷺ had to set out in a certain direction for jihad, he would leave Madinah marching in some other direction, so that onlookers would not find out where he was really headed (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and others).

## Living it

**When your evidence is answered with force, that is a verdict on them, not on you.** Ibn Kathir's line — that they resolved to seize him by force once the proof had been established against them — is a diagnostic. Coercion arriving in place of a reply is what a losing position looks like.

**Calling people to Allah is allowed to be strategic.** Ibrahim chose his day, his timing, his wording. Maʿārif's judgement is that "this method of considered ambiguity for the purpose in sight is based on nothing but wisdom — and no reasonable objection can be raised against it."

**But strategy that never gets to the plain truth is not this strategy.** Maʿārif answers the worry that his star-gazing might have encouraged his people's astrology by pointing out that "it was after a short while that Ibrahim laid bare every possible error of their conduct before his people." The whole manoeuvre existed to buy him the chance to say it plainly. If our tact never arrives at the message, it is not his tact.

**And what is built against you is not outside Allah's hand.** They plotted; He made. Their design against Ibrahim survives in the Qur'an only as a plot that came to nothing, while the man they meant to burn is the one whose proof Allah made supreme and supported. That is the comfort ayah 98 is offering to anyone standing where he stood, with far less at stake.

passages.title: A son granted, and the command both accepted
passages.tafsir:
What holds these five ayat together is a single movement of surrender: a man gives up his people, asks Allah for a family in their place, is granted a son — and is then asked to give that son back. And it ends, in ayah 103, with *both* of them submitting.

## Ayah 99: walking away from everything

Ibn Kathir explains that this comes after Allah had helped His close friend Ibrahim, peace be upon him, against his people, and after Ibrahim had given up hope that they would ever believe, despite all the mighty signs they had witnessed. So he emigrated away from them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail that stings: he said this at a time when he was totally disappointed by his countrymen — nobody except his nephew Lut, peace be upon him, was willing to believe in him.

**"I am going to my Lord."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the statement to mean that he will leave the abode of disbelief and go to a place whereto Allah has commanded him to go, a place where he will be able to worship his Lord in peace. He set out accompanied by his wife Sarah, may Allah be pleased with her, and his nephew Lut, peace be upon him; after passing through different areas of Iraq, he finally reached Syria.

## Ayah 100: the prayer of a man with no family left

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibrahim had no children until then, and that this is precisely why the prayer of ayah 100 follows the departure of ayah 99. Ibn Kathir's reading of **"My Lord, grant me from the righteous"** is that he was asking for obedient children *in compensation for his people and relatives whom he had left behind*. He asks not simply for a son, but for offspring "from the righteous" (*min aṣ-ṣāliḥīn*).

## Ayah 101: "a forbearing boy"

The prayer was answered, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, and Allah gave him the good news of the birth of a son. But look at the single adjective Allah chooses in ayah 101: *ḥalīm*, forbearing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: by saying "forbearing," it was indicated that this newborn would demonstrate such patience, self-control and forbearance in his life as would be exemplary in the world.

On the background of the birth, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that when Sarah, may Allah be pleased with her, realised she was not being blessed with children, she took herself to be barren; Pharaoh had given his daughter Hajirah, may Allah be pleased with her, as a gift to Sarah so that she could help her with household chores, and Sarah in turn passed Hajirah on as a gift to Ibrahim, who married her. The son mentioned here was born to Hajirah, and he was named Ismaʿil, peace be upon him.

## Which son was it?

Ibn Kathir treats this as settled: this child was Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, for he was the first child of whom glad tidings were given to Ibrahim, and he was older than Ishaq.

**The arithmetic.** The Muslims and the People of the Book agree, and it is stated in their own Book, that Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, was born when Ibrahim was eighty-six years old, and Ishaq was born when Ibrahim was ninety-nine.

**Their own wording.** According to their Book, Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice his *only* son — and in another text, his *firstborn* son. Ibn Kathir argues that the name Ishaq was then falsely inserted, which goes against what their own Scripture says; the insertion was made because Ishaq is their ancestor while Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, is the ancestor of the Arabs, and out of jealousy the phrase "only son" was changed to mean "the only son who is with you," since Ismaʿil had been taken with his mother to Makkah. Ibn Kathir calls this a case of falsification and distortion, because the words "only son" cannot be said except of one who has no other son. He adds: the firstborn son has a special status that is not shared by subsequent children, so the command to sacrifice *him* is a more exquisite test.

**The argument from the Qur'an itself.** Ibn Ishaq said he often heard Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Qurazi say that the son Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice was Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, reasoning from the Book of Allah: when Allah finishes the story of the son who was to be sacrificed, He *then* says, "And We gave him the glad tidings of Ishaq — a Prophet from the righteous," and elsewhere, "So We gave her glad tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, of Yaʿqub" (11:71). Allah mentions the son and the son of the son. He would not have commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice Ishaq when He had promised that this very son would in turn have a son.

Ibn Ishaq reports that Muhammad bin Kaʿb put this to ʿUmar bin ʿAbd al-ʿAziz when he was Khalifah, while with him in Syria. ʿUmar answered, "This is something about which I have never given any thought, but I see that it is as you say," and then sent for a Jew who had become a Muslim, committed to Islam, and whom he thought had been one of their scholars. Asked which of the two sons of Ibrahim was commanded to be sacrificed, the man replied: "Ismaʿil. By Allah, O Commander of the faithful, the Jews know this, but they were jealous of you Arabs because it was your father about whom Allah issued this command."

Ibn Kathir then stacks up the transmission: Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Mujahid, ash-Shaʿbi, Yusuf bin Mihran, and al-Hasan al-Basri — who did not doubt it — along with a longer list gathered by Ibn Abi Hatim including ʿAli, Abu Hurayrah and Saʿid bin al-Musayyib, may Allah be pleased with them all. ʿAbdullah, the son of Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal, records asking his father directly which son was to be sacrificed, Ismaʿil or Ishaq, and Ahmad answered: "Ismaʿil" — mentioned in Kitab az-Zuhd. Ibn Abi Hatim said he heard his own father say, "The correct view is that the one who was to be sacrificed was Ismaʿil, peace be upon him."

Imam Ahmad recorded, through Safiyyah bint Shaybah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for ʿUthman bin Talhah, may Allah be pleased with him, and told him: *"I saw the horns of the ram when I entered the House, and I forgot to tell you to cover them up; cover them up, for there should not be anything in the House which could distract the worshipper."* Ibn Kathir treats this as independent evidence that the one to be sacrificed was Ismaʿil, peace be upon him: the Quraysh had inherited the horns of the ram that Ibrahim sacrificed, passed down from generation to generation until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent — and ash-Shaʿbi said plainly, "It was Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, and I saw the horns of the ram in the Kaʿbah." And Allah knows best.

## Ayah 102: "when he was old enough to work with him"

Ibn Kathir explains *fa-lammā balagha maʿahu as-saʿy* as the boy growing up and beginning to go about and walk with his father, and reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid bin Jubayr, ʿAta' al-Khurasani, Zayd bin Aslam and others that it means he became a young man and was able to work as his father did. Commentators put his age at thirteen years at that time; some others say he had crossed the age of puberty (Tafsir Mazhari, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows why Allah includes this clause at all: it measures the weight of the test. He was commanded to sacrifice the son he had so wistfully prayed for at a time when the boy was old enough to walk by the side of his father, and the days when he could become his father's right arm were not far. Ibn Kathir fills in the geography — Ibrahim used to go every so often to check on his son and his mother in the land of Faran, that is, Makkah, to see how they were doing; it was said that he used to ride on al-Buraq, and Allah knows best.

**Why a dream, and not a spoken command?** ʿUbayd bin ʿUmayr said, "The dreams of the Prophets are revelation," and then recited this very ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Qurtubi that from some narrations it appears the dream was shown on three consecutive days, and then gives two reasons for this mode of revelation.

First, from Tafsir Kabir: a command given through a dream could leave a great deal of room for interpretations and excuses by the human self. Ibrahim took none of them. He simply bowed down before the command of his Lord, without interpretation and without hesitation.

Second: the purpose was neither that Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, actually be slaughtered, nor that Ibrahim be bound to complete it, but that he do everything on his part that leads up to it. Had the command been given verbally, it would have disclosed that the actual slaughter was not intended — and the element of test would have remained missing. So he was shown in a dream that he was slaughtering his son; he understood it as slaughter and was set for it literally and comprehensively; and so the element of trial went the full circle, and the dream also came true.

**"So look — what do you think?"** Ibn Kathir says Ibrahim told his son in order to make it easier for him, and also to test his patience and resolve at a young age in obeying Allah and obeying his father. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands it: Ibrahim himself had no hesitation about carrying out the divine command; he wanted to test how far his son was ready to face this trial, and — as is the way of the noble prophets, who are prepared to carry out divine commands at all times but always opt for methods based on wisdom and all possible convenience — he wanted to spare them both the difficulty of doing it unannounced. So what he said was in the spirit of a tender consultation: let the boy become aware of the command of Allah in advance, so that he is prepared to endure the pain well before the hour comes, and so that if any hesitation emerged in his heart there would still be time to help him understand.

## The son's answer

**"O my father, do what you are commanded."** Ibn Kathir renders it plainly: obey the command of Allah and sacrifice me.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches something remarkable: Ibrahim had not referred to any *command* from Allah at all — he had mentioned only a dream. It is Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, who supplies the word "commanded." He understood that the dream of a prophet is revelation, and that this dream was therefore in reality a form of divine order. That is the kind of intelligence and knowledge Allah blessed him with at such a tender age.

**A point of belief.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān uses this to answer those who deny *waḥy ghayr matluww* — "revelation that is not recited" — holding that revelation is only what has been revealed in the Book of Allah, and so that the authority of Hadith does not stand. The command to sacrifice came through a dream, and Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, declared it in very clear words to be the command of Allah. If unrecited revelation is nothing, then where did this command come from, and in which Scriptures was it revealed?

**"You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient."** Ibn Kathir: I will be patient, and will seek the reward for that with Allah — and he believed in what had been promised. Ibn Kathir then points to Allah's own testimonial about him: "And mention in the Book Ismaʿil. Verily, he was true to what he promised, and he was a Messenger, a Prophet. And he used to enjoin on his family the Salah and the Zakah, and his Lord was pleased with him" (19:54–55).

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the manners packed into that short sentence. First, by saying *in shā' Allāh* he entrusted the matter to Allah, so his promise carried no flair of a boastful claim. Second, he could have said "you will find me enduring," but he said "you will find me *one of those* who endure patiently" — the hint being that this endurance is no feat of his alone; there have been many patient servants before him, and he hopes to be counted among them. Thus he removed any trace of pride, arrogance, egotism or conceit. The lesson Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes from it: no matter how much confidence one has in oneself, one should never make tall claims that smack of pride. If something of the kind must be said, weigh the choice of words, and shift the focus off one's own person onto what shows trust in Allah.

## Ayah 103: "then when they had both submitted"

*Fa-lammā aslamā.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *aslama* as to submit, to bow down, to become obedient, to be rendered ready to carry out the command — so the plain sense is that the father resolved to slaughter the son, and the son to be slaughtered by him. Two people, one surrender.

Ibn Kathir records two readings. One: both of them had pronounced the Shahadah and remembered Allah — Ibrahim because he was about to offer a sacrifice, and Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, because he was about to die. The other, held by Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, as-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq and others: they submitted to and followed the command of Allah — Ibrahim obeying the command of Allah, and Ismaʿil obeying Allah and his father.

**The sentence that is never finished.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a grammatical observation. The word used here is *lammā*, "when" — but its complement, the clause that completes the condition, is never mentioned. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the gap as a hint towards the uniqueness of this bold act of self-submission undertaken by father and son — so unique that words simply fail to convey a fuller description.

**"And he laid him down upon his forehead."** Ibn Kathir's explanation is that he placed him facedown so that he could slaughter him from behind and not have to see his face at the time of slaughter, so that it would be easier for him. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr, ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said it means he turned him upside down on his face.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a lexical refinement. The word *jabīn* is applied to the two curvatures of the forehead, while the middle part of the forehead is called *jabhah*. So on the wording, the explanation reported from Ibn ʿAbbas — that he laid him down on his side in a manner that one edge of the forehead was touching the ground — is lexically weightier, and this is the sense in which Maulana Thanavi translated it; other respected commentators have explained it as laying him down face down. Whatever the case, the reason given in historical accounts for this manner of laying him down is the same: initially Ibrahim had laid him down face up, but once he started moving the knife on his throat it would not cut despite repeated efforts, because by the will of Allah a copper plate had come as a barrier in between. It was then the son himself who requested to be laid on his side face down — because when his father looked at him his filial compassion unnerved his hand, and because the boy himself began to feel nervous when he looked at the knife. (Tafsir Mazhari, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.) Allah knows best.

## The scene, as the sources describe it

Two accounts fill in what the ayah leaves silent. Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the rituals were enjoined upon Ibrahim, the Shaytan appeared to him at the Mas'a and raced with him, but Ibrahim got there first; then Jibril, upon him be peace, took him to Jamrat al-ʿAqabah, where the Shaytan appeared and Ibrahim stoned him with seven pebbles until he disappeared; then he appeared at al-Jamrah al-Wusta, and he stoned him with seven pebbles. Then he laid his son prostrate on his face. Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, was wearing a white shirt and said, "O my father, I do not have any garment in which I can be shrouded apart from this; take it off me so that you can shroud me in it." He started to take it off — and then he was called from behind. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same tradition of the Shaytan trying three times to turn Ibrahim away, each time driven off with seven pebbles, and notes that pebbles are thrown at the three pillars at Mina to this day in memory of it.

The second, from Tafsir Mazhari as related in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is what the boy said when father and son reached the place of sacrifice: tie me down well enough so my body does not toss and turn; keep your dress protected, lest drops of my blood spoil it and reduce your reward with Allah, and lest my mother see the blood and be smitten with sorrow; sharpen your knife and run it fast over my throat, so that my last breath comes easy on me, for death is hard; and when you return to my mother, pay my respects to her, and if you wish to take her my shirt you are welcome to do so — perhaps it would give her the comfort she needs. His father, like a mountain of fortitude, answered: "Son, what a good helper you are for me in this task assigned by Allah." Then he kissed his son and, with wet eyes, he tied him.

## What the passage asks of us

Ibrahim's arc in these ayat is one of open hands: he releases his people (99), he asks rather than schemes (100), and when the gift he begged for is demanded back he does not bargain over it (102–103).

The passage also gives us the shape of good obedience. Ibrahim does not merely obey; he obeys *well* — telling his son first, consulting him gently, sparing him what could be spared. And Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, does not merely consent; he consents beautifully — naming it as Allah's command, saying *in shā' Allāh*, and refusing to claim patience as a personal distinction.

And notice where the passage stops: a son laid down, a father's hand steady, and a sentence deliberately left unfinished. Ayah 103 does not resolve the tension; it holds it open, and asks us to stand in it with them.

passages.title: The call, the vision fulfilled, and the ransom
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the moment the knife is stopped. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) has already done everything a father can be asked to do — he has told his son, the son has consented, both have surrendered, and the boy is lying face down under his father's hand. Ayah 104 is the voice from above; ayah 105 is the verdict on what he did; ayah 106 names what the whole episode was; ayah 107 is Allah's answer to a father who had nothing left to give. What holds them together is what Ibn Kathir says plainly about the purpose of the command: it was given **primarily to reward Allah's close friend for his patience and resolve**. The boy was never the object; the father's surrender was.

## How the passage was reached

Ibn Kathir sets the scene from the ayat just before. After Allah had helped His close friend against his people, and after Ibrahim gave up hope that they would ever believe despite the mighty signs they had witnessed, he emigrated away from them saying, *"Verily, I am going to my Lord. He will guide me"* — and then made the prayer, *"My Lord! Grant me (offspring) from the righteous"* (ayah 100). Ibn Kathir explains this as asking for obedient children **in compensation for the people and relatives he had left behind**. Hold that in mind: the son in this story is a prayer answered, the replacement for everything Ibrahim walked away from. That is what the command in ayah 102 asked him to hand back.

Allah answered with *"glad tidings of a forbearing boy"* (ayah 101). Ibn Kathir notes a tender detail about the years that followed: Ibrahim used to go every so often to check on his son and the boy's mother in the land of Faran — that is, Makkah — to see how they were doing. It was said that he used to ride on Al-Buraq, travelling there swiftly, *and Allah knows best*.

Then, when the boy *"was old enough to walk with him"* — which Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, Zayd bin Aslam and others explained as meaning **he had become a young man, able to work as his father did** — the dream came.

Ibrahim told him. 'Ubayd bin 'Umayr said, "The dreams of the Prophets are revelation," and recited this very ayah — so the dream was not a private impression to be weighed and doubted; it was a command. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibrahim told his son rather than surprising him for two reasons: **to make it easier for him**, and to test the boy's own patience and resolve, young as he was, in obeying Allah and obeying his father. The son passed: *"O my father! Do that which you are commanded"* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, *obey the command of Allah and sacrifice me* — *"if Allah wills, you shall find me of the patient,"* that is, *I will be patient and will seek the reward for that with Allah*.

Then ayah 103: *"when they had both submitted themselves, and he had laid him prostrate on his forehead."* On "both submitted," Ibn Kathir reports two readings: that both pronounced the Shahadah and remembered Allah — Ibrahim because he was about to offer a sacrifice, Isma'il because he was about to die — or that they both submitted to and followed the command of Allah, Ibrahim obeying Allah and Isma'il obeying Allah and his father. The second was the view of Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, As-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq and others. As for laying him on his forehead: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said it means **"he turned him upside down on his face"** — and Ibn Kathir explains the mercy in the detail. He placed him facedown so that he could slaughter him from behind and **not have to see his son's face at that moment, so that it would be easier for him.**

That is the posture Ibrahim is in when ayah 104 sounds.

## Ayah 104: "We called out to him, O Ibrahim!"

Notice what the call consists of: his name. *"O Ibrahim!"* Nothing about the boy, nothing about the knife — the man himself, addressed by name from above, in the instant of his greatest obedience.

In the report from Ibn 'Abbas recorded by Imam Ahmad, the detail is that he was **called from behind** him — which fits exactly the posture just described, Ibrahim facing away from his son's face. (Ibn Kathir notes that Hisham mentioned this hadith at length in *Al-Manasik*.)

## Ayah 105: "You have already fulfilled the vision"

It is a stunning thing for Allah to say to a man who has not completed the deed. Two explanations in the sources open it up:

**Ibn Kathir:** it means *"the purpose of your dream has been fulfilled by your laying down your son to sacrifice him."* The dream's aim was reached the moment he laid the boy down; the cutting was never the point.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** presses further: in accomplishing the task entrusted to him in obedience to the command of Allah, **he left nothing undone — in fact he did it perfectly, to the letter.** And here is the beautiful observation: this is more likely so **because in the dream too it was shown that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is simply moving his knife to slaughter his son.** He had been shown the act of the knife, and the act of the knife is precisely what he performed. And, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, now that the test was over, he should let the boy go.

As-Suddi and others add that he did pass the knife over Isma'il's neck and it did not cut him at all, because a sheet of copper was placed between them — and Ibrahim was called at that point.

Then: *"Indeed, this is how We reward the doers of good."* Ibn Kathir's gloss on this reward is not primarily about Paradise: *"this is how We deal with those who obey Us in things that are difficult for them; **We make for them a way out.**"* He anchors it in the promise Allah makes elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And whosoever has Taqwa of Allah, He will make a way for him to get out (from every difficulty). And He will provide him from (sources) he never could imagine. And whosoever puts his trust in Allah, then He will suffice him. Verily, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Indeed Allah has set a measure for all things"* (65:2–3). Ibrahim's ram is that ayah made visible.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same lesson out from the repetition of this phrase later in the sūrah (ayah 110): when a servant of Allah bows down before the command of Allah and is ready to sacrifice all personal thoughts and feelings, then ultimately **Allah takes care of him** — he remains safe from whatever could have afflicted him here in this world, and as for the recompense and reward of the Hereafter, that is written down in his book of deeds. Both worlds, for the man who lets go.

## Ayah 106: "That was truly a revealing test"

Ibn Kathir renders the phrase *a manifest trial*: a test whose difficulty is not hidden and whose result is unmistakable. His comment is short and pointed — it was clearly a test when he was commanded to sacrifice his son, **"so he hastened to do it, in submission to the command of Allah and in obedience to Him."** *Hastened.* The passage records no delay, no bargaining. And Allah's own summary of this man elsewhere is one phrase: *"And of Ibrahim, who fulfilled all that"* (53:37).

**A point from the scholars of Usul.** Ibn Kathir notes that on the basis of this ayah and this story, some of the scholars of *usul* (the principles of jurisprudence) held that **it is valid for a ruling to be abrogated before anyone is able to act upon it** — unlike some of the Mu'tazilah. The evidence, he says, is obvious: Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice his son, then abrogated that and pointed out the ransom. Which tells us what the command was *for* in the first place: Ibn Kathir says its purpose had been primarily **to reward His close friend for his patience and resolve** in sacrificing his son. The command was a door for Ibrahim to walk through, not a death sentence for Isma'il.

## Ayah 107: "And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice"

The ayah's own word is *ransomed*. The boy was not simply spared; something was given in his place, and the One who provided it was Allah.

What was the ransom? In the report from Ibn 'Abbas recorded by Imam Ahmad, when the call came from behind him, **"Ibrahim turned, and saw a fine, horned, white ram."** Ibn 'Abbas added, "We used to look for similar types of rams."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers what the reports say: on hearing this voice from the heavens Ibrahim looked up and saw Jibra'il (peace be upon him) with a ram; and from some reports it appears that it was the same ram offered in sacrifice by Habil, the son of Adam (peace be upon him) — *and Allah knows best*. In short, a present of this ram of Paradise was made to Ibrahim, and he sacrificed it in place of his son as Allah commanded. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas that it was **"a ram which had grazed in Paradise for forty years."**

Why is it called *great*? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Tafsīr Mazharī and others) gives the reason: because **it had come by way of mercy from Allah, and no one can entertain any doubt about the acceptance of its sacrifice.** Its greatness lies not in its size but in its source and its certainty. A sacrifice sent by Allah cannot be rejected by Allah.

## Which son was it?

Ibn Kathir treats this at length and states plainly that it was Isma'il (peace be upon him). His arguments and the reports he cites:

- Isma'il was **the first child of whom glad tidings were given to Ibrahim**, and older than Ishaq. The Muslims and the People of the Book agree, and it is stated in their own Book, that Isma'il was born when Ibrahim was eighty-six and Ishaq when he was ninety-nine.
- Their own Scripture says Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice his **only son**, and in another text his **firstborn** son — but the name Ishaq was falsely inserted there, which goes against what their own Scripture says. Ibn Kathir says the phrase "only son" was changed to mean "the only son who is with you," because Isma'il had been taken with his mother to Makkah; he calls this falsification and distortion, since the words "only son" cannot be said except of one who has no other son. He notes they inserted Ishaq's name because he is their ancestor, while Isma'il is the ancestor of the Arabs. He adds that the firstborn has a special status not shared by later children, so commanding his sacrifice is **the more exquisite test**.
- **Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi's argument from the Qur'an itself:** when Allah finishes the story of the son who was to be sacrificed, He gives Ibrahim glad tidings of Ishaq (ayah 112) — and elsewhere gives glad tidings of *"Ishaq, and after Ishaq, of Ya'qub"* (11:71). Allah mentions the son and the son's son. He would not have commanded the slaughter of Ishaq after promising that this son would himself have a son. So the one commanded could only be Isma'il. Ibn Ishaq said he heard him say this often. When Muhammad bin Ka'b put it to 'Umar bin 'Abd Al-'Aziz during his caliphate in Syria, 'Umar said, "This is something about which I have never given any thought, but I see that it is as you say." He then sent for a man with him in Syria — a Jew who had become a Muslim and was committed to Islam, whom 'Umar thought had been one of their scholars — and the man replied: "Isma'il. By Allah, O Commander of the faithful, the Jews know this, but they were jealous of you Arabs because it was your father about whom Allah issued this command and the virtue that Allah mentioned was because of his patience in obeying the command."
