- **The horns in the Ka'bah.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Safiyyah bint Shaybah, from a woman of Bani Sulaym who was the midwife of most of the people in their household, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for 'Uthman bin Talhah and said to him: *"I saw the horns of the ram when I entered the House (the Ka'bah), and I forgot to tell you to cover them up; cover them up, for there should not be anything in the House which could distract the worshipper."* Sufyan said the horns remained hanging in the House until it was burned, and they were burned too. Ibn Kathir treats this as independent evidence that the one to be sacrificed was Isma'il: the Quraysh had inherited the horns of the ram that Ibrahim sacrificed, passed down from generation to generation until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent — *and Allah knows best*. Ash-Sha'bi likewise said, "It was Isma'il, and I saw the horns of the ram in the Ka'bah."
- A long line of authorities is named for this view: Ibn 'Abbas (reported from him by Sa'id bin Jubayr, 'Amir Ash-Sha'bi, Yusuf bin Mihran, Mujahid, 'Ata' and others; Ibn Jarir also narrated it from him), Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, Yusuf bin Mihran, and Al-Hasan Al-Basri, who did not doubt it. 'Abdullah, the son of Imam Ahmad, asked his father which son was to be sacrificed, and he answered: "Isma'il" — mentioned in *Kitab Az-Zuhd*. Ibn Abi Hatim said he heard his father say, "The correct view is that the one who was to be sacrificed was Isma'il," and listed 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Hurayrah, Abu At-Tufayl, Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ash-Sha'bi, Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi, Abu Ja'far Muhammad bin 'Ali and Abu Salih. Al-Baghawi lists the same position from 'Abdullah bin 'Umar, Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib, As-Suddi, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Mujahid, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi and Al-Kalbi.

## What this asks of us

**Obedience is measured at the point of surrender, not the point of outcome.** Ibrahim was told *you have already fulfilled the vision* before a drop of blood was shed; Ibn Kathir explains that the purpose of the dream was fulfilled by his laying his son down. What Allah accepted was the laying-down. Whatever you are asked to give up for Allah's sake, the deed is complete when your hand is genuinely open — the result belongs to Him.

**The ram is a promise, not a coincidence.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 105 — *We make a way out for those who obey Us in what is hard for them* — is the practical core of the passage, and he ties it to 65:2–3. The way out arrives *after* the surrender, not before it, and it arrives from a direction no one could have calculated: in the reports Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers, a ram brought by Jibra'il (peace be upon him), a ram of Paradise.

**And the son is not a bystander.** A young man who answers his father's impossible news with *"Do that which you are commanded"* — and who, in the report from Ibn 'Abbas recorded by Imam Ahmad, thinks in that moment only of his shroud, telling his father he has no garment to be shrouded in but the white shirt he is wearing and asking him to take it off — is why Ibn Kathir cites Allah's description of him elsewhere: *"he was true to what he promised... and his Lord was pleased with him"* (19:54–55). This trial made two men, not one.

passages.title: Peace upon Abraham and the gift of Isaac
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are the aftermath of the sacrifice — Allah's answer to a man who held nothing back. Having ransomed the son with a great sacrifice (ayah 107), Allah announces what Ibrahim received in return: something left for him among later generations (108), a greeting of peace (109), a rule of divine reward stated openly (110), a testimony to who he was (111), then a second son given as glad tidings, Ishaq (112), with blessing poured on both father and son — followed by a sobering qualification about their descendants (113).

Every ayah is a **gift or a verdict following a trial**. And the last ayah quietly closes the door on anyone who would inherit the reward without repeating the obedience.

## What Allah "left" for him among later generations (108)

The Arabic of ayah 108 is spare: *wa taraknā ʿalayhi fī l-ākhirīn* — "and We left upon him among the later ones." What exactly was left is not stated; the translation supplies "honourable mention", and Ibn Kathir renders the ayah "And We left for him among the later generations". The unnamed object is part of the effect: what Allah left behind for Ibrahim was too broad to fix in one word.

Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the rituals were enjoined upon Ibrahim, peace be upon him, Shaytan appeared to him at the Masʿā and raced with him, but Ibrahim got there first; then Jibril, upon him be peace, took him to Jamrat al-ʿAqabah, where Shaytan appeared and Ibrahim stoned him with seven pebbles until he disappeared; then again at al-Jamrah al-Wusṭā, seven more. Only then did he lay his son prostrate on his face. In the same report, Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, was wearing a white shirt and said, "O my father, I do not have any garment in which I can be shrouded apart from this; take it off me so that you can shroud me in it." Ibrahim had begun to take it off when he was called from behind: *O Ibrahim! You have fulfilled the dream!* He turned and saw a fine, horned, white ram. Ibn ʿAbbas added, "We used to look for similar types of rams." Ibn Kathir notes that Hisham mentioned this hadith at length in *al-Manāsik*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the custom of sacrifice during the Hajj season prevailed among the people of Arabia precisely because this event came to pass within the environs of Makkah. Ibn Kathir adds that the horns of the ram Ibrahim sacrificed were inherited by the Quraysh and passed down from generation to generation until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Safiyyah bint Shaybah that a woman of Bani Sulaym — the midwife of most of the people of their household — told her that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for ʿUthman bin Talhah, may Allah be pleased with him. On one occasion Safiyyah said, "I asked ʿUthman, 'Why did the Prophet ﷺ call you?' He said, 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me:

> **I saw the horns of the ram when I entered the House [i.e., the Kaʿbah], and I forgot to tell you to cover them up; cover them up, for there should not be anything in the House which could distract the worshipper.**'"

Sufyan said the horns of the ram remained hanging in the House until it was burned, and they were burned too. Ash-Shaʿbi, an early authority, said plainly: "I saw the horns of the ram in the Kaʿbah."

So "what We left for him" was not a legend. It was a rite, a place and a relic — and beyond all of them, a pattern of worship. Notice also the Prophet's ﷺ reasoning in that hadith: even a genuine memento of Ibrahim's sacrifice must be veiled if it might pull a worshipper's eye away from Allah.

## "Peace be upon Abraham" (109)

Ayah 109 is short: *salāmun ʿalā Ibrāhīm* — Ibn Kathir renders it, *"Salam (peace!) be upon Ibrahim!"* A man had just laid his son face-down in obedience; the reply, once the ransom was provided, is a greeting of peace.

Its placement is its commentary. Ayah 106 had called the episode *a manifest trial*; ayah 107 answered it with the ransom; ayah 108 left something of Ibrahim among the later generations — and now this. Ibn Kathir says outright that the purpose of the original command had been primarily to reward Allah's close friend for his patience and resolve. This greeting is part of what that reward looks like.

## "This is how We reward the good-doers" (110)

Ayah 110 states a general law — and the passage states it twice, once already at ayah 105 as the call came, and again here after the whole affair is over. Ibn Kathir's gloss: it means **"this is how We deal with those who obey Us in things that are difficult for them; We make for them a way out."** He cites the promise:

> "And whosoever has Taqwa of Allah, He will make a way for him to get out (from every difficulty). And He will provide him from (sources) he never could imagine. And whosoever puts his trust in Allah, then He will suffice him. Verily, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Indeed Allah has set a measure for all things." (65:2–3)

("Taqwa" is the care of a servant who keeps Allah in view.)

The command was real, the knife was real, and the way out arrived from a direction no calculation could have produced. Note the order: the way out came *after* the submission. Ibrahim was not shown the ram and then asked to obey.

Ibn Kathir draws a legal point too: on the basis of this ayah and this story, some of the scholars of *uṣūl* (the principles of jurisprudence) have stated that it is valid for a ruling to be abrogated before anyone is able to act upon it — unlike some of the Muʿtazilah. The evidence: Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice his son, then abrogated that and pointed out the ransom.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsīr Mazharī and others, explains why the ransom animal was called *ʿaẓīm*, "great" (ayah 107): because it had come by way of mercy from Allah, and no one can entertain any doubt about the acceptance of its sacrifice. Hadith reports mention that Ibrahim, on hearing that voice from the heavens, looked up and saw Jibril with a ram; from some reports it appears it was the same ram offered in sacrifice by Habil (Abel), son of Adam — and the source itself pauses there to say, *Allah knows best.* Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, described it as "a ram which had grazed in Paradise for forty years."

## "He was truly one of Our faithful servants" (111)

Ayah 111 gives Ibrahim his title. Not conqueror, not even father of prophets — *one of Our believing servants*. Everything in the story flows from those two words. He **believed**, so a dream was enough to move him: the early authority ʿUbayd bin ʿUmayr said, "The dreams of the Prophets are revelation," and recited this very passage. And he was a **servant**, so the command did not have to be explained to him before he complied. Ibn Kathir's repeated description of him as Allah's close friend rests on that foundation rather than replacing it.

The son shows the same two qualities in miniature. Ibrahim laid the matter before him — "So look what you think!" — which he did, Ibn Kathir says, in order to make it easier for him, and also to test his patience and resolve, at a young age, in obeying Allah and obeying his father. The answer, *"O my father! Do that which you are commanded"*, means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "obey the command of Allah and sacrifice me"; and *"if Allah wills, you shall find me of the patient"* means "I will be patient and will seek the reward for that with Allah." Allah's later testimony to him — *he was true to what he promised … and he used to enjoin on his family the Salah and the Zakah, and his Lord was pleased with him* (19:54–55) — was earned on that ground.

## The glad tidings of Ishaq (112) — and the question of which son

Ayah 112: *"And We gave him the glad tidings of Ishaq — a Prophet from the righteous."* Ibn Kathir notes that having given the glad tidings of the one who was to be sacrificed, Allah immediately follows with mention of the glad tidings of his brother Ishaq, as is also mentioned in Sūrah Hūd (11:71) and Sūrat al-Ḥijr (15:53–55). On the word *nabiyyā* ("a Prophet") he comments: it means that from him there will come a righteous Prophet.

This ayah is the hinge of a famous scholarly question: **which of Ibrahim's two sons was the *dhabīḥ* — the one commanded to be sacrificed?**

**The disagreement is real.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly that there is a severe difference of opinion among commentators and historians about it. That this son was Isḥāq has been reported (in the listing it takes from Usmani) from among the Companions by ʿUmar, ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAbbās, ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAbbās and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, and from among the Successors by Saʿīd Ibn Jubayr, Qatādah, Masriq (Masrūq), ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil, Zuhrī and Suddiyy. Counter to this, it has been reported that the son was Ismaʿīl — from among the Companions by ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Hurayrah and Abū ṭ-Ṭufayl, and from among the Successors by Saʿīd Ibn Musayyab, Saʿīd Ibn Jubayr, Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Mujāhid, ʿUmar Ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Shaʿbī and Muḥammad Ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī. Maʿārif notes that ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd Ibn Jubayr appear in *both* groups, because reports of both views are attributed to them. Among the later commentators, Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī preferred the first view, while Ibn Kathir and others not only went by the second but refuted the first.

**Where the weight lies.** Maʿārif concludes that in terms of the descriptive arrangement of the Qur'an and the strength of the narrations, the weightier view is that it was Ismaʿīl, and offers four arguments:

1. **The order of the text.** The Qur'an reports the whole event of the sacrifice and only then, in ayah 112, gives the glad tidings of Isḥāq — which tells us the son to be sacrificed was someone other than Isḥāq, whose birth was announced afterwards. Ibn Kathir reports Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī making the same argument from the Book of Allah, and Ibn Ishaq says he heard him say it often.
2. **The promise of a grandson would have removed the trial.** Isḥāq's glad tidings included that he would be a prophet, and in Sūrah Hūd, *"So, We gave her the good news about Isḥāq, and about Yaʿqūb after Isḥāq"* (11:71) — son and grandson together. Ibrahim would therefore have understood that this son would live to have offspring, so slaughtering could not bring death to him. There would have been no major trial, and no ground for the praise Allah gives him.
3. **He was the firstborn.** The prayer for offspring came as Ibrahim migrated from his homeland (ayah 100), the glad tidings of the forbearing boy answered it (ayah 101), and the command came when that same boy was old enough to work alongside him (ayah 102) — a chain that points to the first son. Ibn Kathir adds that the firstborn has a special status not shared by subsequent children, so the command to sacrifice him is a more exquisite test. All the sources agree Ismaʿīl was the elder: Ibn Kathir notes that the Muslims and the People of the Book agree, and it is stated in their Book, that Ismaʿīl was born when Ibrahim was eighty-six; for Isḥāq, the Tafsir Ibn Kathir text here gives ninety-nine, while the Genesis passage Maʿārif quotes gives a hundred (Maʿārif concludes Isḥāq was fourteen years younger).
4. **The place.** It is nearly settled that the event took place within the environs of Makkah — hence the Arabian custom of sacrifice at Hajj, and the ram's horns hanging in the Kaʿbah. It was Ismaʿīl who lived in Makkah, not Isḥāq.

**On the counter-reports.** Ibn Kathir's assessment, as Maʿārif quotes it, is that these sayings evidently all came from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, who on embracing Islam in ʿUmar's time began relating reports from his old books; others heard them and started passing them on — material Ibn Kathir judged the ummah does not need a single word of. And he closes, as always, *Allah knows best.* Both commentaries also hold that the name Isḥāq was inserted into the received biblical text out of rivalry over ancestry. Ibn Kathir's core argument is linguistic: that text says "your only son", and "only son" is applied only to a son whose father has no other son; rereading it as "the only son present with you" (since Ismaʿīl and his mother were not there) is a distortion. Maʿārif adds that in the very passage of Genesis where Isḥāq's birth is foretold, it is also said of Sarah, "she shall be a mother of nations; kings of people shall come from her" (17:16), and of Isḥāq, "I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his descendants after him" (17:19) — a son already promised nations from his progeny could not then be ordered to be sacrificed.

Ibn Kathir records a striking exchange. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī mentioned this to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz while he was Caliph, when he was with him in Syria; ʿUmar replied, "This is something about which I have never given any thought, but I see that it is as you say." He then sent for a man there, a Jew who had become a Muslim and was committed to Islam and was thought to have been one of their scholars, and asked him which son it was. The man answered: "Ismaʿīl. By Allah, O Commander of the faithful, the Jews know this, but they were jealous of you Arabs because it was your father about whom Allah issued this command and the virtue that Allah mentioned was because of his patience in obeying the command."

Ibn Kathir cites ʿAbdullāh, son of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said, "I asked my father about which son was to be sacrificed — was it Ismaʿīl or Isḥāq?" He said, "Ismaʿīl" (mentioned in *Kitāb az-Zuhd*). Ibn Abī Ḥātim said, "I heard my father say, 'The correct view is that the one who was to be sacrificed was Ismaʿīl,'" and reported the same from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Hurayrah, Abū ṭ-Ṭufayl, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, ash-Shaʿbī, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī and Abū Ṣāliḥ. Al-Baghawī lists the same view from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, as-Suddī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī and al-Kalbī.

**Why it matters — and why it should not be over-fought.** The passage's own subject is obedience, not genealogy. But the answer does matter: if the *dhabīḥ* was Ismaʿīl, then the trial, the stoning at the Jamarāt, the sacrifice at Hajj and the honour Allah announces in ayah 108 all belong where the sources place them, and the pilgrim's own actions retrace that ground. Maʿārif closes: in the light of these proofs it is almost certain that Ismaʿīl was the *dhabīḥ* — "Allah is Pure and He knows best."

## Blessing on both — and the warning in its tail (113)

Ayah 113 opens its hands to both sons: *"We blessed him and Isḥāq."* The rivalry described above is a human disease, not a divine verdict. And then, in the same breath, it refuses to bless anyone automatically: *"And of their progeny are (some) that do right, and some that plainly wrong themselves."*

Ibn Kathir says this is like the ayah about Nuh, peace be upon him: *"O Nuh! Come down (from the ship) with peace from Us and blessings on you and on the people who are with you, but people to whom We shall grant their pleasures (for a time), but in the end a painful torment will reach them from Us."* (11:48) Blessing on a father is not an estate his descendants inherit.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion sharply. Refuted through this ayah, it says, is the false pride of the Jews that being among the progeny of these noble prophets is in itself sufficient to bless one with merit and salvation. The ayah openly declares that having a lineal connection with a man of virtue is not a sufficient guarantee of one's salvation: **that depends on one's own beliefs and deeds.**

Notice the words chosen. The good among the progeny are called *muḥsin* — the singular of the *muḥsinīn*, "the doers of good", whom ayah 110 promised to reward. That reward was never attached to Ibrahim's name; it was attached to a description, and anyone who fits the description qualifies. The other kind is *ẓālimun li-nafsihi mubīn*: one who wrongs — and the one he wrongs is *himself*, plainly.

## Living it

- **The way out comes after the submission.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 110 is a promise about difficulty, not about ease: obey in the thing that is hard, and Allah makes a way out, and provides from sources one could never have imagined (65:2–3). What is asked for first is the obedience, not the calculation.
- **Ask to be counted among the *muḥsinīn*.** Maʿārif names the pride ayah 113 refutes — that descent from these noble prophets is by itself enough for merit and salvation — and the principle covers anyone tempted to lean on a pedigree: salvation depends on one's own beliefs and deeds. Ayah 111 gives Ibrahim's real credential: *one of Our believing servants*.
- **Let nothing compete with Allah — not even a relic of devotion.** The Prophet ﷺ had the horns of the ram covered so that nothing in the House would distract a worshipper. If that could distract, so can a great deal else we keep in front of us.
- **Speak to your children as Ibrahim spoke to his son.** He told him, Ibn Kathir says, to make it easier for him and to test his patience and resolve. And the boy answered with *"if Allah wills"* — confident in Allah, never in himself.

passages.title: Moses and Aaron favoured, delivered, and guided
passages.tafsir:
These nine ayat are a roll-call of the favours Allah placed on Musa and Harun (peace be upon them): prophethood, rescue, victory, a Book, guidance, and finally a name that outlives them. What holds the passage together is that every single verb belongs to Allah — *We favoured, We delivered, We helped, We gave, We guided, We left* — and the sequence closes not with a description of what the two brothers achieved but with a greeting of peace over them and a statement of who they were: "They were truly two of Our faithful servants" (ayah 122).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes this as "the third event" relating to Musa and Harun, notes that it "has appeared in details at several places" in the Qur'an, and adds that "here it serves as an indicator." So the passage is not retelling the story; it is pointing at it. A whole lifetime of struggle is compressed into a handful of verbs. The purpose of compressing it this way, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is to show "how Allah Taʿala helps out His sincere and obedient servants, and how He bestows so many of His rewards on them."

## Two kinds of favour

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a simple key that unlocks the shape of the passage. Allah's favours are of two kinds:

- **Positive favours** — those that bring benefit. This is what ayah 114 announces in summary: "And We certainly showed favour to Moses and Aaron."
- **Negative favours** — those that "save from loss or harm." These are spelled out in the verses that follow.

So ayah 114 is the headline, and everything after it is the itemised account. It is worth pausing on that, because we are far quicker to notice the gifts we were given than the disasters we were spared. This passage counts both as favour. Being rescued from something is a gift in exactly the same sense as being handed something.

Ibn Kathir identifies the first of the favours in ayah 114 as **prophethood** itself — "Allah tells us how He blessed Musa and Harun with prophethood." Before the rescue, before the victory, before the Book, the favour is that these two men were chosen to carry Allah's message at all.

## The great distress — what exactly they were delivered from

Ayah 115 says they and their people were delivered "from the great distress." The Qur'an leaves the phrase general; Ibn Kathir fills it in from the wider Qur'anic account. The distress was "the oppression of Fir'awn and his people," who:

- **killed the sons** of the Children of Israel and spared the women — a policy aimed at ending a people by ending its next generation;
- **forced them to do "the most menial tasks"** — degradation as a way of life, not merely occasional cruelty.

Notice how ayah 115 widens the frame: it is not only the two prophets who are delivered but "them **and their people**." Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah saving Musa and Harun "along with those who believed." The prophets are not lifted out of a drowning crowd; the community that believed with them is carried out with them. Deliverance here is not a private transaction.

And note that Allah does not minimise what they went through in order to call the rescue a favour. He names the distress "great." What the passage teaches is not that the faithful are spared hardship, but that Allah's help arrives, and that it is decisive when it comes.

## "It was they who prevailed"

Ayah 116 — "We helped them so it was they who prevailed" — is the turning of the whole story. Ibn Kathir: "ultimately He caused them to prevail over them and to seize their lands and their wealth and all that they had spent their entire lives amassing."

Two things are worth feeling here. First, the order of the ayah: Allah's help is named first, and the prevailing follows from it. Ibn Kathir's wording says the same thing — it was *He* who "caused them to prevail." The victory is not a separate achievement standing alongside Allah's aid; it is what Allah's aid produced. Second, the ones described as prevailing are precisely the people who had been at the bottom: the despised community whose sons were being killed and who were set to the lowest labour. "It was they who prevailed."

Ibn Kathir's detail about the wealth carries its own lesson: everything Fir'awn's people "had spent their entire lives amassing" ended up in the hands of the people they had oppressed. A lifetime of accumulation, transferred by Allah's decree.

## The Book that makes things clear

Ayah 117: "We gave them the clear Scripture." Ibn Kathir identifies it plainly: "Then Allah revealed to Musa the Clear and Mighty Book, which is the Tawrah" — the Torah as Allah revealed it to Musa.

To show what that clarity consists of, Ibn Kathir brings in another ayah about the same Book:

> "And indeed We granted to Musa and Harun the criterion (of right and wrong), and a shining light." (21:48)

Two images sit inside that verse. *Al-Furqān* — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "the criterion (of right and wrong)" — is what separates right from wrong so that the two can no longer be confused. And *ḍiyāʾ*, "a shining light," is what lets you see where you are walking. A revealed Book does both jobs at once: it tells you which is which, and it lights the road.

Notice, too, whom the gift is credited to. The Book came down upon Musa — Ibn Kathir says "Allah revealed to Musa the Clear and Mighty Book" — yet both ayah 117 and the verse Ibn Kathir cites name **both brothers** as the recipients: "We granted to Musa and Harun the criterion... and a shining light." Harun is not an assistant on the margins of the story. The whole passage speaks of the two together — favoured together, delivered together, given the Book together, guided together, greeted together in ayah 120.

## Guided to the Straight Path

Ayah 118: "and guided them to the Straight Path." Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayat 117–118 together is a single short phrase that carries the weight of a whole discussion — he says it means guidance "with regard to words and deeds."

That is, guidance is not only knowing the right thing; it is being brought to say it and to do it. A person can hold an accurate map and still walk the wrong way. Allah's favour on these two prophets included both halves: the clear Book (knowledge), and being led along the straight road (speech and action shaped by that knowledge).

There is something quietly humbling here too. Musa and Harun are prophets, recipients of revelation — and still the ayah says that *Allah* guided them. Guidance is never self-generated, at any rank. It is listed among the favours precisely because it is a gift.

## A name left behind among later generations

Ayah 119: "And We blessed them with honourable mention among later generations." Ibn Kathir explains: it "means, that after they died they would be mentioned in good terms and spoken of highly."

What was left behind is not property but standing: a place in the esteem of people who would come long after them and had never met them. And Allah Himself is the one who left it — "We left for them among the later generations." It is not the residue of ambition or self-promotion; no publicity effort put it there.

Then Ibn Kathir notes that Allah "explain[s] this further" in what immediately follows. Ayah 120 is the content of that honourable mention:

> **"Peace be upon Moses and Aaron."**

That is the good mention Allah left among the later generations — a greeting of peace, recorded in Allah's own Book, and so carried to every generation that reads it. Two men from an oppressed people, whose sons were killed and who were forced into the lowest labour, are given a line of peace by Allah Himself.

And it is worth noticing that when we read ayah 120 aloud, we are not merely reporting that peace was sent upon them; we are joining in it.

## "Thus do We reward the doers of good"

Ayah 121 turns the specific case into a rule: "Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers" — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "Verily, thus do We reward the doers of good."

The words "thus" and "this is how" point back over everything from ayah 114 onward: *this* — rescue, victory, revelation, guidance, honoured remembrance — is what Allah's reward looks like. And the recipients are named not as "Musa and Harun" but by a category: *al-muḥsinīn*, the doers of good. Ayah 121 deliberately holds the door open — the two prophets are presented as an instance of a standing divine practice, not an exception to it. Whoever enters the category is dealt with by the same rule. This is exactly what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from the passage as a whole: the purpose is to show "how Allah Taʿala helps out His sincere and obedient servants, and how He bestows so many of His rewards on them."

## The title that comes last

Ayah 122 is the seal: "They were truly two of Our faithful servants" — Ibn Kathir's rendering, "Verily, they were two of Our believing servants."

After prophethood, deliverance, victory, scripture, guidance and lasting honour have all been listed, the final word about Musa and Harun is not "prophets", not "victors", not "recipients of the Tawrah" — but **believing servants of Allah**. And the possessive is striking: "**Our** servants." To belong to Allah, and to be described by Allah as His, is the honour on which all the other honours rest.

Read the passage backwards and it explains itself: they were Allah's believing servants (122), and so they were among the doers of good whom Allah rewards in just this way (121), and so honourable mention and peace were left upon them among all later generations (119–120), and so they were guided, given the Book, made victorious and delivered (115–118) — all of it gathered under the opening announcement, "We certainly showed favour to Moses and Aaron" (114).

## Living it

**Count the escapes, not only the gifts.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's two categories of favour are a practical lesson in gratitude: alongside the favours that "bring benefits" are the favours that "save from loss or harm." The harm that never reached you is a favour of exactly the same kind as the good that did.

**Do not measure Allah's help by the weight of the distress.** The Children of Israel endured the killing of their sons and forced degradation before "We saved them... from the great distress" was written over their story. Allah Himself called that distress "great" — and the deliverance still came.

**Ask for guidance in deeds, not only in knowledge.** Ibn Kathir's "words and deeds" makes a good self-audit: not only *do I know the straight path*, but *am I speaking and acting on it* — and it is Allah who grants both.

**Let the good name be Allah's to give.** What survived of Musa and Harun in the memory of later generations was left there by Allah — "We left for them among the later generations." Work for His pleasure, and let the remembrance take care of itself.

**Aim at being one of the doers of good.** Ayah 121 states a standing practice, not a one-off. Whoever enters that category is inside the promise.

And when you next recite ayah 120, say it as a greeting and mean it: *Peace be upon Moses and Aaron.*

passages.title: Elias calls his people away from Ba'l
passages.tafsir:
These ten ayat give us the whole mission of the prophet Ilyas (Elias) in a handful of words: a man sent to a people who had swapped the Creator for an idol called Ba'l, who put one burning question to them, was rejected, and was then honoured by Allah for all time. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is the fourth prophetic account in this run of the surah, and the ayat themselves lay out a clear shape — **call, rejection, and vindication** — with the closing seal in ayat 131–132 being one Ibn Kathir says has already been explained earlier in the surah.

## A prophet the Qur'an barely describes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that Ilyas is named in the Qur'an in only two places: Surah al-Anʿam (6:85), where his name simply appears in a list of righteous prophets with no story attached, and here in Surah aṣ-Ṣaffat (37:123 and 37:130). This passage is therefore the only place in the Qur'an where anything of his mission is told.

That brevity is deliberate. Maʿārif states the principle plainly: *the noble Qur'an is no book of history*. Rather than narrate the details of Ilyas's long struggle, it restricts itself to what is necessary for taking a lesson. Nothing about his personal background appears in the Qur'an or in authentic hadith; the many colourful details in books of tafsir come mostly from Israʼili narratives — reports carried over from the earlier scriptural traditions.

**Who was he?** Ibn Kathir records that Qatadah and Muhammad bin Ishaq said "Ilyas is another name for Idris," and that Ibn Abi Hatim recorded the same from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him; Ad-Dahhak held this too. Wahb bin Munabbih instead gave a lineage: "Ilyas bin Yasin bin Finhas bin Al-ʿIzar bin Harun bin ʿImran" — placing him in the line of Harun. Maʿārif reports a further view, held by some, that there is no difference between Ilyas and Khadir, then says that researchers have refuted these identifications: the Qur'an mentions Idris and Khadir separately in a way that leaves no room for declaring them the same. What Hafiz Ibn Kathir judged correct, Maʿārif says, is that they are two separate messengers (al-Bidayah wa-n-Nihayah 1/339).

## The world he was sent into

Historical and Israʼilite reports, Maʿārif says, almost agree that he was sent to the Bani Israʼil after Hizqil (Ezekiel) and before Al-Yasaʿ. Ibn Kathir likewise says Allah sent him to the Children of Israel after Hizqil.

By then the kingdom of the Bani Israʼil had split in two: Yahudiyah (Judah), with its capital at Baytul-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and Israʼil, with its capital at Samaria (present-day Nablus). Ilyas was born at Jalʿad in Jordan. The king of Israʼil is named Ahab in the Bible, and Ajib or Akhib in Arab historical and exegetical writing. His wife — named Isabelle in these accounts — worshipped the idol Ba'l, and it was she who set the whole nation on the path of idolatry by raising a huge altar dedicated to Ba'l in the land of Israʼil. It was into that atmosphere, with idolatry backed by the throne itself, that Allah commanded Ilyas to go, preach pure monotheism, and turn the Israelites away from idol worship.

That background gives ayah 124 its weight. **"Will you not fear Allah?"** was no comfortable sermon; it was said to a people whose queen had made idolatry state policy and who, by these accounts, harassed him in all sorts of ways — Ahab and Isabelle going so far as to plan his killing, until he took refuge in a far-out cave for a considerably long period.

## The famine and the fire

Ibn Kathir relays from Wahb bin Munabbih, from the People of the Book: the people had begun worshipping the idol Ba'l; Ilyas called them to Allah and forbade them to worship anyone besides Him; their king believed in him and then apostatised; they persisted, and *not one person among them believed in him*. So he prayed against them, and Allah withheld the rain for three years. They then asked him for relief and promised they would believe if the rain came. He prayed for them, the rains came — and they persisted in their disbelief. At that point he asked Allah to take him to Himself. Al-Yasaʿ bin Akhtub had grown up under his care. Ibn Kathir then reports the account of a horse of fire brought to him, his being clothed with light and covered with feathers, and flying with the angels — then immediately adds his own caution: **"This is what was narrated by Wahb bin Munabbih from the People of the Book; Allah knows best how true it is."**

Maʿārif gives the fuller account, noting that the most exhaustive treatment among the customary books of tafsir is in Tafsir Mazhari on the authority of ʿAllamah al-Baghawi, that its events have almost all been taken from the Bible, and that parts of it in other tafsirs are related on the authority of Wahb Ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Ahbar — both mostly reporters of Israʼili material. In that telling, Ilyas prayed for famine to strike his people, so that a miracle at his hands in lifting it might bring them to belief. Famine came. Then, by Allah's command, he met Ahab and told him the famine was there because of disobedience to Allah, and that abstaining from it even at that late hour could lift the punishment. He proposed a test: "you say your god Ba'l has four hundred and fifty apostles in this part of Israʼil. Gather them together before me on a day of your choice. Let them offer their sacrifice in the name of Ba'l, and I shall offer my sacrifice in the name of Allah. The one whose offering the heavenly fire would come and burn to ashes will be the one whose faith will be true."

They gathered at Mount Carmel. The false apostles of Ba'l offered their sacrifice and remained busy with their entreaties before Ba'l from morning till afternoon — no answer came. Then Ilyas offered his, and fire came from the heavens and reduced it to ashes. Many people fell prostrate in sajdah; the truth lay manifest before them. Yet the apostles of Ba'l remained adamant, and Ilyas had them killed in the valley of Kishon. Heavy rains followed and the whole region turned verdant.

And still Isabelle was not ready to learn her lesson. She turned more hostile and prepared to have him killed, so he left Samaria and went into hiding again. After some time he began preaching in Judah, the other Israelite country, where the epidemic of idolatry had gradually reached; its king Jehuram also refused to listen, until he was destroyed in fulfilment of Ilyas's prophecy. A few years later Ilyas returned to Israʼil and tried once more to reform Ahab and his son Ahaziah, who clung to their misdeeds until foreign intrusions and fatal diseases overtook them. Thereafter Allah recalled His prophet back unto Him.

Set that whole history beside ayah 127 — **"But they rejected him, so they will certainly be brought forth"**. Decades of struggle, a public miracle, drought and rain, kings and queens: all of it compresses into *fa-kadhdhabūhu*, "so they denied him." The Qur'an keeps only the moral spine.

## The question in ayah 124, and the argument in 125–126

Ilyas opens not with information but with a question: *alā tattaqūn* — rendered "Will you not have Taqwa?" and "Will you not fear Allah?" Ibn Kathir gives the sense: *do you not fear Allah when you worship others instead of Him?* It works on the conscience rather than by argument: it asks a person to look at what he is doing and feel the danger in it.

Then in ayah 125 comes the contrast: **"Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the Best of creators?"**

**Ba'l.** Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, along with Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah and As-Suddi, said that *Ba'l* means "lord." ʿIkrimah and Qatadah said this is the language of the people of Yemen; another report from Qatadah says it is the language of Azd Shanuʼah. ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam narrated from his father that it is the name of an idol worshipped by the people of a city called Baʿlabak (Baalbek), west of Damascus. Ad-Dahhak said simply, "It is an idol which they used to worship." Ibn Kathir sums the phrase up: "will you worship an idol?"

Maʿārif fills in the word's ordinary sense — *baʿl* literally means husband, master — and its long history: it was worshipped in Syria as far back as the time of Musa and was the most popular idol-god there; the once-famous Syrian city of Baʿlabakk (Baalbek, ancient Heliopolis, in present-day Lebanon) was named after it. Maʿārif also mentions that some people think Hubal, the well-known idol of the pre-Islamic people of Hijaz, was this very Ba'l (Qasas-ul-Qurʼan 2/28).

**"The Best of creators."** The phrase *aḥsan al-khāliqīn* needs care. Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, says it never means that there could be — Allah forbid — some other real creator alongside Him. The drive and sense of the statement is that He is the one most exalted of all those false objects of worship which the people had taken to as being some sort of creator. Some commentators, Maʿārif adds, take *khāliq* here in the sense of *ṣāniʿ*, "maker": He is far ahead of and far better than all other makers. And what do other makers actually do? They take different components that already exist and put them together. **Bringing something out of nothingness into existence is simply not under their power and control — and it is under His.** He has the inherent power to make what is not, become what is (Bayan-ul-Qurʼan).

Ayah 126 then closes the argument by naming Him: *Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers*. Ibn Kathir's comment: "He is the One Who is deserving of your worship alone, with no partners or associates." Ilyas does not appeal to novelty; he appeals to the Lord who was already their fathers' Lord — the very Lord that idolatry had displaced.

**Living it: the word "creation."** Maʿārif draws a concrete ruling out of this ayah. *Khalq* means to bring something from the state of non-being into the state of being solely on the strength of the creator's inherent power; that attribute is particular to Allah alone, and ascribing it to anyone else is not permissible. On this basis Maʿārif objects to the common modern habit of calling a writer's articles, a poet's compositions or a painter's paintings their "creations." Call them what they are — articles, effort, imagination, research work, or whatever else applies — but Allah is *al-Khāliq*, the Creator, and that is Him alone.

## Who is exempted, and who is honoured (127–132)

Ayah 127 ends the account of the deniers: they rejected him, *fa-innahum la-muḥḍarūn* — "they will certainly be brought forth." Ibn Kathir: brought forth for the punishment on the Day of Reckoning. Maʿārif adds that they will have to taste the consequence of having belied Allah's true messengers, and that it could refer both to the punishment of the Hereafter and to their sad end within this world — the rulers of both Israʼil and Judah in fact faced destruction after rejecting Ilyas.

Ayah 128 carves out the exception: **"except the chosen servants of Allah."** Ibn Kathir explains these as those who believe in Him alone. Maʿārif adds a precise point of vocalisation: the word is *mukhlaṣīn*, pronounced with a fathah on the letter *lām*, meaning *chosen, elected, people divinely identified as special*. So, Maʿārif says, it is more appropriate to translate it as "the chosen" rather than "the sincere": people whom Allah has elected to receive the honour of having obeyed Him perfectly and who thereby made themselves deserving of the best returns and rewards from Him.

Ayah 129 — **"And We left for him among the later generations"** — means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that "he is praised and spoken of highly." A man whom, by Ibn Kathir's report, not one person in his own nation believed in is given a good name in every generation after him. That is this passage's answer to what looks, from the outside, like failure in daʿwah.

Ayah 130 pronounces the honour itself: *salāmun ʿalā Il Yāsīn* — "Peace be upon Elias." The unusual form of the name puzzles readers. Ibn Kathir explains it as a dialect variation: one might likewise say *Ismaʿīn* for *Ismaʿīl*; this is the dialect of Bani Asad, who say *Mīkāl*, *Mīkāʼīl* and *Mīkāʼīn*, *Ibrāhīm* and *Ibrāhām*, *Isrāʼīl* and *Isrāʼīn*, *Ṭūr Sīnāʼ* and *Ṭūr Sīnīn* — "all of that is fine." Maʿārif says the same: *Il Yāsīn* is the very name of Ilyas, since the people of Arabia frequently add the letters *yāʼ* and *nūn* to non-Arab names — as *Sīnāʼ* (Sinai) can take the form *Sīnīn* — and here too two letters have been added.

Ayat 131 and 132 close with the same seal used for those others: **"Indeed, this is how We reward the good-doers. He was truly one of Our faithful servants."** Ibn Kathir notes that the meaning of this has already been discussed earlier in the surah.

## Is Ilyas still alive? A lesson in handling reports

The lengthy narrative in Tafsir Mazhari from ʿAllamah al-Baghawi says Ilyas was lifted towards the heavens mounted on a horse of fire and is alive there like ʿIsa. ʿAllamah as-Suyuti also reported several narrations from Ibn ʿAsakir, al-Hakim and others indicating that he is alive. It is reported from Kaʿb al-Ahbar that four prophets are still alive: two on the earth — Khadir and Ilyas — and two in the heavens — ʿIsa and Idris (ad-Durr-ul-Manthur 5/285–286). Some went so far as to say that Khidr and Ilyas get together in Baytul-Maqdis during Ramadan and keep fasts (Tafsir Qurtubi 15/116).

But, Maʿārif says, authentic scholars like Hafiz Ibn Kathir have not declared these narratives to be sound. Of narratives of this nature he wrote that this is one of "those Israʼili narratives that are neither confirmed nor falsified. Instead, what is obvious is that its soundness is remote" (al-Bidayah wa-n-Nihayah 1/338). He adds that Ibn ʿAsir has reported several narratives of people who met Ilyas, but none of these is satisfactory — either because the chain of authority cited is weak, or because the people to whom the events are attributed are unknown (al-Bidayah wa-n-Nihayah 1/339).

Maʿārif traces where the idea came from. It is fairly evident, it says, that the notion of Ilyas being lifted to the heavens was taken from Israʼili narratives: the Bible says a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them and that Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven (2 Kings 2:11). For this reason the belief arose among the Jews that he would return to the earth, so that when Yahya was sent as a prophet they doubted whether he was Ilyas — and it appears in the Bible that when they asked him, "Are you Elijah?", he said, "I am not" (Gospel of John 1:21). Scholars like Kaʿb al-Ahbar and Wahb Ibn Munabbih, well versed in the religious background of the People of the Book, would have described these narratives before Muslims, and from there the notion found currency among some. **Otherwise there is nothing in the Qur'an or the Hadith that provides any proof of his being alive or having been raised up to the heavens.**

The one narrative that exists is in the *Mustadrak* of al-Hakim, which says the Prophet ﷺ met Ilyas on his way to Tabuk — but this report is, as hadith experts hold, *mawḍūʿ*: fabricated. Hafiz adh-Dhahabi's verdict was blunt: "In fact, this is fabricated. Cursed be whoever fabricated it. I had never imagined that the inadvertence of al-Hakim could overtake him to the extent that he would admit this thing as sound" (ad-Durr-ul-Manthur 5/286). A believer should therefore not pass that story on as a hadith.

In short, Maʿārif concludes, it is not proved from any authentic Islamic report that Ilyas is alive, and in this matter the safest and sanest course is to observe silence. With Israʼili narratives in particular one should follow the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ: *neither confirm, nor falsify these.* And the reason Maʿārif gives is freeing: **the Qur'an has a purpose — that it be understood, that it provide lessons and give good counsel — and that purpose can be achieved fully without settling such questions at all.** And Allah is Pure and High — He knows best.

## What the passage leaves with us

A prophet was sent to a people who had taken an idol for a lord, and he asked one question: will you not fear Allah? He was denied. Not one of them, in Ibn Kathir's report, believed in him. And Allah's verdict on that life is *salāmun ʿalā Il Yāsīn*: peace be upon him, honourable mention among all later generations, and a place among "Our faithful servants."

For anyone who has ever spoken the truth where nobody wanted to hear it, ayat 129–132 are the promise: what the ayat attach the reward to is being a *muḥsin* and a believing servant — not the response of the audience.

passages.title: Lot delivered while his town is destroyed
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat tell the story of Lūṭ (Lot), peace be upon him, in the shortest possible compass: a messenger sent, a household rescued, one woman left behind, a town destroyed — and then, in the last two ayat, the address swings round from the ancient past to the people of Makkah who were listening, because the ruins of that town lay on the road their own caravans travelled. What holds the passage together is that turn. Everything in ayat 133–136 is told so that the question of ayah 138 can land: **you pass by this in the morning and at night — will you not then reflect?**

## Why the story is told so briefly

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is the fifth event in the sūrah's run of accounts, this one relating to Sayyidnā Lūṭ, peace be upon him, and observes that because the event has already appeared at several places earlier in the Qur'an, no more details are needed here.

That is worth pausing on. This is not a shortened story so much as a *referenced* one. The listener is assumed already to know the episode, so it is compressed to its bare structural bones — messenger, rescue, exception, destruction — and the passage spends its real weight elsewhere: on the two ayat of direct address at the end. When you feel the passage moving fast, that speed is purposeful. The narrative is the run-up; the admonition is the jump.

## Ayah 133: "And Lot was indeed one of the messengers"

The passage opens not with something Lūṭ said or did, but with a statement of who he was: he was indeed one of the messengers.

Ibn Kathir opens his comment in the same register. Under the heading "The Destruction of the People of Lut (Lot)," he writes that Allah tells us He sent His servant and Messenger Lūṭ, peace be upon him, to his people, and they denied him — and that Allah then saved him from among them, him and his family, with the exception of his wife.

Notice what that one sentence of Ibn Kathir establishes before anything else happens. The town was not overthrown out of nowhere. A messenger was sent. A message was delivered. Only then did they deny it. The whole moral logic of ayah 136 rests on this opening line of ayah 133 — and on the fact that the man sent was Allah's servant and Messenger, not a self-appointed voice.

## Ayat 134–135: the rescue, and the one left behind

"˹Remember˺ when We delivered him and all of his family" (134). Ibn Kathir renders it: "When We saved him and his family, all." The deliverance is stated as complete — *all* of them — which is exactly what makes the next ayah land like a stone:

"except an old woman, who was one of the doomed" (135).

Ibn Kathir identifies her plainly: she was his wife, and she was destroyed along with her people.

Two things here repay attention.

**The ayah names her by her age, and Ibn Kathir supplies the relationship.** The text before us says only "an old woman." It is Ibn Kathir who tells us this was Lūṭ's wife. So the one bond that might have looked like a guarantee of rescue — marriage to a prophet of Allah — is precisely the bond that did not save her. She is not counted among the family who were brought out. She is counted, in Ibn Kathir's words, among *her people*, who were destroyed. Nearness to a prophet of Allah is not, by itself, shelter.

**"Among those who remained behind," or "one of the doomed."** The sources in front of us render the same phrase both ways: the translation of the ayah has "one of the doomed," while Ibn Kathir's rendering reads "who was among those who remained behind." The two are describing one fact from two angles. She was not among those who went out; she was among those the punishment fell upon. To be left behind on the night Allah's decree arrives is, in this account, to be among the doomed — and Ibn Kathir states the outcome without softening it: she was destroyed along with her people.

There is also something to notice in the ordering of the passage itself. The rescue in ayah 134 is mentioned before the destruction, and ayah 136 begins with "Then" — the ruin of the rest is placed after the deliverance of the household, not before it.

## Ayah 136: "Then We ˹utterly˺ destroyed the rest"

The translation of the ayah carries the force: *utterly* destroyed. Ibn Kathir adds a detail the ayah leaves folded up — Allah destroyed them **with different kinds of punishments**. Not one blow, but several.

Then he says something that turns the passage from history into geography. Allah, he writes, made their vicinity **a foul, stinking lake** which is on a well-travelled route where people pass by night and day. He identifies the place: the Dead Sea, which lies close to the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, on the highway between Arabia and Syria.

That is the hinge of the whole passage. On Ibn Kathir's account the punishment did not simply end when the town fell. Its trace was left in the landscape — brackish, lifeless, foul-smelling — beside a road that people were still travelling, by night and by day, long afterwards.

The wording "the rest" is worth a moment too. The town's population is identified only by contrast with the handful who were brought out. In the reckoning of that night, the rescued household is the reference point, and everyone else is the remainder.

## Ayat 137–138: the road you already travel

"You ˹Meccans˺ certainly pass by their ruins day — and night. Will you not then understand?"

Here the Qur'an stops narrating and turns to face the people listening. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the setting explicit: the people of Makkah are being particularly admonished, because they passed by the site of Sadūm (Sodom) day and night while travelling with their trade caravans to the country of Syria — and Sadūm was the place where this grave event came to pass, an event full of vital lessons, yet they failed to learn any of them.

Sit with the force of that. According to Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the evidence was not a distant rumour requiring their trust. It was on their trade route. They went past it, and went past it again, and drew nothing from it. The failure named in these ayat is not a failure of access to information. It is a failure to reflect on what was already in plain view.

**Why morning, and why night?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the time of morning and evening was particularly mentioned because the people of Arabia generally used to pass through there during those very hours. It then quotes Qāḍī Abū al-Saʿūd, from Tafsīr Abī al-Saʿūd: "Perhaps, this site of Sodom was located at a stage on this route that those who departed from here did so in the hours of the morning and those who arrived here did so at the time of the evening."

So the two times of day are not decoration. On this explanation they are the ordinary rhythm of a real caravan journey — the hour you set out and the hour you pulled in. Whichever end of the day it was, that place was what you passed. It is hard to imagine a more exact way of saying: you cannot claim you never saw it.

## "Will you not then reflect?"

Ibn Kathir gives the meaning of the closing question directly: "will you not learn a lesson from them and how Allah destroyed them, and realize that a similar end awaits the disbelievers."

Two things in that short gloss are worth holding onto.

First, what is being asked for is a piece of thinking. Not merely a shudder, and not merely a memory of an old catastrophe, but the deliberate drawing of a lesson: connect what you rode past this morning to the warning you are hearing now. The question at the end of ayah 138 — "will you not then reflect?", "will you not then understand?" — appeals to that faculty in the listener, and Ibn Kathir spells out precisely what its exercise would produce.

Second, notice that Ibn Kathir carries the conclusion forward into the present: **a similar end awaits the disbelievers.** On his reading the ruin beside that road is not only a record of what happened to somebody else long ago. It is a warning about what still lies ahead for those who reject the message.

## Living it

**Proximity is not reflection.** On Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account the people of Makkah had the closest possible access to the evidence — it sat on their own trade route, morning and evening — and they still failed to learn anything from it. Seeing a thing and thinking about it are not the same act. Each of us has our own version of that road: the graveyard we drive past, the illness in the family, the collapse of someone who once looked untouchable. Ayah 138 asks whether any of it is actually being reflected upon, or merely passed.

**Do not lean on your associations.** Ayah 135 is the hardest line in the passage precisely because of who the woman was. Ibn Kathir tells us she was the wife of Lūṭ, peace be upon him, and that she was destroyed along with her people. Marriage, lineage, community, a reputation borrowed from the piety of those near you — none of it stands in for one's own standing before Allah.

**And the deliverance is mentioned first.** Before "Then We ˹utterly˺ destroyed the rest" comes "when We delivered him and all of his family." Ibn Kathir's summary keeps the same order: Allah saved him from among them, him and his family — and destroyed the rest. For a believer surrounded by a society that has rejected the truth, that ordering is itself a consolation. Hold to the message; the rescue is Allah's to arrange, and in this account He arranged it completely.
