# Sūrah aṣ-Ṣāffāt 139–148: Yūnus, the fish, and the city that believed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is the last event described in this sūrah — the story of Yūnus (peace be upon him) in a handful of strokes: a prophet who set off before he was told to, a storm, a drawn lot, a fish, a whispered glorification in the dark, a bare shore, a plant of shade — and finally a city of a hundred thousand who believed. What holds it together is a single movement: a slip, its consequence, and a rescue tied to a lifetime of devotion — ending in the one community named in the Qur'an whose faith at the eleventh hour was accepted.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this event, with its full details, has appeared towards the later part of Sūrah Yūnus, and Ibn Kathir points back to Sūrat al-Anbiyāʼ (21:87–88); here the Qur'an gives the compressed version.

## Ayah 139: a messenger, first and always

The passage opens by fixing his rank: **"And Jonah was indeed one of the messengers."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a question commentators and historians debated: was Yūnus made a messenger long before his encounter with the fish, or only afterwards? Some held his mission came after the event. But in view of the apparent order and style of the Qur'an, and from most hadith narrations, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges it more likely that he was invested with prophethood earlier, and the episode of the fish came later. That ordering matters: what follows is not the story of a man becoming a prophet, but of a prophet being disciplined.

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on the passage with a hadith reported in the Two Sahihs, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "It is not right for any person to say I am better than Yunus bin Matta." Whatever the Qur'an is about to say of him — the flight, the blame, the fish — he remains a messenger of Allah, above the reach of our comparisons.

## Ayah 140: the word that stings — *abaqa*

**"When he fled to the overloaded ship."** The verb chosen is أَبَقَ (*abaqa*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it comes from إِبَاق (*ibāq*), which means specifically the escaping of a slave from his master — not simply "he travelled" or "he departed", but the flight of one who owes obedience. Allah used this word of Yūnus, it explains, because he had started off without waiting for the revelation from his Lord. And it adds: the noble prophets are the close ones among the servants of Allah, and the slightest slip from them causes the swiftest grip. Hence this strong expression, *abaqa*.

This is the Qur'an's own measure of intimacy: nearness to Allah does not soften His correction, it sharpens it. Note too that the ayah says he fled *to the ship* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering is "he ran towards the boat already loaded." Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said of الْفُلْكِ الْمَشْحُونِ (*al-fulk al-mashḥūn*), the laden ship, "It was filled with cargo." A boat already at its limit — which is exactly why the storm that follows becomes a problem of weight.

## Ayah 141: the drawn lot

**"Then he drew straws"** — فَسَاهَمَ (*fasāhama*), which Ibn Kathir glosses as drawing lots. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: the boat was caught by a storm while in the middle of the waters, and it was feared that its excessive weight might cause it to sink, so it was decided that one person from the boat should be cast into the waters, and lots were drawn to determine who.

The second half of the ayah, فَكَانَ مِنَ الْمُدْحَضِينَ, Ibn Kathir explains as "among those who have been overcome." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the root sense: إِدْحَاض (*idḥāḍ*) literally means to defeat someone, to make him fail or lose. The Qur'an describes a prophet of Allah as the one who *lost*.

**A ruling drawn from the ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on when drawing lots is legitimate. Lots are a method of selecting somebody to do something; through them one can neither prove someone's right, nor indict someone as a criminal. If two people differ about the ownership of some property, ownership cannot be decided by lots. But where a person is entirely entitled, Sharīʿah-wise, to opt for any one of several permissible courses of action, and the choice is simply his, then rather than going by his own will and preference he may arrive at a decision by drawing lots — and that is not merely permissible but better. The example given: someone who has more than one wife and is going on a journey has the right to take whichever wife he elects to take with him; if he draws lots instead, that is better, so that no one is disheartened. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Prophet ﷺ used to do that.

Applied to the ship: the purpose of the lot was not to label anyone a culprit. To save a whole boat-full of passengers, anyone could have been cast into the waters; the lot merely settled which.

**Was it suicide?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers directly: it was his name that came up in the draw and he threw himself into the waters, but no one should raise the objection that this was some sort of suicide plunge, for it is possible that the shore was near and he intended to swim ashore.

## Ayah 142: swallowed, and "blameworthy"

**"Then the whale engulfed him while he was blameworthy"** — the ayah as it stands in Ibn Kathir's text reads, "Then a big fish swallowed him as he had done an act worthy of blame." The Qur'an does not soften it, and neither does it enlarge it beyond what was said in ayah 140.

Ibn Kathir gives the scene in full. The ship was being pounded by the waves on all sides and they were at risk of drowning, so they drew lots — whoever lost would be thrown overboard so as to lighten the load. Yūnus lost the draw three times, yet they did not want to throw him overboard. He took off his garment so that he could throw himself into the sea, and they tried to stop him. Then Allah commanded a large fish from the Green Sea (that is, the Mediterranean) to cleave the oceans and come and swallow Yūnus — without cutting his flesh or breaking his bones. The fish came, Yūnus threw himself overboard, and it swallowed him and took him away, travelling through all the seas with him.

Two details are worth holding onto. The fish was *commanded*: what looks like a catastrophe of nature is an appointment. And "without cutting his flesh or breaking his bones" — the punishment was a confinement, not a mauling.

Ibn Kathir continues: when Yūnus had stayed for some time in the fish's belly, he thought that he had died; then he moved his head and legs and arms, and saw that he was alive. He prayed in the belly of the fish, and one of the things he said in his prayer was: "O Lord, I have taken as a place of worship to You a place which no other person has reached."

**How long?** The scholars differed, and Ibn Kathir simply lists them: three days (Qatādah); seven days (Jaʿfar aṣ-Ṣādiq, may Allah be pleased with him); forty days (Abū Mālik); and Mujāhid, narrating from ash-Shaʿbī, "It swallowed him in the morning and cast him forth in the evening." Ibn Kathir's own verdict: **and Allah knows best** how long exactly it was.

## Ayat 143–144: the hinge of the whole passage

**"Had he not ˹constantly˺ glorified ˹Allah˺, he would have certainly remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected."** Everything turns on مِنَ الْمُسَبِّحِينَ — "of those who glorify" — and the commentators offer two readings.

**First view: his life of worship before the crisis.** Ibn Kathir reports the view that it means: had he not already done righteous deeds during his time of ease. This was the view of aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk bin Qays, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Wahb bin Munabbih, Qatādah and others, and it was the view favoured by Ibn Jarīr. Ibn Kathir supports it with the hadith narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "Remember Allah during times of ease and He will remember you during times of difficulty."

**Second view: the words he cried in the dark.** Ibn Kathir also reports that what is meant is the glorification recorded elsewhere: *"But he cried through the darkness ˹saying˺: 'Lā ilāha illā Anta, You are glorified! Truly, I have been of the wrongdoers.' So We answered his call, and delivered him from the distress. And thus We do deliver the believers"* (21:87–88). This was the view of Saʿīd bin Jubayr and others.

The two readings do not really compete. The narration Ibn Kathir cites next joins them into one scene.

**The duʿāʼ at the Throne.** Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Anas bin Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) — and Ibn Kathir remarks that he knows of nothing narrated from Anas that he did not attribute to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — that when it occurred to the Prophet Yūnus (upon him be peace) to call upon Allah in these words in the belly of the great fish, he said, "Lā ilāha illā Anta, You are glorified! Truly, I have been of the wrongdoers." This call went and hovered around the mighty Throne. The angels said, "O Lord, this is the voice of one who is weak but known, in a faraway strange land." Allah, may He be exalted, said, "How do you know this?" They said, "O Lord, who is he?" Allah said, "My servant Yūnus." They said, "Your servant Yūnus, from whom there kept coming acceptable deeds and supplications which were answered?!" They said, "O Lord, will You not have mercy on him for what he did during his time of ease, and save him from this trial and tribulation?" He said, "Of course." So He commanded the great fish, and it cast him forth on the naked shore.

Read the passage through that narration and ayah 143 opens up. The years of accepted deeds were not consumed and gone; they were *recognised*. And in the divine reply — "Of course" — there is the whole tenderness of the passage.

**A caution on ayah 144.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns against a misreading: it is wrong to assume from "until the Day they are resurrected" that had Yūnus not been making *tasbīḥ*, that fish would have gone on living right through the last day of Qiyāmah. The sense, rather, is that the very belly of that fish would have been made his grave.

**And a practical consequence.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from the ayah that *tasbīḥ* — proclaiming the purity of Allah, declaring Him free of every imperfection — and *istighfār* — seeking His forgiveness — have a proven efficacy of their own. The very words Yūnus recited in the belly, *lā ilāha illā Anta subḥānaka innī kuntu min aẓ-ẓālimīn* ("There is no god but You — Pure are You — Indeed I was among the wrongdoers", 21:87), were the means by whose blessing Allah delivered him from that trial, and he came out safe and sound. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it has been continuously reported from the pious elders that when they faced any distress, individual or collective, they would recite this *tasbīḥ* one hundred and twenty-five thousand times, and by virtue of its *barakah* Allah would have the distress removed from them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites, from Tafsīr Qurṭubī, a narration from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ (may Allah be pleased with him) appearing in Abū Dāwūd, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that any Muslim who recites the prayer Yūnus made in the belly of the fish — *lā ilāha illā Anta subḥānaka innī kuntu min aẓ-ẓālimīn* — for any permissible objective, his duʿāʼ will be answered.

## Ayat 145–146: bare ground, and a plant of shade

**"But We cast him onto the open shore, worn out, and caused a squash plant to grow over him."** Ibn Kathir glosses فَنَبَذْنَاهُ as "We threw him out." Of بِالْعَرَاءِ, Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) and others said it refers to land in which there is no vegetation and no buildings; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: an open land with no trees. وَهُوَ سَقِيمٌ — "while he was sick" — means, Ibn Kathir says, weak of body; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some narrations tell us he had become very weak from having remained confined in the belly of the fish, and that he had no hair left on his body.

A prophet delivered from the sea onto an empty plain, too weak to stand, without shelter of any kind — and the very next thing Allah reports of Himself is not a command but a kindness: He grew a plant over him.

On يَقْطِين, Ibn Kathir lists a long line of early authorities who all said it means squash: Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Wahb bin Munabbih, Hilāl bin Yasāf, ʿAbdullāh bin Ṭāwūs, as-Suddī, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī and several others. Some mentioned why this plant in particular suits a man in his condition: it grows quickly; its leaves offer shade because of their large size and smooth texture; flies do not come near it; and its fruits provide good nourishment, edible raw or cooked, both pulp and peel. Ibn Kathir also reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to like squash and would look for it wherever it was on the serving dish.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a linguistic note: *yaqṭīn* signifies every such tree that has no trunk, and it appears in hadith narrations that it was a gourd creeper. The purpose of having a tree grow there was to provide shade for Yūnus. But the Qur'an calls it a شَجَرَة — a tree — which points to one of two possibilities: either Allah made this very gourd plant grow with a trunk by way of a miracle, or it was some other tree up which the creeping plant was made to wind its way, so that it could provide a thick shade; otherwise, having enough shade from a winding plant alone would have been difficult.

Every property of the plant answers a need of the man lying under it.

## Ayat 147–148: the city that believed

**"We sent him to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed, so We gave them enjoyment for a while."** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 147 as a return: it is as if, after he came forth from the fish, he was commanded to go back to those to whom he had been sent in the first place — and they all believed in him.

**"Or more."** Makḥūl said they numbered one hundred and ten thousand — reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Ibn Jarīr said that some of the scholars of Arabic, the people of Basrah, took it to mean "up to one hundred thousand or more," and he interpreted this ayah as he interpreted *"and became as stones or even worse in hardness"* (2:74), *"they fear men as they fear Allah or even more"* (4:77), and *"and was at a distance of two bows' length or even nearer"* (53:9). In all of these, the meaning is: not less than that, but rather more.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān meets the difficulty — Allah is Knowing and Aware, so why should the number appear uncertain? Two answers are offered. Quoting Mazharī: the statement is made in congruity with the view of common people — if an average person had seen them, he would have said their number was one hundred thousand or somewhat more than that. And Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī (Bayān ul-Qurʼān): nothing is being doubted in the text itself; they could accurately be called both — if you eliminate the fraction, one hundred thousand; if the fraction is taken into account, more than one hundred thousand.

**Why their faith was accepted.** Ibn Kathir explains فَمَتَّعْنَاهُمْ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ as: until the time of their appointed end. And he brings the ayah that names this community as unique: *"Was there any town that believed, and its faith at that moment saved it? — except the people of Yūnus; when they believed, We removed from them the torment of disgrace in the life of this world, and permitted them to enjoy for a while"* (10:98). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads إِلَىٰ حِينٍ to mean that so long as they did not revert to their *kufr* and *shirk*, no punishment visited them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic about *why* the punishment was averted: it was averted because these people had started believing **on time** — before it actually materialised. It uses this to reject the claim of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad Qadiani, who had challenged his adversaries that divine punishment would descend on them by such and such time should they continue to oppose him; instead their opposition grew stronger and no punishment came, whereupon he claimed it had been removed from them because they were really scared in their hearts, just as it had been removed from the people of Yūnus. This ayah declares that interpretation false: the people of Yūnus stayed safe from the punishment because of their *īmān* — whereas his adversaries never believed in him at all.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer.

**Do not run ahead of your Lord.** The whole chain of events begins with a prophet who started off without waiting for the revelation from his Lord. If *abaqa* is the word used of Yūnus, the rest of us should hesitate before assuming our own timing is Allah's.

**Store up worship in the good days.** This is the reading of ayah 143 that Ibn Jarīr favoured and that the narration from Anas dramatises: the deeds of your time of ease are what plead for you in your time of trial. "Remember Allah during times of ease and He will remember you during times of difficulty."

**When you are in the dark, glorify Him and own your wrong.** The words are handed to us: *lā ilāha illā Anta subḥānaka innī kuntu min aẓ-ẓālimīn.* No claim of innocence, no bargaining — the purity of Allah affirmed, and one's own wrongdoing admitted. And the promise attached to that rescue in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʼ was never restricted to a prophet: *"And thus We do deliver the believers."*

passages.title: The lie that Allah fathered daughters
passages.tafsir:
After the long procession of prophets that fills most of Sūrah aṣ-Ṣāffāt, the sūrah turns back to the matter it began with: pure monotheism, and the demolition of the shirk set against it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this pivot — the prophetic stories "provided some good counsel and some lessons to learn," and now the text returns to affirming *tawḥīd* (Allah's absolute oneness) and refuting *shirk* (ascribing partners to Him). What holds ayat 149–157 together is that they are a single sustained cross-examination of one specific pagan claim: that the angels are Allah's daughters. Nine ayat, and almost every one of them is a question. The passage does not merely deny the claim; it takes the claim apart, demanding of its holders the one thing they never had — a reason.

## The belief in the dock

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out what the Arabs of that time actually held: the angels were the daughters of Allah, and the daughters of the chieftains of the jinn were the mothers of those angels. It adds, on the authority of the scholar its text names as ʿAllāmah Whidi (citing *Tafsīr Kabīr*), that this was not a Quraysh peculiarity — it also prevailed among the tribes of Juhainah, Banū Salamah, Banū Khuzāʿah and Banū Malīḥ. A regional creed, then, not a fringe opinion.

Ibn Kathīr is careful to count what is stacked inside this single creed. Three separate things, he says, were said about the angels, forming "the utmost disbelief and falsehood": that they were the daughters of Allah and that Allah had offspring at all — exalted and sanctified be He above that; that this offspring was female; and then that these supposed daughters were worshipped instead of Allah. Any one of the three, he says, would on its own be enough to condemn a person to spend eternity in Hell. The passage is not fussing over a detail of angelology. It is pulling down an entire structure.

## Ayah 149: "Ask them"

The passage opens with a command to the Prophet ﷺ: *fa-stafti-him* — "Now ask them." Ibn Kathīr glosses the word precisely: it means "quiz them by way of denunciation." This is not a question asked in ignorance, hoping for information. It is the question of a prosecutor who already knows the answer and wants the accused to hear himself say it. Everything that follows in ayat 149–157 is that cross-examination.

And the first question is the sharpest: **"Are there daughters for your Lord, and sons for them?"** Notice the order — Allah's alleged share is named first, theirs second, set side by side so the reader cannot miss the arithmetic. Ibn Kathīr places beside it the parallel from Sūrah an-Najm: "Is it for you the males and for Him the females? That indeed is a division most unfair!" (53:21–22).

Why is that division unfair *by their own lights*? Because of what the Qur'an elsewhere records about them. Ibn Kathīr quotes it: "And when the news of the birth of a female child is brought to any of them, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with inward grief" (16:58). His face darkens. He swallows his rage. Ibn Kathīr adds that this upsets him, and that he would only choose sons for himself. And then — Ibn Kathīr puts the question in the mouth of the text itself — "how can they attribute to Allah the share that they would not choose for themselves?"

That is the opening blow, and it lands without needing a single point of revealed doctrine. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises it plainly: this belief of yours is already wrong in terms of your own recognised practice and customs, since you yourselves regard daughters as a source of shame; and what is a source of shame for you personally, how could it be proved to be good for Allah?

## The four doors, closed one by one

The real architecture of this passage is an argument about **evidence**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays it out as a formal exercise: a claim like this could be proved in one of three ways — (1) observation, (2) report, meaning the word of an entity or person whose veracity is established, or (3) reason. The passage walks through all three, then adds a further possibility — a revealed scripture — and closes that door too. Read this way, ayat 150 through 157 stop being a scatter of rhetorical questions and become a single tight case.

**Door one: observation (ayah 150).** *"Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?"* Ibn Kathīr's gloss is one sentence and it is devastating: how did they decide that the angels are female when they did not witness their creation? Maʿārif makes the same point — you simply have not seen Allah creating angels in a way that could have given you knowledge of their nature, so you have no proof from observation. Ibn Kathīr sets alongside it the ayah from az-Zukhruf: "And they make the angels females who themselves are servants of the Most Gracious. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned!" (43:19) — and he specifies that they will be questioned about that on the Day of Resurrection. Note the word Allah uses of the angels there: **servants** of the Most Gracious. Not offspring. Servants. And note the terrifying calm of "their testimony will be recorded": what they said about the unseen is being written down as testimony they will have to answer for.

**Door two: report (ayat 151–152).** If you did not see it, perhaps someone trustworthy told you? *"Indeed, it is one of their fabrications to say, 'Allah has children.' They are simply liars."* Ibn Kathīr reads the two halves separately: "it is of their falsehood" means it is a part of the lies they tell; "Allah has begotten" means that offspring have been born to Him; and then, "verily, they are liars." So the claim is condemned twice over — the statement is a fabrication, and the people making it are liars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows exactly why both halves are needed for the argument. A report only counts as proof when one goes by the word of people who are trustworthy and whose veracity is well established. Here the opposite is the case: those who hold this belief are liars, so "nothing they say can be a binding argument." The chain of transmission for this creed is its own refutation.

**Door three: reason (ayah 153).** *"Has He chosen daughters over sons?"* The verb is the language of selecting and preferring — Ibn Kathīr pairs it with al-Isrāʼ: "Has then your Lord preferred for you sons, and taken for Himself from among the angels daughters? Verily, you indeed utter an awful saying" (17:40). His gloss on ayah 153 is a simple "what would make Him choose daughters rather than sons?" Maʿārif spells out why this is the rational prong: *in your own view*, daughters have a lower status than sons. Now think of the great Being of Allah, who holds the superior-most status in the entire universe — how could such a Being like to have something of a lower status? On their own scale of values the claim is not merely false; it is incoherent.

Then ayah 154 stops arguing and simply stares: *"What is the matter with you? How do you judge?"* Ibn Kathīr: "what kind of reasoning makes you say that?" There is a moment in every cross-examination when the questions run out and only astonishment is left. This is that moment. And ayah 155 follows it with the invitation that so often accompanies the Qur'an's rebukes — *"Will you not then be mindful?"* Remember. Think again. The door back is open.

**Door four: a revealed Book (ayat 156–157).** *"Or do you have any compelling proof? Then bring us your scripture, if what you say is true!"* Ibn Kathīr glosses the "plain authority" of ayah 156 as simply "evidence to prove what you say," and ayah 157 as: produce evidence for that derived from a Book revealed from heaven by Allah, to prove that He has taken offspring as you claim — adding the verdict, "what you say is totally irrational." Maʿārif frames it as the one likelihood left unexplored: perhaps you have been blessed with some scripture from the heavens through the medium of revelation (*waḥy*) in which you were asked to believe as you do? Then come out and show us the proof — where is that revelation, and where is that Book?

The silence that answers is the point. Not one of the four doors opens. They did not see it; they cannot cite anyone truthful who told them; their own reasoning contradicts it; and no revelation supports it. All that is left is what the Qur'an already named it in ayah 151: a fabrication.

## An *ilzāmī* answer — and what it does *not* concede

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here for a point of method that is easy to miss and important to get right, because a careless reading of ayat 149 and 153 could leave the impression that the Qur'an shares the pagan estimate of daughters.

It does not. What this passage uses is an *ilzāmī* answer — a reply that refutes an opponent's claim through the analogy of some *other* view of things the opponent himself already holds. Maʿārif is explicit that in doing this "it is never necessary to concede that we too subscribe to this other view, in fact, there could be occasion when that other view is also incorrect." It is put to use functionally, only to drive some sense into an adversary bent on obstinacy. So when Allah argues from their conviction that the existence of daughters is a cause of disgrace, Maʿārif says outright that this does not mean it is so with Allah — nor does it mean that, had they called the angels sons of Allah rather than daughters of Allah, the belief would have been correct.

That last clause is the guard rail. The problem was never the gender assigned; it was the assigning of offspring at all. And so Maʿārif points to the answer the Qur'an gives in its own voice, underneath the argument-from-their-premises: Allah is independent and need-free, and neither does He need any children, nor does it befit His Most Exalted State of Being. Two denials, not one — the first says there is no need in Him that offspring could answer, the second says the very notion is unworthy of Him. The *ilzāmī* argument dismantles their claim from inside; that statement of Allah's absolute independence destroys it from above.

Ibn Kathīr's own commentary on ayat 151–152 keeps breaking off into the same note. He cannot state the pagan claim without immediately adding, of Allah, "exalted and sanctified be He above that." That is the posture the passage leaves us in: not a counter-speculation about what the angels are, but the declaration that Allah is far above what was said of Him.

## Living it

**Do not speak about the unseen without knowledge.** The single question that undoes the whole pagan creed in ayah 150 is *were you there?* Their testimony about the angels will be recorded, and Ibn Kathīr says plainly that they will be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection (43:19, as he cites it here). Claims about angels, about the jinn, about what Allah wills or loves, about the fate of particular people — these are not areas for confident guessing. Ayah 157 sets the standard for anything asserted about Allah: *bring your Book*.

**Learn the method of the passage.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson explicitly: with people bent on obstinacy it is more appropriate to answer *ilzāmī* — to show them that their own accepted premises will not carry the belief they are defending. That is an argument available before any shared scripture exists. But note the discipline that comes with it. Maʿārif insists we do not thereby concede the premise we borrowed, and it makes sure the reader also hears the real answer in its own terms, so the borrowed argument is never mistaken for the doctrine.

**Test what you inherited.** Whole tribes held this belief — Juhainah, Banū Salamah, Banū Khuzāʿah, Banū Malīḥ, and Quraysh besides. Numbers and ancestry authenticated nothing. Ayah 155 puts its demand to every one of them, and to us: *afalā tadhakkarūn* — will you not then be mindful? The four questions of this passage make a serviceable examination of any conviction we carry about Allah and His religion. Did I see it? Did someone truthful and reliable convey it? Does it stand to reason? Is there a Book behind it? If the answer to all four is no, no amount of inheritance or company will hold it up on the Day when testimony is read back.

passages.title: Alleged kinship with jinn; the angels' own witness
passages.tafsir:
This passage closes a long argument. From ayah 149 onwards Allah has been cross-examining the idolaters about their claim that the angels are His daughters — asking what reasoning makes them say such a thing, demanding a plain authority, and finally telling them to produce their Book if they are truthful (ayah 157). Ibn Kathir sums up the force of that last demand: produce evidence derived from a Book revealed from heaven by Allah — because what you are saying is totally irrational.

Ayat 158–166 finish the case in four movements: the invented genealogy (158), Allah's own declaration that He is far above it (159–160), the statement that their falsehood has no power over anyone (161–163), and finally the testimony of the very creatures they slandered — the angels speak in their own voice (164–166).

## Ayah 158: "a kinship between Him and the jinn"

**What exactly did they claim?** Ibn Kathir preserves the conversation that makes this ayah concrete. Mujahid said: "The idolators said that the angels were the daughters of Allah. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said, 'Then who are their mothers?' They said, 'The daughters of the leaders of the Jinn.'" Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said the same.

So the invention had a second storey built on the first: having made the angels daughters, they had to supply mothers, and they reached for the chieftains of the jinn — as though, Allah forbid, there were a marital bond and offspring resulting from it. That is how Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out this first interpretation.

**A second explanation, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān considers weightier.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises an honest difficulty with the reading above: the ayah speaks of *kinship* (Arabic *nasab*), and the marital relationship of a husband and wife is not based on kinship.

For that reason it prefers a second interpretation, reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Hasan al-Basri and ad-Dahhak (referring the reader to Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qurtubi and Tafsir Kabir): some of the people of Arabia believed that, Allah forbid, Iblis was a *brother* to Allah — Allah being the creator of good and Iblis the creator of evil. Brotherhood *is* kinship, and this reading fits the word exactly. It is this very false belief, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that the ayah refutes: the idea of two powers, a maker of good and a maker of evil, standing in some relation of equality.

Both readings are worth holding, because the same second half of the ayah refutes both.

**"But the jinn know well that they are to be brought forth."** Who is meant by "they"?

- **Ibn Kathir:** "but the jinn know" means *those to whom this is attributed*; and what they know is that those who say such things will be brought forth for punishment on the Day of Reckoning, "because of the lies and falsehood that they uttered without knowledge."
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** allows both possibilities: "they" may be the idolaters who took jinn and shayāṭīn as equals of Allah — the jinn themselves know these people will be brought before Allah to be punished; or "they" may be the jinn themselves. On that second reading the argument is devastating in its simplicity: the shayāṭīn and jinn you have attached to Allah *already know very well* that they face a terrible fate in the Hereafter. Iblis is perfectly aware of his own evil end. Someone who himself believes he must taste his punishment could hardly be the equal of Allah — and to take him to be so, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is certainly a gross lack of good sense.

Notice the logic. It does not appeal to a text the idolaters rejected. It appeals to what the accused parties themselves know. The very beings they promoted to divinity are themselves awaiting a summons.

## Ayat 159–160: the only fitting response is tasbīḥ

**"Glorified is Allah far above what they claim."** Ibn Kathir glosses ayah 159: exalted, sanctified and glorified be He far above having any offspring, and far above what the wrongdoers and heretics attribute to Him.

This is worth pausing on. After all the cross-examination, the Qur'an's final answer to a lie about Allah is not another argument — it is **subḥān Allāh**, a declaration that He is utterly free of what is being pinned on Him. *Tasbīḥ* — glorification — is not vague praise; as Ibn Kathir's wording shows, it is the specific act of declaring Allah exalted and sanctified above every defect attributed to Him. A believer who hears something false said about Allah has this response ready before any debate begins.

**"But not the chosen servants of Allah" (160).** Ibn Kathir explains the grammar: the pronoun in "they attribute" refers to *all of mankind*, and then Allah excludes from that indictment those whom He chooses — whom Ibn Kathir identifies as "the ones who follow the truth revealed to every Prophet who was sent."

So the sweep of ayah 159 is wider than the idolaters being addressed. Humanity at large has said unbefitting things about its Lord; the exception is not a nation or a lineage but a stance — following the truth that the Prophets brought. And note where the initiative lies in the phrase itself: as the sources render it, these are the servants *whom He chooses*. They are not self-made saints; they are people Allah selected.

## Ayat 161–163: your falsehood cannot capture anyone

"Surely you and whatever you worship can never lure anyone away from Him — except those destined to burn in Hell."

Ibn Kathir's reading is direct: the only ones who will believe what you say and follow your misguided ways of false worship are those who are *more* misguided than you and are created for Hell. He brings two parallels from the Qur'an: those who have hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, who are "like cattle, nay even more astray" (7:179) — this, he says, is the parable of people who follow the ideas of shirk, disbelief and misguidance; and "Certainly, you have different ideas. Turned aside therefrom is he who is turned aside" (51:8–9) — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, the one who is misled by it is the one who is turned aside.

Read this way, the ayah is as much a limit set on falsehood as a condemnation of it. It states what the actual reach of this propaganda is: it can only take hold of a heart that has already closed itself off. Falsehood has no independent power to steal a soul that is looking for the truth.

## Ayat 164–166: the angels take the stand

Now comes the most striking turn in the passage. Ibn Kathir introduces it precisely: Allah here declares the angels to be *above* the position attributed to them by those who disbelieved in them and told lies about them — that they are His daughters.

And He does it by letting them speak. Ayah 164 is in the first person plural — "There is not one of *us* without an assigned station." The beings about whom the idolaters had invented so much give their own account of themselves, and it contains three things: a station, a rank, and an occupation. Daughterhood is not among them.

**"A known station" (164).** Ibn Kathir: each one has his own place in the heavens and in the places of worship, which *he does not overstep*. That last clause is the heart of it. An angel's dignity lies in staying exactly where he was assigned.

On the density of that worship, Ibn Kathir cites ad-Dahhak's Tafsir, in which Masruq used to narrate from ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no place in the lower heaven without an angel standing or prostrating in it." Ibn Kathir adds that it was reported that Ibn Masʿūd said, "In the heavens there is one heaven in which there is no space a hand span wide but there is the forehead or the foot of an angel on it," and then recited this ayah; Saʿīd bin Jubayr said something similar. Picture the sky above you as a floor with no unoccupied handspan — every inch of it a place of prostration.

**"We are indeed the ones lined up in ranks" (165).** Ibn Kathir: it means we stand in rows to worship — and he links it straight back to the oath of this very sūrah, *wal-ṣāffāti ṣaffā*, "By those ranged in ranks," noting "as we have already seen in the Ayah." The sūrah swore by them at its opening; near its close they identify themselves as the ones sworn by. The frame of the whole sūrah closes shut.

This is also where the passage reaches down into the mosque. Ibn Kathir reports from Abu Nadrah: when the iqāmah had been given, ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, would turn to face the people and say, "Make your rows straight, for Allah wants you to follow the ways of the angels." Then he would recite *wa innā la-naḥnu al-ṣāffūn*, and say, "Move back, O so-and-so; move forward, O so-and-so." Then he would go forward and say *Allāhu Akbar*. Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir.

And in Sahih Muslim it is narrated from Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We have been favored above mankind in three things: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for us; and its soil is a means of purification for us."

So the straight row in tonight's ṣalāh is not a matter of tidiness. It is this ummah given a share in the angelic form of worship — the very thing the idolaters could never have guessed about the angels while they were busy assigning them a gender and a mother.

**"And we are indeed the ones glorifying His praise" (166).** Ibn Kathir puts the angels' words into full sentences: "we stand in rows and glorify the Lord, praising Him, sanctifying Him and declaring Him to be above any faults or shortcomings. We are servants of Him and in need of Him, humbling ourselves before Him."

Read that against ayah 159. Allah answered the slander by declaring Himself exalted and sanctified above what they attribute to Him — and by Ibn Kathir's gloss, the angels describe their own permanent occupation in exactly those terms: praising Him, sanctifying Him, declaring Him above any fault. They are not junior partners in divinity; they are *ʿibād*, servants, in need of Him and humbling themselves before Him. The idolaters tried to attach the angels to Allah by blood. The angels answer that their only relation to Him is servitude — and that this is their glory.

## What the passage asks of us

**Speak about the unseen only from revelation.** The demand in ayah 157 — bring your Book — sets the standard, and Ibn Kathir spells it out: produce evidence derived from a Book revealed from heaven by Allah, because otherwise what you say is totally irrational. Claims about angels, jinn, the next world and above all about Allah Himself are not open to guesswork. Ibn Kathir reminds us, citing 43:19, that such testimony about the angels "will be recorded, and they will be questioned" — meaning, he says, they will be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection.

**Let *subḥān Allāh* be your reflex.** When something unworthy of Allah is said in your hearing, the passage models the response: declare Him exalted above it — in your heart and on your tongue — before you argue.

**Know your own maqām.** Every angel has a known station he does not overstep, and that is precisely what makes him honourable. A believer's dignity likewise lies in faithfully occupying the place Allah has assigned — in the row, in the family, in the duty of the day — rather than reaching for a rank not given.

**Straighten the row.** ʿUmar's practice, and the hadith in Sahih Muslim, turn ayah 165 into something you do five times a day: standing shoulder to shoulder, straight, deliberately following the ways of creatures whose whole existence is ranked worship and tasbīḥ.

passages.title: They wished for a Reminder, then rejected it
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat expose one of the most uncomfortable habits of the human heart: asking Allah for guidance and then turning away when it arrives. The Quraysh of Makkah used to say, before the Prophet ﷺ came to them, that if only they had a Reminder like the earlier communities had, they would be Allah's devoted servants. Ayah 170 records what actually happened when that Reminder came: **"But now they reject it."** What holds the four ayat together is that single arc — the wish (167–168), the promise attached to it (169), and the broken promise with its consequence (170).

## Where this comes in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the transition plainly: after the preceding ayat have laid out proofs of the basic beliefs of Islam, "these verses now mention the obstinacy of the disbelievers." The shift is from argument to character. The proofs have been given and the idolaters' slander against the angels answered — Ibn Kathir notes that the words of ayat 164–166 place the angels far above the position the disbelievers had invented for them, that they are the daughters of Allah. And now Allah turns to the deeper problem. The issue was never a shortage of evidence. It was a will that had already decided.

## Ayah 167: what they used to say

**وَإِن كَانُوا لَيَقُولُونَ — "They certainly used to say."**

Notice two things in how this is rendered. First, the emphasis: "They *certainly* used to say," "And *indeed* they used to say." Allah is not passing on a rumour about them; He is putting on record, with emphasis, words they really did speak.

Second, this is not one remark on one afternoon. It is what they *used to say* — a settled line of talk, the kind of thing a community repeats often enough that everyone has heard it. That matters for ayah 170, because a claim you make about yourself many times over is judged accordingly.

## Ayah 168: what kind of "Reminder" they wanted

**لَوْ أَنَّ عِندَنَا ذِكْرًا مِّنَ الْأَوَّلِينَ — "If only we had a Reminder like ˹those of˺ earlier peoples."**

*Dhikr* means a "reminder" — and Ibn Kathir shows how concrete the wish was. He explains that they used to wish — before you, O Muhammad, came to them — "that they would have someone to remind them about Allah and what happened in earlier times, and to bring them the Book of Allah." So the wish had three parts: a person to remind them, knowledge of Allah and of what befell the nations before, and a revealed Book of their own.

Notice what the wish quietly admits. "Like earlier peoples," "as had the men of old" — this concedes that other communities had received scripture and that the Arabs had not. Ibn Kathir cites the passage where Allah quotes exactly this complaint: *"Lest you should say: 'The Book was sent down only to two sects before us, and for our part, we were in fact unaware of what they studied'"* (6:156–157). They knew scripture existed elsewhere. They felt the lack. And in their own telling, that lack was the only thing standing between them and true devotion.

## Ayah 169: the promise they made about themselves

**لَكُنَّا عِبَادَ اللَّهِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ — "we would have truly been Allah's devoted servants."**

This is the heart of the passage: not a wish for information but a claim about their own hearts. *Give us what they had, and see what we become.* The renderings before us are "Allah's **devoted** servants" and, in Ibn Kathir's translation, "the **chosen** servants of Allah" — and either way, they were not claiming a modest improvement. They were claiming the highest rank of servanthood, on credit, on the strength of a condition that had not yet been met.

Ibn Kathir sets beside it the ayah in which they went further and swore to it: *"And they swore by Allah their most binding oath that if a warner came to them, they would be more guided than any of the nations (before them); yet when a warner came to them, it increased in them naught but flight (from the truth)"* (35:42). And the parallel he also cites: *"Or lest you should say: 'If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than they'"* (6:156–157). Read together, a pattern emerges that the Qur'an itself records more than once: the loudest self-confidence about what we would do *if* is the least reliable evidence about what we will do *when*.

There is also a quiet contrast running through this passage. Two groups speak in the first person here. In ayat 164–166 the angels say *"there is not one of us but has his known place… and verily, we indeed are those who glorify"* — a servanthood being performed, in rank and in praise, at this very moment. Ibn Kathir explains their words as meaning: we stand in rows and glorify the Lord, praising Him, declaring Him to be above any faults or shortcomings, "servants of Him and in need of Him, humbling ourselves before Him." In ayah 169 the Quraysh also say "we" — but their servanthood exists only inside a sentence that begins with "if only." One "we" is standing in a row; the other is standing on a hypothetical.

And that contrast is not left in the heavens. In Sahih Muslim it is narrated that Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"We have been favored above mankind in three things: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for us; and its soil is a means of purification for us."** Actual devotion has a shape you can stand in.

## Ayah 170: the one word that undoes it all

**فَكَفَرُوا بِهِ — "But ˹now˺ they reject it."**

The turn is in that single word, *now*. The Reminder came — exactly the thing they had asked for — and their response was disbelief. And "it" is not something else: it is the very *dhikr* of ayah 168. They did not reject some substitute for their wish. They rejected the thing itself.

**فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ — "so they will soon know."**

Ibn Kathir calls this "a definite and stern threat because of their disbelief in their Lord and their rejection of His Messenger ﷺ." It is the tone of a warning too grave to itemise. And the passage he cites from Sūrah al-Anʿām spells out the verdict on this posture, along with what follows it: *"So now has come unto you a clear proof from your Lord, and a form of guidance and a mercy. Who then does more wrong than one who rejects the Ayat of Allah and turns away therefrom? We shall requite those who turn away from Our Ayat with an evil torment, because of their turning away"* (6:156–157). The proof arrived; the turning away was theirs.

## Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the end of the passage as consolation as much as warning. These people, it says, used to crave the coming of some prophet from Allah so that they could follow him; but when he did come, "they started confronting him with a posture of obstinacy and hostility." So the Prophet ﷺ is comforted here: he should not worry about the pain these people cause him. The time was coming very soon when he would prevail and his oppressors would be defeated and punished.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this was not deferred entirely to the Hereafter. That it will unfold comprehensively there is already settled; but in this world too, it notes, Allah showed the spectacle that in every campaign from the battle of Badr up to the conquest of Makkah His blessed Messenger came out victorious and his adversaries were disgraced. "They will soon know" was answered, in part, within the lifetime of the man they mocked.

## Living it

**Watch the conditional promise.** The Quraysh's sentence — *if only we had X, we would be Allah's devoted servants* — is a sentence we still say. If only I had more time, a better teacher, Arabic, a quieter house, a different job, I would be a serious worshipper. The passage does not call such a wish a lie. It calls it untested. What settles a person's case is not the wish but what they do on the day the missing thing is handed to them.

**The excuse has already been closed.** The Reminder they asked for exists, in our hands, recited in our homes. Ibn Kathir quotes Allah's answer to every version of this complaint: *"So now has come unto you a clear proof from your Lord, and a form of guidance and a mercy"* (6:156–157). Whatever else we may plead on the Day of Judgement, we cannot plead that no reminder reached us.

**Rejection can be quiet.** Notice how 35:42 describes the outcome when the warner finally came: it "increased in them naught but flight from the truth." Not always an argument — sometimes just movement away, a turning aside, a life arranged so the Reminder never quite gets a hearing.

**And if you are the one being turned away from**, ayah 170 speaks to you as well. The consolation Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds here — that the pain of being rejected is not the end of the matter, and that the outcome is already settled with Allah even when it is not yet visible — was given first to the Prophet ﷺ, and it holds for anyone who carries the truth to people who asked for it and then would not have it.

passages.title: Allah's promise that His messengers prevail
passages.tafsir:
These nine ayat close Sūrah aṣ-Ṣāffāt by drawing one conclusion from everything before them. Ibn Kathir titles the section "The Promise of Victory and the Command to turn away from Idolators," and reads ayah 171 as pointing back over the sūrah: the messengers "would prevail over their people who disbelieved in them and went against them, and how Allah destroyed the disbelievers and saved His believing servants" — a pattern, he says, that Allah "has already stated." What the passage now adds is that this pattern was never a series of accidents. It was the working out of something already settled with Allah.

And because it is settled, the Prophet ﷺ is told what to do in the meantime: step back, be patient, and watch.

What holds the passage together is the movement from a settled promise (171–173) to a practical instruction (174–175), to a word about those who demand the punishment (176–177), and back to the same instruction repeated (178–179). Promise, patience, warning, patience again.

## "Our Word has already gone forth" (171)

Every rendering in front of us puts this in the past tense: "Our Word has already gone forth," "Our Word has gone forth **of old**," and, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's translation, "Our Word has already gone ahead in favor of Our servants — the messengers." Allah's **kalimah**, His Word, was already there ahead of the events.

Ibn Kathir explains it exactly this way: "it has already been stated in the first decree that the Messengers and their followers will ultimately prevail in this world and the Hereafter." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same sense: "it stands predetermined with Allah that His chosen servants, that is, the prophets would be the ones to prevail."

Ibn Kathir sets two other ayat beside this one — "This is like the Ayah":

- **"Allah has decreed: 'Verily, it is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious.' Verily, Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty."** (58:21)
- **"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth."** (40:51)

That second ayah matters for reading 172 correctly. The promise is not for prophets alone. Ibn Kathir says the first decree covers "the Messengers **and their followers**," and 40:51 names "Our Messengers and those who believe" together.

**Ayah 172 — إِنَّهُمْ لَهُمُ الْمَنصُورُونَ.** Notice how the renderings before us all put this as something *done for* them rather than something they pull off: "that they would surely be **helped**," "they verily would be **made** triumphant," and in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's translation, "they are the ones who will have **Allah's support**." The triumph is help given. Ibn Kathir's gloss keeps both worlds in view: "in this world and in the Hereafter, as We have already stated that they would prevail over their people who disbelieved in them and went against them."

**Ayah 173 — وَإِنَّ جُندَنَا لَهُمُ الْغَالِبُونَ.** Here the frame widens from the messengers to **جُندَنَا**, "Our army" — and Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and decisive: they "would ultimately prevail."

## The honest difficulty: but some prophets did not win

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection a thoughtful reader should raise. If it "stands predetermined with Allah that His chosen servants, that is, the prophets would be the ones to prevail," then — "this may raise a difficulty, for in the mortal world, some prophets did not."

The answer given there has two parts.

**First**, in most cases the victory *was* visible: "the majority of prophets consists of the noble souls whose people belied them and met their punishment while they were kept safe from it." That is precisely the pattern Ibn Kathir says has already been narrated — the people destroyed, the prophet delivered.

**Second**, for the few who "could not prevail outwardly and physically right up to the end of their tenure in this world," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says they nonetheless "always enjoyed ascendancy in the field of logic and argument, and the ultimate intellectual victory remained always theirs." The physical traces of that ascendancy were, "due to some consideration of wisdom, such as a trial, or its likes," deferred until the Hereafter.

Then comes the image, attributed there to sage Thanavi, that makes the point land. Picture a highway robber who starts harassing a high appointee of the state while the appointee is on a journey. The officer "would never, by virtue of his Allah-given intellectual sobriety, stoop to the low-down robber," until he reaches the capital of his state, "where the robber will be seized and punished." During those hours on the road the robber has the upper hand — but "simply due to this temporary ascendancy, neither can we call that robber an authority, nor that authority a subject. In fact, given the true state of affairs, that robber — despite this temporary ascendancy — is still a subject, while that man of authority — despite his temporary lack of ascendancy — is still the authority he had been all along."

That is the theology of this passage in one picture. Apparent power is not the same thing as actual standing, and a delay in enforcement is not a reversal of the verdict.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) "has expressed this more briefly and lucidly": **those who are not helped to ascend in the present world are helped to ascend in the Hereafter** — cited there from Bayān ul-Qurʼān, the Tafsīr of Sūrah al-Māʼidah.

## "Our army" is a description you have to earn (173)

The most searching comment in the sources is about the word *jundanā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns that "no group of people achieves this supremacy or ascendancy, whether in the present world or in the Hereafter, simply by having particular racial traits, or by belonging to a religion only in name."

The promise is attached to a *description*, and the description is **enlistment**. It "actually happens only when every human being makes himself a member of 'the army of Allah'," which "necessarily implies that he or she should be committed to the obedience of Allah in every department of life as the objective of his or her life." The words *Our army*, it says, are "telling us very clearly that the person who embraces Islam will have to enter into a solemn pledge to devote his or her entire life in waging a struggle against the forces of self and Satan — and his or her supremacy, whether material or moral, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, depends on this condition."

So the ayah is at once the most comforting and the most demanding in the passage. Allah's forces cannot lose. The only real question is whether you are in them.

## "So turn away from them for a while" (174–175)

**فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّىٰ حِينٍ.** The instruction comes directly after the promise, and Ibn Kathir unpacks it as: "bear their annoyance with patience and wait until an appointed time, when We shall cause you to prevail and will grant you victory."

So "turning away" here is not indifference and not abandoning the message; it is bearing what they do without being dragged into it. And **حَتَّىٰ حِينٍ** — "for a while," "until an appointed time" — is left unnamed. The promise is certain; the date is not given. Patience is asked for exactly in that gap.

**وَأَبْصِرْهُمْ فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ (175).** The command is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir: "watch them and see what will happen to them by way of punishment for their opposition towards you and their disbelief in you." Then the same seeing is turned back on them — **فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ**, "and they shall see" — which Ibn Kathir notes Allah says "as a threat and a warning." He is to watch what befalls them; what they will see is what befalls themselves.

## "Do they seek to hasten Our punishment?" (176)

**أَفَبِعَذَابِنَا يَسْتَعْجِلُونَ.** Ibn Kathir explains: "they seek to hasten on the punishment because they disbelieve in you, and Allah is angry with them because of that and will make them suffer the consequences, and because of their disbelief and stubbornness, He will hasten on the punishment."

There is a terrible symmetry in that. Their demand for speed comes out of disbelief and stubbornness — and it is answered, but as a consequence of that disbelief, not as a favour to their curiosity.

## The morning that is spoken of (177)

**فَإِذَا نَزَلَ بِسَاحَتِهِمْ فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنذَرِينَ** — "Then, when it descends in their courtyard, evil will be the morning for those who had been warned."

Two words in the ayah carry the verse.

**سَاحَة (*sāḥah*)**: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word "literally means a courtyard," and that the expression *nazala bi-sāḥatihi*, "descended in his courtyard," "is an Arabic idiom that denotes the appearance of a calamity **face to face**" — not rumoured on the horizon, but standing in your own yard. As-Suddī, quoted by Ibn Kathir, glosses "when it descends in their courtyard" as meaning **in their homes**. Ibn Kathir's own summary: "when the punishment comes down to the place where they are, terrible will be the day of their punishment and destruction."

**صَبَاح (*ṣabāḥ*)**, the morning, is specified rather than any other hour. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "the time of morning has been specified, as an attack would usually come at that hour among the people of Arabia." It adds, on the authority of Mazharī, that this was also the practice of the Prophet ﷺ: "should he reach the territorial jurisdiction of some enemy at the time of night, he used to postpone his attack until the morning."

So the dread in the ayah is not abstract. It is the dread of the hour at which, in that world, an army arrived.

## From the Sunnah: the morning of Khaybar

Ibn Kathir reports that it was recorded **in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs** that Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "On the morning of Khaybar, when the people came out with their tools (to go about their daily work) and saw the (Muslim) army, they went back and said, 'Muhammad by Allah! Muhammad and the army!'" The Prophet ﷺ said:

> **Allāhu Akbar! Khaybar has been destroyed. Then, when it descends in the courtyard of any people, evil will be the morning for those who had been warned!**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same words, saying that "according to Hadith narrations, when the Holy Prophet ﷺ attacked the fort of Khaibar during the morning hours, he said: *Allahu Akbar, Khaibar is destroyed. Verily, when we descend on the courtyard of a people, the morning of those who had been already warned is too bad.*"

Ibn Kathir brings this report here because the Prophet ﷺ himself spoke the ayah's words at that hour — the courtyard, the dawn, the people who had already been warned, coming out with their tools to an ordinary working day.

## "So turn away from them for a while, and watch" (178–179)

The command returns almost word for word. Ibn Kathir simply says: "This is a reiteration of the command stated above. And Allah knows best."

One small difference in the wording is worth noticing. In 175 it is **وَأَبْصِرْهُمْ** — "watch *them*"; in 179 it is **وَأَبْصِرْ** — "watch," with no object named. In both ayat the closing words are the same and are about them, not him: **فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ**, "and they shall see."

Repetition here is not filler. It is how the sūrah leaves the Prophet ﷺ — and every reader after him — holding the same posture on the last line as on the first.

## Living it

- **Read your own hardship through ayah 171.** Ibn Kathir calls it "the first decree": the outcome was stated before the opposition ever began.
- **Take "turn away" as a discipline, not a mood.** It means, in Ibn Kathir's words, to "bear their annoyance with patience and wait" — while continuing to carry the message.
- **Do not read delay as defeat.** Thanavi's traveller does not stop being the man of authority because a robber holds the road for a stretch of the journey.
- **Audit your enlistment.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt that no one inherits this victory by racial traits or "by belonging to a religion only in name"; the promise attaches to those who make obedience to Allah the objective of life "in every department," in the daily struggle against self and Satan.
- **Never demand that a warning be proved.** Ayah 176 shows people trying to hasten the punishment out of disbelief and stubbornness. Ayah 177 shows it standing in the courtyard at dawn.

passages.title: Closing glorification, peace, and praise
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the closing seal of Sūrah aṣ-Ṣāffāt: Allah declares Himself utterly beyond the false descriptions the idolaters had been throwing at Him, sends peace upon the messengers who spoke about Him truthfully, and closes with praise belonging to the Lord of all the worlds. What holds them together is that they are one movement of speech — a purification, a greeting, and a praise. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, Allah has compressed all the subjects of this sūrah into these three verses.

## A whole sūrah folded into three lines

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens its comment on this passage with a striking admission: it would take volumes to explain this beautiful finale properly. It then traces how each line of the finale reaches back into the body of the sūrah:

- The sūrah began with a description of *tawḥīd* — the Oneness of Allah — and the essence of that argument was that Allah is free of everything the *mushriks* (those who associate partners with Allah) attribute to Him. So the first of these closing lines serves as an indicator pointing back to that whole detailed discussion.
- The sūrah then recounted events relating to the noble prophets, and the second line is a hint back over all of that.
- After that, the beliefs, doubts, and objections of the disbelievers were refuted very openly and explicitly — both in terms of report and in terms of reason — and alongside that came the declaration that supremacy will ultimately be the lot of the people of truth. Whoever listens to those statements with good sense and insight, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is bound to end up praising Allah. And so it is on exactly that note of praise that the sūrah is concluded.

Read this way, the passage is not a polite sign-off appended to the end. It is the sūrah's own conclusion, drawn in the reader's presence. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes what these three ayat state between them: the basic beliefs of Islam — *tawḥīd*, the Oneness of Allah, and *risālah*, prophethood — are mentioned clearly, while mention of the Hereafter comes up as a corollary. Confirming these was the real purpose of the sūrah.

## What the glorification is doing

*Subḥāna rabbika* — "Glorified is your Lord." Ibn Kathir's opening line is worth sitting with: **Allah glorified Himself here**, and stated that He is far above what the lying wrongdoers say about Him; glorified and sanctified and exalted be He far above what they say.

*Tasbīḥ* — the act of glorifying Allah, saying *subḥān Allah* — is not merely praise. As Ibn Kathir explains, tasbīḥ **implies a declaration of being free from all shortcomings**. It is a clearing away, a denial: whatever deficiency has been imagined about Allah, He is above it and clear of it. That is why the word arrives at exactly this point, immediately after the false attributions have been recounted.

**Rabb al-ʿIzzah.** Ibn Kathir explains this phrase as **the Owner of might and power Whom none can resist**; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "Lord of great might and honor." Both senses sit in the two renderings together — unassailable strength, and the honour that belongs to such strength. To call Allah the Lord and Owner of ʿizzah is to say that might is not something He borrows or shares: it is His to own, and, in Ibn Kathir's words, none can resist it.

**"Above what they attribute to Him."** *ʿAmmā yaṣifūn* — Ibn Kathir glosses it as: **from what these lying fabricators say**. The verb is about *describing*, giving Allah qualities. This is what the sūrah has been exposing throughout: descriptions that make Allah less than He is. The ayah does not argue with those descriptions one by one at this point. It simply lifts Allah clear of the whole category.

## Two ways of speaking about Allah

Now hold the first two lines of the passage side by side, because the second explains the first.

*Wa salāmun ʿalā al-mursalīn* — "And peace be upon the messengers." Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as: **may the peace of Allah be upon them in this world and in the Hereafter** — not a wish confined to their earthly lives, but peace extended over both realms. And then he gives the reason, which is the hinge of the whole passage: **because what they say about their Lord is sound, correct and true.**

So two groups have spoken about Allah. One group described Him falsely — and in Ibn Kathir's words they are the lying fabricators, the ones He is far above. The other group described Him truthfully — and the response to them is *salām*, peace, in this world and the next. The dividing line between them, the thing Ibn Kathir names as the reason for the greeting, is **speaking soundly and truly about Allah**. That is a sobering standard. What we say about our Lord is not a minor matter of vocabulary; on Ibn Kathir's reading it is the very ground on which these two lines separate people.

The sūrah recounted the prophets' stories one after another. Here they are gathered into a single greeting.

## The Prophet ﷺ inside that greeting

Ibn Kathir relates that Saʿīd bin Abī ʿArūbah narrated that Qatādah said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **'When you send Salām on me, send Salām on all the Messengers, for I am one of the Messengers.'**"

Ibn Kathir notes that this **was recorded by Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim**.

This is a beautiful piece of instruction, and it flows straight out of the ayah. The Prophet ﷺ places himself inside the very word the ayah uses — *al-mursalīn*, the ones sent — rather than outside it. He is not asking to be greeted separately, above the line; he asks that the greeting sweep in all the messengers, because, as he himself says, he is one of them. The humility of it is part of the teaching. And practically, it means that when a believer says *wa salāmun ʿalā al-mursalīn*, he has sent peace upon Muḥammad ﷺ along with all of his brothers among the messengers.

## Why the glorification and the praise travel together

*Wa al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn* — "And praise be to Allah, Lord of all the worlds."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and expansive at once: **praise be to Him at the beginning and end of all things.** Praise is not just the closing formality after a matter is finished; it frames a matter at both ends.

Ibn Kathir then explains why the two ideas of this passage keep appearing side by side: **because tasbīḥ implies a declaration of being free from all shortcomings**, glorification and praise appear together here and in many places in the Qur'an. The logic is worth making explicit, and it binds the first line of the passage to the last. Glorification clears away everything unworthy of Allah — the negative half. Praise affirms what is truly and worthily His — the positive half. Deny the falsehood, affirm the perfection: that is why the two words travel together in the Qur'an, and it is exactly the shape of these three ayat, with peace upon the truthful messengers standing between them.

## Carrying the passage into life

Because these three lines summarise right belief and right speech about Allah so completely, the sources record them being used precisely as a closing.

**After the prayer.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites ʿAllāmah al-Qurṭubī, who on his own authority reports this saying of Sayyidnā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him): "I have heard it many times from the Holy Prophet ﷺ that he, after the Ṣalāh was over, used to recite these verses." So the closing of the sūrah became a closing for the prayer — a small habit worth reviving, and easy to carry: three short ayat, already memorised by anyone who reads this sūrah.

**At the end of any gathering.** Ibn Kathir records that Abū Muḥammad al-Baghawī noted in his Tafsīr that ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: *"Whoever wants a greater measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let him say at the end of any gathering:*

> **Subḥāna rabbika rabb al-ʿizzati ʿammā yaṣifūn — wa salāmun ʿalā al-mursalīn — wa al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same saying of Sayyidnā ʿAlī with reference to Imām al-Baghawī — "Whoever wishes to have the best of return filled to the brim on the Day of Judgment should recite this at the end of every sitting attended" — and adds, citing Tafsīr Ibn Kathir, that Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported this very saying from a narration of Shaʿbī that ascends to the Holy Prophet ﷺ.

**On the general principle.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what the passage teaches by example: it is naturally expected of a true Muslim that he or she would conclude **every article, every address, and every sitting** by admitting and stating the greatness of Allah and by saying words of praise for Him. The end of a sūrah teaches you how to end a piece of writing, a talk, a meeting, a conversation.

**A related but distinct formula.** Ibn Kathir mentions that other hadiths, concerning the expiation for any wrongs that may have occurred during a gathering, prescribe words that glorify and praise Allah, affirm that there is no deity except Him, and seek His forgiveness while turning to Him in repentance. He notes that he has written a chapter dealing exclusively with that topic. It is worth keeping the two clear: our three ayat are recorded as a closing of exalted praise, while that supplication is specifically framed around expiating whatever may have slipped into the sitting.

## Holding the passage together

If you want one sentence for these three ayat, it is this: *say nothing false about Allah, honour those who said true things about Him, and give Him the praise.*

That is why the sūrah — which spent so long on what the idolaters attribute to Allah, the accounts of the noble prophets, and the ultimate supremacy of the people of truth — ends here rather than with a warning. Someone who has actually listened to all of that with good sense and insight, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is bound to arrive at praise. The passage does not so much command us to praise as show us where honest thought lands. Purify the thought of Allah, send peace on the ones who carried the truth, and praise the Lord of all that exists.

*And Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, knows best.*
